M Amirul Islam with Shirin Sharmin Choudhury, Tania Amir, Monzil Murshid, Advocates ----- For the Petitioner. 
Mizanur Rahman, Deputy Attorney-General with Zaman Akter; Assistant Attorney-General ----- For the State.
parties:
Kalandiar Kabir  ----- Petitioners
Vs.
Bangladesh and others ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
Md Hamidul Haque J: This Rule was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the detenu Shahriar Kabir now detained in Dhaka Central Jail should not be brought before this Court so that it may satisfy itself that he is not being held in custody illegally and without any lawful authority.

<u>2. Mr M Amirul Islam appeared on behalf of the petitioner, he has challenged the validity of the order of detention on several grounds which we like to discuss one by one. First argument of Mr M Amirul Islam is that the detenu was arrested under section 54 of the Code of Criminal Procedure but there was no reason to arrest the detenu under that section of the Code of Criminal Procedure. In this connection, he has taken us through the provisions of section 54 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and has argued that under nine circumstances as mentioned in the above section, a police officer may arrest a person without a warrant and without any order from a Magistrate. We cannot accept the argument of Mr Islam. It is true that under nine circumstances a person may be arrested under section 54 of Code of Criminal Procedure by police without any warrant. Seven circumstances are not applicable but we have found that the provisions of this section shall also apply when a police officer receives any credible information that a person may be concerned in any cognizable offence or receives any credible information or has a reasonable suspicion that a man might have committed an act in any place out of Bangladesh which if committed in Bangladesh would have been punishable as an offence. So we are of the view that arrest of the detenu under section 54 of the Code of Criminal Procedure was not illegal in view of the above power given to the police officer under section 54 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.</u>

3. Mr Islam has argued that a detention order cannot be passed with a view to prevent the activities of the detenu which may endanger public safety and public order. In this connection, he referred to some cases including the case of Mostafizur Rahman vs Bangladesh as reported in 51 DLR (AD) 1. It is true that in this case the Appellate Division and in some other cases the High Court Division held the view that the Government has no authority to detain a person for maintaining the public safety and public order. Mr Islam referred to the grounds for detention Annexure J of supplementary affidavit and has pointed out that in the last part it is mentioned that in consideration of the overall law and order situation in the country the authority was satisfied that the detenu should be detained under section 3(2) of the Special Powers Act. 1974. It appears to us that Mr Islam only considered the first portion of that paragraph but not the paragraph as a whole. To consider this question the same paragraph is quoted below:

“উপরোক্ত অনুচ্ছেদে বর্ণিত অবস্থা এবং দেশের আইন শৃঙ্খলা পরিস্থিতির সামগ্রিক বিবেচনায় নিম্নস্বাক্ষরকারীর নিকট সন্তোষজনক ভাবে প্রতীয়মান হইয়াছে যে, আইনশৃঙ্খলা  বিঘ্নিতকরণ জনিত ক্ষতিকর কার্যকলাপ হইতে আপনাকে বিরত রাখার নিমিত্তে ১৯৭৪ সালের বিশেষ ক্ষমতা আইনের ৩ (২) ধারার বিধান অনুসারে জনস্বার্থে অন্তরীন রাখা প্রয়োজন”

4. On perusal of the above paragraph we find that in addition to reference of overall law and order situation, it is also mentioned that in order to prevent the detenu from endangering the law and order situation by his prejudicial activities, the detention was necessary. From the use of the under lined expression, we are of the view that the order of detention cannot be said to be invalid on the ground as argued by M Islam.

5. Mr Islam also argued that the materials recovered and seized at the time of his arrest may come within the omitted clause (g) of section 2 of the Special Powers Act, 1974 but after omission of that clause (g), possession of those materials cannot be considered as prejudicial act within meaning-of section 2(f) of the Special Powers Act, 1974.

<u>6. It is true that clause (g) of section 2 of the Special Powers Act was omitted by Act 18 of 1991. The purpose was probably to ensure freedom of expression as embodied in our Constitution. However, on perusal of section 2 (f) which explains the meaning of 'prejudicial act' we find that such act is an act which is intended or likely to prejudice the sovereignty or defence of Bangladesh; prejudice the maintenance of friendly relationship with foreign states; prejudice the security of Bangladesh or endanger public safety or the maintenance of public order; create or excite feelings of enmity or hatred between different communities or classes of people; interfere with or encourage or incite interference with the administration of law or maintenance of law and order, etc. In this case, we find from the ground for detention that on the recovery of some cassettes the authority decided to detain him under section 3(2) of the Special Powers Act with a view to prevent him from doing any prejudicial act within meaning of section 2(f). The possession of the materials created a suspicion in the mind of the authority that detenu might engage in any activities as referred to above. So, according to us, in spite of omission of clause (g), the authority had the scope to detain the detenu, on the ground as mentioned in Annexure J. At that stage, obviously, no proof of future participation was necessary. This aspect was taken into consideration in the case of Salim Hasan vs Bangladesh (45 DLR 318) and following is the observation of the court:</u>

<u>" .......a preventive detention is to prevent a person on a mere suspicion that some crime had been done and the same would be repeated and is not a question of proving an allegation by evidence which must be done when a proceeding is drawn under the Penal Code"</u>

7. Mr Islam has also argued that the detention was malafide and, as such, the grounds of detention were not supplied to the detenu and the learned Advocate had to make a prayer before the court for allowing them to procure copy of the grounds and to give them an opportunity to meet the detenu for consultation. There is some substance in this argument of Mr Islam.

8. This matter came up for hearing on 12-12-2001. The order of detention was passed on 25-11-2000. The provision for furnishing the ground is contained in section 8 of the Special Powers Act 1974. The purpose of furnishing the grounds to the detenu is to afford him an opportunity to submit a representation against order of his detention. At the time of hearing on 12-12-2000 the learned Deputy Attorney-General submitted that the grounds were supplied to the detenu but the learned Advocate for the petitioner submitted that he had no information that the grounds were actually supplied. After hearing the parties, the court then passed an order directing the authority to allow two lawyers of the detenu to meet the detenu and to allow the detenu to consult his lawyers. Mr Islam has referred to paragraph 7(1) of the supplementary affidavit and has submitted that the grounds were only shown to the detenu and was allowed to read the same but it was taken back and kept in the office.

<u>9. Now, from Annexure A, we find that it was supplied to the detenu on 8-12-2001. We cannot approve of the action of the authority. This court had to interfere by passing an order to give an opportunity to the lawyers to meet the detenu to get instruction from him and to procure the copy of the grounds supplied to the detenu. However, as the learned Advocates were ultimately allowed to meet the detenu in compliance with the order of the court, we think that the detenu ultimately got the opportunity to file a representation against the order of his detention but this subsequent conduct of the authority cannot be considered to hold that the initial order of detention was malafide.</u>

10. Lastly, the most important argument of Mr Islam is that after detaining the detenu under section 3(2) of the Special Powers Act, a specific criminal case has been started over the self-same facts and, as such, he has argued that there cannot be two parallel proceedings against the same person. In support of his views Mr Islam referred to some decisions of this court and also a decision of the Supreme Court of India. The first case which was cited by Islam is the case of Shahidul Haque vs Government of East Pakistan reported in 20 DLR 1005. Next, he cited the case of Mrs Tahera Islam vs Secretary, Ministry of Home, Bangladesh reported in 1988 BLD 262 = 40 DLR 193. The Indian case cited by him is the case of Biram Chand vs State of Uttar Pradesh reported in 1974 AIR (SC) 1161. We will discuss the question as to whether there can be two parallel proceedings against the same person later on after taking into consideration the submissions of the learned Deputy Attorney-General and Assistant Attorney- General.

11. Mr Islam has also argued that after starting a regular case against the detenu on the self-same facts, there was no scope of extending the detention and this extension shows that it was done without application of mind.

12. Mr Mizanur Rahman, the learned Deputy Attorney-General with Mr Zaman Akter the learned Assistant Attorney-General has submitted that the activities of the detenu comes within definition of "prejudicial act" because the detenu was acting against the sovereignty and security of Bangladesh. They have also submitted that there was nothing malafide in the order passed by the Government. It is also argued that there may be a valid detention order in spite of pendency of a case and in this connection they referred to the cases of Habiba Mahmud vs Bangladesh reported in 45 DLR (AD) 89, the case of Nasima Begum vs Bangladesh reported in 49 DLR (AD) 102, the case of Nasima Begum vs Home Ministry reported in 1983 BLD 140.

<u>13. The question whether parallel proceedings may be continued or not came up for decision in so many cases before the Indian Supreme Court. In the case of Biram Chand vs State of Uttar Pradesh, a Division Bench of Supreme Court of India held that the if the authority concerned makes an order of detention under the Act and also prosecutes him in a criminal case on the self-same facts that would be totally barred. The following is the observation of the Court: "The detaining authority cannot take recourse to two parallel and simultaneous proceedings nor can take recourse to a ground which is the subject matter of criminal trial" There is another case reported in the same volume of AIR 1974 at 2154. This is the case of H Saha vs State of West Bengal. In this case the Bench was constituted with five Judges including the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court of India. In this case, the Court has observed that the preventive detention and prosecution are not synonymous. The purposes are different, the power of preventive detention is precautionary power exercised in reasonable anticipation and this mayor may not relate to an offence and it is not a parallel proceeding. The court further observed the order of preventive detention could be made with or without prosecution and in anticipation or after discharge or even acquittal. Similar view was taken by our Appellate Division in the case of Habiba Mahmud vs Bangladesh (45 DLR AD 89). The following observation was made in that case: "Even after his acquittal in a criminal case a person may be detained under the Act. In that case, the detaining authority will have to satisfy the court that the necessity for a preventive measure survives and that the acquittal was on technical ground or on benefit of doubt." In this case, it is also held that where the allegations against the detenu are of serious nature, the detaining authority may consider those allegations and despite pendency of a criminal case, can make an order of detention. In the case of Nasima Begum vs Bangladesh as reported in 49 DLR (AD) 102, the Appellate Division also made almost similar observation. It has been observed that if the criminal cases are taken to be just illustrative of the detenu's background, the other statements in the grounds of detention are nothing but general statements as to the character of the detenu. Considered with the background thus given, the allegation of character will stick. So we have found that criminal case or pendency of criminal cases are not considered to be valid grounds for detention but if these are mentioned as background of the detenu in that case reference of such cases will not make a detention order invalid.</u>

14. We like to mention here that in the above cases which we have discussed the question of reference of pending cases came up for decision. In the instant case before us, in the grounds of detention there is no reference of any pending case. The case against the present detenu was started on 8-12-2001 with the filing of a first information report by a police inspector and officer in charge of Airport police station. Mr Islam has argued that as after passing the order of detention under section 3(2) of the Special Powers Act over the self-same facts, a regular criminal case has been started with specific allegations under some sections of the Penal Code, the detention cannot be continued and this, according to him, will amount to two parallel prosecutions. Exactly on this question, there are three decisions of this court reported in 20 DLR, 40 DLR and 45 DLR Mr lslam has argued that these decisions are consistent on the point and in these decisions this court took the view that when a specific case is started in respect of the self-same facts, the same activities of a person should not be taken as grounds for making an order of detention against him.

15. We have perused the first decision of this court in the case of Shahidul Hoque vs the Government of East Pakistan as reported in 20 DLR 1005. Of course, this case relates to an order of detention passed under Rule 32(1)(b) of the Defence of Pakistan Rules. In the detention order there was a reference of a meeting held on 13-7-1967 in which the detenu delivered a speech with a view to excite the workers of a Spinning Mill. In respect of the same incident, a specific case was started by the manager of the mill by lodging a First Information Report. Under such circumstances, a Division Bench of the High Court of East Pakistan made the following observation: "When a specific case has been started in relation to the alleged activities of the detenu on a certain date, the same activities should not, in fairness, be taken as a reasonable basis for making an order of detention". This view was followed in the case of Mrs Tahera Islam vs Secretary, Government of Bangladesh reported in 1988 BLD 262 and also in 40 DLR 193.

16. We have also perused the case of Salim Hassan vs Bangladesh as reported in 45 DLR 318. In this case similar question came up for decision. In a long judgment, the court took into consideration many earlier decisions of this Court and also of the Indian Supreme Court. After taking into consideration the decision of our Court and Indian Court, the Court made the following observation:

"Having considered those decisions and after considering the submissions of the learned Advocates of both the parties our view would be that in a detention matter the activities complained of may also provide for a criminal offence and punishable under the law and for that only there would exist no law for the same matter to be considered sufficient for a detention under the Special Powers Act when there are other specific independent grounds for detention, but where a criminal proceedings is essentially on the same subject matter and no other matter than the criminal proceeding, then the proceeding under the normal law of the land would be allowed to be continued and the specific case would negative the necessity of any detention order except it could be shown on evidence or from records that proceeding would come to a fiasco because there is no possibility of any evidence to be produced in court in spite of attempts made by the prosecution for him to be punished eventually and there is a possibility of his immediately repeating the same activity in similar manner. A criminal proceeding thus would not bar a detention order but there are some limitations and we have spelt out those as aforesaid. It therefore depends on the facts and circumstances of each and there is no absolute formula which is to be followed.

17. In the above case, the grounds for detention were the verbatim copy of that was stated in the complaint petition. Considering all the decisions and the facts and circumstances of the above case, the Court finally found that the continuation of the detention order was bad in law and the detenu was kept in detention in an illegal manner.

18. The other case of this Court which we like to refer is the case of Golam Kabir vs Government of Bangladesh as reported in 27 DLR 199. In this case also, in addition to the order of detention passed by the Government under section 3(2) of the Special Powers Act, two First Information Reports were also lodged against the detenu under certain provisions of the same Act. The Court has observed that the Special Powers Act has combined both punitive and preventive measures. It is also observed that there is no bar to prosecute a person who is alleged to have committed any of the offences defined or mentioned in the Act, if he is also preventively detained.

19. In the above, we have referred to the cases on the point decided earlier by this Court and also by the Indian Supreme Court. In the case reported in 45 DLR 318 this court considered many decisions of different Courts of the sub-continent on this point. It appears to us that the decision taken in cases reported in 20 DLR, 40 DLR and also in 45 DLR is consistent. In the last decision, this Court observed that where a criminal proceeding is initiated on the same subject matter, then the proceeding under the normal law would be allowed to continue and such specific case would negative the necessity of any detention order except it could be shown on evidence or from records that the proceeding would come to fiasco because there is no possibility of any evidence to be produced in Court in spite of attempts made by the prosecution and there is possibility of his immediately repeating the same activities in a similar manner. We have quoted the relevant observation of the court in this judgment earlier; the above observation was made in line with the decision given by the Supreme Court of India in the case of Borjahan vs the State of West Bengal reported in 1972 AIR (SC) 2256. The relevant portion of the judgment delivered in that case was also quoted in the judgment reported in 45 DLR 318.

20. We have also given our anxious thought to the question raised and have considered the decision of the different Courts including this Court. We are of the view that we may follow the view taken by this Court in the cases reported in 20 DLR, 40 DLR and 45 DLR. The position was considered very carefully in the last case and the observations given in that case appears to us to be most appropriate. Though passing of an order of detention after a criminal case is instituted on the self-same facts and allegation is not barred by specific provision of Special Powers Act or by any other law but in view of earlier judicial pronouncements we accept the view that when a specific case has been started in relation to the self-same facts, the same activity should not, "in fairness" be considered as a ground for detention. Of course, there is slight difference between the facts of those cases with the facts of the present case before us. In the reported cases criminal case was either started immediately before passing of the order of detention or on the date of detention on the self-same facts. In the instant case, the criminal case was started after 13 days from the date of passing of the order of detention and, as such, there is no reference of any case in the grounds of detention itself.

<u>21. On perusal of the grounds in Annexure J and the certified copy of the First Information Report which was produced before us at the time of hearing, we find that the case was started on the self-same allegations or facts as mentioned in the grounds for detention (Annexure J). The learned Deputy Attorney-General have pointed out that the occurrence took place outside the territory of Bangladesh and it may be difficult to prove the allegations in the criminal case against the present detenu and for that reason continuation of detention is necessary. We cannot accept this view. Time has not yet come to decide whether evidence will come or not but we have found that the criminal case has been started on the self-same fads and allegations as mentioned in the grounds for detention. The law will take its own course in respect of the criminal case but we are of the view that the starting of the specific case negatived the necessity of continuation of detention. So, according to us, though initially the authority had the scope of and reason for passing the order of detention when the detenu was found in possession of the materials as mentioned in the grounds of detention, but after starting of the specific case, continuation of detention will be bad in law and illegal.</u>

22. Before we part with, we like to make some observation on the allegation made by Mr Islam about the ill treatment meted out to the detenu. Mr Islam after referring to paragraph 7(d) and 17(c) of the supplementary affidavit, submits that the detenu is not a convict or a prisoner and, as such, there is no scope of treating him in inhuman manner. The respondents did not file any affidavit-in-opposition denying the above statement made in supplementary affidavit. However, we are not actually required to decide in this Rule what treatment was actually meted out to the detenu but we are concerned about the legal right which a detenu is supposed to enjoy. A detenu has neither been found guilty by any Court of law for commission of any offence nor he is standing trial for any alleged offence but he is detained only to prevent him from doing any prejudicial act in future.

23. In the Jail Code, detail procedure has been laid down as to what treatment should be meted out to convicts and under trial prisoners. Under that Code on commission of any offence in jail itself or on violation of any rules, there are provisions of punishment of a convict or under trial prisoner. There is no scope of torturing even a convict or under trial prisoner. In the jail there is no separate provision for a detenu and no rule as to how he is to be treated. The Jail Code was prepared during British time. At that time there were state prisoners. Unfortunately, though several decades passed, no initiative was taken by any Government during this long period to make the Jail Code up to date. Though the Governments are found to be over zealous about preventive detention, but no steps were taken to determine how a detenu should be treated. Even if the old rules of the Jail Code are applied which is contained in chapter 32 of the Jail Code, a detenu should receive much better treatment.

24. Mr Amirul Islam referred to 3(three) decisions of the Indian Supreme Court where the Supreme Court made some specific observation as to the right of prisoners. The cases referred to are the case of Francis Coralie vs Union Territory of Delhi reported in AIR 1981 746, the case of Sunil Batra (II) vs Delhi Administration 1980 (SC) 1579, the case of the Sunil Batra vs Delhi Administration reported in 1980 Supreme Court Cases 488.

25. Very important decision has been given in the two cases of Sunil Batra by the Supreme Court regarding jail reforms and treatment towards the prisoners including the convicts and under trial prisoners. The Court in its long judgment after making special reference to Articles 19 and 21 of the Indian Constitution made recommendation for immediate reforms with some specific suggestions.

26. In the case of Francis Coralie vs Union Territory of Delhi, the question of right of a detenu detained under section 5 of the Conservation of Foreign Exchange, and Prevention of Smuggling Activities Act came up for decision. Some restrictions were imposed in the above Act about the interview of the detenu with the legal adviser and members of the family. In this case, the Court also decided the question whether a person preventively detained has any rights.

27. In the above cases, the Court decided what is meant by "right to life". In the Francis Coralie case, the Court (Bhagawati, J) observed as follows:

"We think that right to life includes the right to live with human dignity and all that goes along with it, namely, the bare necessaries of life such as adequate nutrition, clothing and shelter over the head and the facilities for reading, writing and expressing oneself in diverse forms. Every act which offends against or impairs human dignity would constitute deprivations pro tanto of this right to life any form of torture or cruel or inhuman or degrading treatment would be offensive to human dignity and constitute an inroad to his right to live and it would, on this view, be prohibited by Article 21 unless it is in accordance with procedure prescribed by law, but no law which authorises and no procedure which leads to such torture or cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment can ever stand the test of reasonableness and non-arbitrariness; it would be plainly unconstitutional and void as being violative of Articles 14 and 21"

<u>28. Article 14 of the Indian Constitution provides equality before law and equal protection of law. Article 21 provides that no person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to the procedure established by law. Article 30 of our Constitution is similar to Article 21 of the Indian Constitution and Article 27 is similar to Article 14 of the Indian Constitution. So, we think that the above observations of the Indian Supreme Court apply in our context if we consider those with reference to Articles 27 and 30 of our Constitution. However, we could not find any decision of our courts on the point of treatment of the prisoners with reference of these two Articles. So, we like to remind the authority that the treatment towards the prisoners should be human and in accordance with the rules because a prisoner remains a human being and is entitled to be treated as such. This is more important while treating a detenu. A detenu is neither a convict found to be guilty of an offence by a competent court nor an under trial prisoner who stands trial for commission of an offence under any existing penal law. Under the existing rules of the Jail Code, a state prisoner is to receive treatment like civil prisoner. But this does not sufficiently cover the status of a detenu. So, we like to suggest that the Government should frame rules regarding the detenu keeping in mind that he still retains some right under Articles 27 and 30 of the Constitution in spite of his detention.</u>

<u>29. Lastly, as we have mentioned earlier, we cannot approve the action of the authority about the manner in which copy of the ground was supplied to the detenu and the difficulty he had to face in having consultation with his lawyer and meeting members of his family. The right to consult a lawyer is given under clause (1) of Article 33 but clause (3)(b) provides that provision of clause (1) shall not apply if a person is detained for preventive detention. However, clause (5) of this Article provides that grounds should be communicated as soon as may be and the detenu shall be afforded an opportunity of making a representation against the order. This provision of affording an opportunity to submit representation would be meaningless unless a detenu gets an opportunity to consult a lawyer. As regard the opportunity of meeting the members of the family, we like to emphasise that such opportunity should be given denial of which will amount to denial of his rights which he should enjoy in spite of preventive detention. In this connection, we may again refer to the decision of the Indian Supreme Court as made in the case of Francis Coralie in which the Supreme Court had to issue instruction upon the authority to allow the members of the family of the detenu to meet him twice in a week.</u>

<u>30. In view of our discussion, the present Rule is liable to be made absolute. We have found that there was valid ground for passing the initial order of detention but at the same time we have found that there is no valid ground for continuation of the detention after starting of the case on the self-same facts and allegation with reference to which the order of detention was passed.</u>

<u>In the result, the Rule is made absolute. It is declared that the detenu Shahriar Kabir, son of late Mr Siddiqullah of Ga-16 Mahakhali, PS Gulshan, District Dhaka now detained in Central Jail, Dhaka is being held in custody without any lawful authority and he be set at liberty forthwith if not wanted in any other case.</u>

End.

lawyer:
HN Nandi, Advocate ----- For the Petitioner. 
A Salam Khan, Advocate ----- For the Opposite Parties.
parties:
Bainchitala Islamia Junior Madrasha ------ Petitioner
vs.  
Md Abdur Rashid & others ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
Syed Amirul Islam, J: This Rule arises out of an application filed under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure and is directed against the order No. 15 dated 22-2-95 passed in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 54 of 1985 by the learned District Judge, Jhenidah allowing an application for addition of parties.

2. The petitioner as plaintiff instituted Title Suit No. 16 of 1081 for declaration that the petitioner is the successor of the defunct Bainchitola Islamia Junior Madrasha and for declaration of Title to the Suit land appended to the plaint, in the court of the Subordinate Judge, Jessore which was registered as Title Suit No. 26 of 1979 and subsequently after the establishment of the subordinate Judge's court at Jhenidah it was transferred to the new court and renumbered as Title Suit No. 16 of 1981. In that suit one Badaruddin was made defendant No. 7 and the summons of the suit was served on the defendants in due course and thereafter the suit was decreed ex parte by the Judgment and decree dated 20-11-82. After passing of the aforesaid ex parte decree the defendant Nos. 6 and 7 namely, one Harun Ali and Badaruddin filed an application under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure which was registered as Miscellaneous Case No. 76 of 1982. That Miscellaneous Case was resisted by the present petitioner by filing a written objection wherein have asserted that the summons of the suit was duly served on the defendants and the learned trial Court after recording evidence and hearing die parties dismissed the aforesaid Miscellaneous Case No.76 of 1982 vide its Judgment and order dated 23-4-85 and being aggrieved by the aforesaid Judgment and order dated 23-4-85 the defendant No. 7 Badaruddin preferred Miscellaneous Appeal No. 54 of 1985 before the learned District Judge. During the pendency of the aforesaid Miscellaneous Appeal one Khondoker Moulana Mesbahul Alam Azad Khandani filed an application under Order 1 rule 10 of the case claiming himself as Secretary of Bainchitala Islamia Junior Madrasha, for adding him as appellant in the aforesaid appeal, That application was allowed by the appellate Court and against the order the petitioner preferred a revisional application before the High Court Division Which was registered as Civil Revision No. 216 of 1985 in the then Jessore Bench of the High Court Division and ultimately, it was re-numbered as Civil Revision 3602 of 1991(Dhaka). A Single Bench of this High Court Division by its order dated 2-8-94 made the Rule absolute ex parte after hearing the petitioner as none entered appearance on behalf of the opposite party. During the pendency of the Civil Revision before this court Badaruddin died on 22-12-92. After the disposal of the aforesaid Civil Revision the record of the Lower Court was sent to the appellate Court below and the record was shown to the learned Advocate for the defendant appellant on 8-1-95Thereafter on 22-1-95 the heirs of said. Badaruddin filed an application under Order 1 rule 10 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for adding them as appellants in place of Badaruddin as his heirs. In that application they stand that although the record of the case was shown to the learned. Advocate on 8-1-95 but the learned Advocate did not make any correspondence with the opposite parties and they came to know about the abatement of the appeal from the secretary of the petitioner and as such they filed the application for adding them as appellants on 22-2-95. It appears from the record that none was found to move that application and the learned appellate Court below on consideration of the contents of the application allowed the same and added the opposite parties as appellants under they Order 1 rule 10 of the Code by the impugned order dated 22-2-95. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid order the petitioners preferred this revisional application to call in question the legality and propriety of the aforesaid order passed by learned appellate Court below and obtained the instant Rule.

3. Mr. HN Nandi, the learned Advocate appearing (or the plaintiff-petitioner, submits that the learned appellate Court below committed an error of law In allowing the application filed by the opposite parties in view of the facts that the petitioners did not assert in their application under Order 1 rule 10 of the Code that they have inherited the said suit property as heir of their deceased father defendant No.7 Badaruddin. The learned Advocate further submits that in their application, on the other hand, they asserted that they wanted to be added as appellants to protect the interest of their deceased father and at the same time they asserted that their father was Borgadar of the suit land under the Bainchitala Junior Madrasha and after his death they have taken Borga of the suit land from the said Madrasha. These assertions are contradictory and conflict with one another. The learned Advocate further submits that in view of the fact that the opposite parties have failed to show that they have succeeded to the Estate of their deceased father, they can neither be added as appellants under the provisions of Order I rule 10 nor under Order 22 rule 4 of the Code of Civil Procedure because in both the cases, it is the requirement of law that they must show that they have succeeded to the estate left by their deceased father. The learned Advocate further submits that the petitioner has made Badaruddin and others defendants in the interest of justice and for greater interest of the plaintiff-petitioners and.in the application filed under Order 9 rule 13 deceased Badaruddin himself asserted that he was simply entrusted by the Bainchitala Junior Madrasha to manage the property and there is nothing on record to show that, that right of management has devolved upon the opposite parties on the death of said Badaruddin. In this connection he refers to the decision reported in PW 1974 (Lahore) 312.

4. Mr A Salam Khan, the learned Advocate appearing for the added opposite parties, on the other hand, submits that there is no dispute between the parties that the opposite parties are heirs of deceased defendant Badaruddin and since Badaruddin was defendant No.7 in the suit the opposite parties as heirs of Badaruddin are, as of right, entitled to be added as appellants in the aforesaid miscellaneous appeal under the provisions of Order I rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure and in that view of the matter the appellate Court below rightly relying on the decision reported in 22 DLR 500 and 42 DLR 481 has allowed the application. The learned Advocate further submits that misquoting of section cannot stand in the way of a party to get the desired relief. In the instant case although the application was filed under Order I rule 10 of the Code but, in fact they were substituted in place of deceased defendant appellant by virtue of the provisions of Order XXII rule 4 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The learned Advocate relying on the decision reported in 32 DLR (AD) 96, further submits that it is now well settled that on setting aside the order of the lower appellate Court by High Court Division, the appeal before the learned appellate Court became pending and after arrival of the records an opportunity for substitution of the heirs of the deceased appellant is available to the party concerned and, in that view of the matter, the appellate Court below rightly substituted the opposite parties as heirs of deceased defendant appellant. The learned Advocate also relies on 22 DLR 500 and submits that in the interest of justice in the instant case the heirs of the deceased appellant can be added as parties in the instant miscellaneous appeal.

5. On a perusal of the impugned order it appears that the appellate Court below relying on the decision reported in 22 DLR 500 and 41 DLR 481 has allowed the application filed by the opposite parties under Order I rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure on the ground that it is an appropriate case where they are entitled to be added as parties.

6. I have gone through the decisions reported in 22 DLR 500 as well as the decision reported in 41 DLR 481 and the facts of those cases are quite distinguishable from the facts of the instant case. In both the cases the heirs of the deceased plaintiff appellant after the abatement of the appeal filed application for adding them as parties and it-has been held that in an appropriate case even if a suit is abated, the heirs of deceased party can be allowed to be added as party, and in both the cases there in no dispute that the heirs of the deceased inherited the Estate left by the deceased plaintiff, but in the instant case it was asserted by the deceased defendant appellant Badaruddin that he was entrusted by the Bainchitala Junior Madrasha to manage the suit property. Even if this statement is hundred percent correct then also on his death the right to manage the suit property does not devolve upon the heirs of deceased Badaruddin in the absence of any positive assertion to the effect that they have been entrusted by the said Madrasha to manage the property on the death of Badaruddin, The right which deceased Badruddin had was a personal right conferred on him by the Bainchitala Junior Madrasha. In the instant case there is no evidence nor there is any assertion made by the opposite parties that after the death of their father they have been entrusted by the said Madrasha to manage the suit property In this connection it may be mentioned that in connection with the aforesaid miscellaneous application Khondoker Moulana Mesbahul Alam Azad Khandani claiming himself as Secretary of the Bainchitala Junior Madrasha tried to implead himself as appellant in the aforesaid miscellaneous appeal and that application for adding him as appellant. was allowed by the appellate Court below but against that order a revisional application was preferred by the plaintiff petitioner before this court which was registered as Civil Revision No. 3602 of 1991 and the Rule in that revisional application was made absolute on finding that the said Badaruddin is not the owner of the suit property and against that ,order an appeal was preferred before the Appellate Division which was dismissed and that the alleged dispute between Bainchitala Junior Madrasha and the plaintiff petitioners attained its finality. In the application filed under Order 1 rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure the opposite parties have now come up with a plea that their father was a Borgadar of the suit land under the aforesaid madrasha and after his death they have taken Barga of the suit land from the said Madrasha. I have already pointed out that Badaruddin himself did not claim to be a Borgadar under the said Madrasha in his application under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code but his heirs for the first time have come up with an application under Order 1 rule 10 of the Code stating that their father was a Borgadar under the Bainchitala Madrasha and on his death they have taken Borga settlement of the suit land from the aforesaid Madrsha. It is alleged that on the death of their father they have taken Borga of the suit land from the said Madrasha and even if it be a fact then also they cannot be added as parties in the instant suit because they have no independent right to call in question the legality and propriety of the decree passed in Title suit No. 16 of 1991 wherein they were not parties.

<u>7. Be it an application under Order 1 rule 10 of the Code or an application for substitution under Order 22 rule 4 of the Code the opposite parties must show that they have inherited the Estate left by their deceased father but it is clear from the assertion made by both deceased Badaruddin in his application under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure and the present opposite parties in their application under Order 1 rule 10 of the Code that no Estate has been left by their father to which they have succeeded on his death. Thus they do not come within the ambit of legal representative as contemplated in rule 4 of Order 22 of the Code. In the case reported in PLD 1974 (Lah) 312, it has been held that the successors of a deceased do not become legal representative within the meaning of rule 4 of Order 22 of the Code if no Estate is left by the deceased to be succeeded by the successors. In the instant case admittedly the suit property is not the personal property of deceased Badaruddin and it did never belong to him. So, no question of inheritance does arise in respect of the suit land by the opposite parties as heirs of deceased Badaruddin. In that view of the matter the application filed by them can neither be allowed under Order I rule 10 or under Order 22 rule 4 of the Code of Civil Procedure and the learned Appellate court below misdirecting himself and on a total misconception of law and facts erroneously allowed the application filed by the opposite parties for adding them as appellants in the Miscellaneous Appeal No. 54 of 1985.</u>

In the result, the Rule is made absolute with a cost of Taka 2,000.00 (two thousand). The Judgment and order No. 25 dated 22-2-95 passed by the learned District Judge, Jhenidah in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 54 of 1995 is set aside and the application dated 22-2-95 filed by the opposite parties is rejected.

End.

lawyer:
Syed Md Dastagir Hossain, Advocate ----- For the Petitioner. 
Nirmalendu Deb, Advocate ----- For Opposite Party No. 1
parties:
Syed Sad Ali ------ Petitioner
vs
Bidhan Chandra Dev and ors ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
MA Aziz J: This Rule is directed against the judgment and order dated 23-9-95 passed in Misc. Appeal No. 3 of 1994 by the learned Additional District Judge, Moulvibazar setting aside the judgment and order dated 29-11-93 passed in pre-emption case No. 4 of 1987 by the learned Subordinate Judge, Moulvibazar allowing pre-emption.

2. The case of the pre-emptor petitioner Syed Sad Ali, in short, is that he instituted a case for pre-emption under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act being Preemption case No. 4 of 1987 in the Court of the Subordinate Judge, Moulavibazar contending, inter alia, that the case property (shop) along with other lands belonged to the. predecessor in interest of proforma opposite parties Nos. 7-20; out of the aforesaid reported a quantum of land measuring 0.07 acres was transferred by registered kabala dated 4-9-83 to the predecessor-in-interest of opposite party Nos. 10-12 namely, Azadur Rahman, Syed Sad Ali and his full brothers namely, opposite party Nos. 4-6 and ever since the petitioner and his brothers (opposite party Nos. 4-6) have been owning and possessing the same and after their purchase they completed the construction work of the shop which at the relevant time was under construction; that the case land is a shop of the pre-emptor petitioner which he acquired earlier by purchase from opposite party Nos. 7 and 8 M Serajul Islam and Md Nazrul Islam. The said Serajul Islam and Nurul Islam transferred the case shop to opposite party No. 1 Bidhan Chandra Dev on the 1st of Ashar 1392 BS corresponding to 16-6-85 and the said deed was registered on 11-9-86 without serving any notice to the petitioner who is a co-sharer to the holding; that having been aware of the transfer the petitioner procured a certified copy of the kabala dated 11-9-86 and tiled an application for pre-emption under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act.

3. Pre-emptee (opposite party No. 1) Bidhan Chandra Dev contested the case by filing a written objection denying all the material allegations and assertions contained in the pre-emption petition stating, inter alia, that the quantum of land in plot No. 269 is 0.19 acres but owing to printing mistake the said quantum was written as 9 decimals; that the said Plot No. 269 belonged to Samar, Azadur Rahman, Ilasur Rahman and Moniruddin and through an amicable partition they got their respective shares demarcated. As a result the other co-sharers had no right, title and interest in the case land; that Sanowar while in exclusive and uninterrupted possession of his share of the land died leaving behind two sons namely, opposite party Nos. 7 and 8 Md Serajul Islam and Md Nazrul Islam. Thereafter those two brothers sold the case land on 16-6-85 to the petitioner which was registered on 11-9-86; that after his purchase the petitioner raised a loan of Taka 1, 00,000.00 by mortgaging the said property with the Rupali Bank Chadnighat Branch on 16-10-85 through a registered mortgage deed on the same date. It was further stated that since the value of the land has gone up, the petitioner (pre-emptor) with a view to grabbing the case land has filed the application for pre-emption false assertions. Hence the pre-emption petition is liable to be dismissed.

4. The learned Subordinate Judge, Moulavibazar by judgment and order dated 29-11-93 allowed pre-emption holding, inter alia, that admittedly the pre-emptor petitioner is a co-sharer by purchase to the holding and the pre-emptee opposite party is a stranger to the said holding and that the case having been filed within the statutory period of limitation the petitioner is entitled to have the case land pre-empted. Having felt aggrieved by the said judgment and order the pre-emptee preferred Misc. Appeal No. 3 of 1994 in the Court of the learned District Judge, Moulavibazar which on transfer was heard and disposed of by the learned Additional District Judge, Molavibazar who by the impugned judgment and order dated 23-9-95 allowed the appeal by setting aside the judgment and order of the trial Court holding, inter alia, that the pre-emptor petitioner Syed Sad Ali though a co-sharer of the holding he is not a co-sharer of the land (shop) transferred and, as such, he is not entitled to pre-empt the case shop. The learned Subordinate Judge relied on a decision reported in 35 DLR (AD) 230 in the case of SM Basiruddin vs Zahurul Islam Chowdhury and others in which case their Lordships departed from the view taken in the case of Manindra Chandra Ghose vs Mujibul Islam reported in 12 DLR 785 which view was endorsed by Mr Sekander Ali, J and concurred by Mr Murshed, J holding that the petitioner appellant (pre-emptor) being co-sharer in the tenancy were also co-sharer in the land which is the subject matter of the pre-emption case. In the 35 DLR case Ruhul Islam, J held according to Hasan, J the words non-agricultural land means a piece of land in joint possession and enjoyment without partition which may form a tenancy or a portion of a tenancy. The learned Judge explained that this interpretation will not throw the land open to unlimited number of persons but to persons who are co-sharer tenants under the same landlord in respect of the undivided land, though such co-sharer tenants may be co-sharer tenants of the tenancy. In the instant case it is found that the case land is demarcated by a boundary wall as per admission made by PW 1 the pre-emptor Syed Sad All himself. The joma remained unaltered. No separate holding was opened by any of the co-sharers and although allegedly there was an amicable partition between the co-sharer that did not ipso facto split up the joma.

5. In the case reported in 35 DLR (AD) the provision of section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and that of section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act were elaborately discussed. The expression co-sharer in the land transferred used in section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act was held to be much narrower and limited in its scope and extent. Under section 24 of the Non Agricultural Tenancy Act, the pre-emptor has to be a co-sharer not only in the holding transferred but also a co-sharer in the land transferred. In the instant case the pre-emptor though a co sharer in the joma was not a co-sharer in the land (i.e. shop) transferred to opposite party No.1 Bidhan Chandra Dev because of the fact that the shop transferred is well demarcated as per admission of the pre-emptor himself.

<u>6. Syed Dastagir Hossain, learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner submits that the case reported in 35 DLR has no manner of application in the instant case firstly, because there being no partition by metes and bounds between the co-sharer and the holding not having been split up, the pre-emptor did not cease to be a co-sharer of the holding and that the expression co-sharer in the tenancy and co-sharer in the land transferred are synonymous and in that view of the matter the petitioner is competent to maintain this petition for pre-emption as he has filed the application for pre-emption within the prescribed time in compliance with all the legal formalities required under the law. Mr Hossain further submits that there has been no splitting up of the joma in accordance with the provision of section 117(1) (c) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. On the other hand Mr Nirmalendu Dev, learned Advocate appearing for the pre-emptee opposite party submits that the appellate Court has pronounced a correct judgment by setting aside the judgment and order passed by the learned Subordinate Judge allowing pre-emption. In support of his contention Mr. Deb has referred to the provision of section 24 of the Non Agricultural Tenancy Act with special emphasis on the expression "co-sharer to the land transferred" unlike the expression appearing in section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act which is a co-sharer in the tenancy or holding. Mr Deb relied on the decision in the case of SM Basiruddin Zahurul Islam Chowdhury and another reported' in 35 DLR SAD) 230 wherein their Lordships took different view from that taken by Sekander Ali, J and concurred by Murshed, J that the expression co-sharer in the holding and co-sharer in the land transferred is synonymous but in the case reported in 35 DLR their Lordships held that the legislature consciously used the expression non-agricultural land in section 24 instead of using the expression tenancy or holding as used in section 96 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. This was done with the purpose of limiting the number of applicants by making it available only to the co-sharers of the land and not of the tenancy, so that distribution among all the co-sharers may not make the land unfit for the purpose for which it was taken and it was observed by Ruhul Islam J. So, according to me, the words non-agricultural land means a piece of land in joint possession and enjoyment without partition which may form the tenancy or a portion of tenancy. This interpretation will not throw the land open to the unlimited number of persons but to persons who are co sharer tenants under the same landlord in respect of undivided land though such co-sharer tenants may be co-sharer tenants of the tenancy.</u>

7. In the reported case, the case land appertaining to a permanent tenure stood recorded in CS. Khatian No. 214 under Mouza Shahar Dacca, owned by Akshoy Kumar Saha Banik and Rangubala Choudhurani, Akshoy Kumar Saha Banik instituted Title Suit No. 126 of 1946 in the First Court of Subordinate Judge, Dacca for partition and by the decree passed in the suit Akshoy Kumar Saha Banik got one-third ((1/3)) share while Rangubala got the remaining two-tbird ((2/3)) share. One Nafisa Khatun by purchasing the interest of Akshoy Kumar Saha Banik became co-sharer of Rangubala. Rangubala created a lease in respect of the 2/3rd share for 99 years by a registered deed of lease dated 23-12-53 in favour of Ayesha Khatun. Respondent No. 2 Nafisa Khatun sold her interest to respondent No. 1 by registered sale deed dated 18-4-72. Ayesha Khatun also sold her interest to the appellant by a registered sale deed dated 10-9-73. Against this sale respondent No. 1 filed the application for pre-emption. The appellant contested the case by filing written objection contending, inter alia, that the respondent No. 2 was not a co-sharer in the tenancy, because the land of the tenure was partitioned by the decree in Title suit No. 126 of 1946 between Akshoy Kumar Saha Banik and Rangubala Choudhurani; and that a separate tenancy was created in favour of Ayesha Khatun by Rangubala by granting permanent lease for 99 years reserving for herself annual rent of Taka 1/-; and that Ayesha Khatun paid rent of Taka 1.00 to the lessor Rangubala till the rent receiving interest was acquired by the Government. The learned Subordinate Judge allowed pre-emption against the appellant and the appeal was dismissed. Thereafter the appellant moved the High Court Division in revision under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure and being unsuccessful moved this court and obtained leave from this court to appeal from the judgment of the High Court Division and their Lordships having considered the provision of section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act allowed the appeal with costs and the order allowing pre-emption was set aside and thus the application for pre-emption was dismissed.

8. In view of the facts, circumstances, the material on records and the decision reported in 35 DLR (AD) 230 referred to above I do not find any cogent reason to interfere with the impugned order. The court of appeal below does not appear to have committed any error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice in setting aside the judgment and order passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Moulavibazar.

In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs.

Let the lower court records be sent down at once.

End.
