full_judgment:
This Rule arises out of an application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure and is directed against the order dated 31-12-1976 passed by the Subordinate Judge, First Court, Bakerganj in Title Suit No.86 of 1975 setting aside the decree dated 29-9-1975 on an application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

2. The petitioner as plaintiff filed Title Suit No. 86 of 1975 in the First Court of Subordinate Judge, Bakerganj on 19-12-1975 for a declaration that they are the owners of the property by virtue of Kolkarsha right against Kartick Chandra and 54 others. The allegations levelled in the plaint of the aforesaid suit, in brief, is that the land described in the schedule of the plaint measuring an area of 16.61 acres of land of mouza Kalashgram PS Kotwali, District Bakerganj was settled to the petitioners by the owners in first part of Baishak, 1354 BS on a rental of Taka 90.00 and since then they are in possession of the same by cultivation, making improvement and enjoying the usufructs. It was agreed between them that the original owners will take necessary steps for getting the said land recorded in the name of the petitioners but the same was not recorded in the name of the petitioners and was illegality recorded in the name of the defendants. The suit was ultimately decreed on compromise against the defendant Nos. 1, 2, 4, 5, 19, 22, 23 and 55 and ex parte against the other defendants. Thereafter the deceased opposite party No.1 Prem Lata filed an application on 13-11-1975 for setting aside the aforesaid decree dated 29-9-75 under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure describing herself as widow of Basanta Kumar Das alleging that the decree was obtained by suppressing summons and that some of the defendants died long before the institution of the suit. Subsequently, the said petition of the opposite party was amended and con verted into an application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure as she was not a party in the suit. The present petitioner filed written objection against the said application stating that the summons was duly served, no fraud was committed and she had no locus standi to file the application and they also asserted that she was the wife of Lialit Fakir and not of Basantra Kumar Das.

3. The deceased opposite party Prem Lata examined 3 witnesses in support for her contention and the petitioners examined two witnesses in the proceeding and the learned Subordinate Judge, by his judgment and order dated 31-12-1978 allowed application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure by setting aside the decree passed on 29-9-75. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid judgment and decree dated 31-11-76 the petitioners have preferred this revisional application and obtained the instant Rule.

4. Mr Abdul Quayum, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff petitioners, submits firstly that in the instant case it is to be decided whether an ex parte decree can be set aside under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure. He submits that when a suit is decreed ex parte there are three (3) remedies available to an aggrieved party namely, the aggrieved party can prefer an appeal against the ex parte decree, secondly, he can file an application for review of the ex parte decree under Order 47 rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure and thirdly, the aggrieved party can file an application under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the ex parte decree and for this proposition of law he refers to and relies on the case reported in 31 DLR (AD) 51. He next submits that it was now well settled that where specific relief is available inherent power of the court under section 151 cannot be invoked and for this purpose he relies on the case reported in 29 DLR (SC) 185. Mr Abdul Quayum then submits that section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure is not an alternative remedy inasmuch as section 151 of the Code does not create any new power, nor does it confer an additional jurisdiction upon a court and for this purpose he relies on the decision reported in 26 DLR 124. The learned Advocate further submits that by passing a decree a court of first instance becomes functus officio and no more remains in seisin of the case and as such the court cannot entertain an application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure to sit over its judgment because if that is allowed that would amount to converting the first court of facts into a last court of facts which is not contemplated by the Code of Civil Procedure. The learned Advocate further submits if there is an allegation of fraud on the basis of which a party wants to get the decree set aside the proper course is to file a separate suit and not an application under section 151 of the Code and for this purpose he relies on the decision reported in 43 CWN 969 wherein it has been held that where there is an allegation of fraud the proper course is to file a fresh suit and not to impugn the ex parte decree by an application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

5. Mr Syed Ziaul Karim, the learned Advocate appeared on behalf of one Jahangir Hossain Howlader, Akram Ali Howlader and Amdad Ali Howlader and earlier filed an application for impleading those persons as parties in this revisional application and it was ordered that the aforesaid application would be considered at the time of hearing of the Rule. Mr Syed Ziaul Karim on 9-8-1995 appeared before this court and submitted that he would not press the said application but his presence may be noted. In that view of the matter the application earlier filed by him for adding his clients as parties has not been gone into and the same is kept with the record without adverting thereto or passing any order thereon and the present judgment is being pronounced in his presence.

6. On a perusal of the impugned order it appears that the predecessor-in-interest of opposite party No.1(ka) namely, Prem Lata, filed an application under Order 9 rule13 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the ex parte decree dated 29-9-1975 which was ultimately converted into an application under section 151 of the Code. In that application the predecessor-in-interest of opposite party No.1(a) namely, Prem Lata asserted that the decree was obtained by suppressing summons and some of the defendants of the aforesaid suit also died long before the institution of the suit. The said application of Prem Lata was resisted by the present petitioners by filing written objection stating, inter alia that the summons was duly served and no fraud I was committed and that Prem Lata has no locus standi to file such application. The trial Court after taking into consideration the materials and evidence on record found that Prem Lata is the wife of Basanta Kumar Das who was one of the defendants of the aforesaid title suit and in that view of the matter the learned trial Court arrived at a finding that she has locus standito file an application under section 151 of the Code to call in question the legality and propriety of the ex parte decree dated 29-9-75. It also appears that the plaintiff petitioners have also raised objection as to the maintainability of the aforesaid application filed under section 151 of the Code and the learned trial Court rejected that contention of the plaintiff petitioners on the ground that the aforesaid application was filed by the predecessors-in-interest of opposite party No.1 (a) on the ground of fraud and fraud vitiates everything and in that view of the matter the learned trial Court found that the application is maintainable under section 151 of the Code. It also appears from a perusal of the impugned order that on consideration of materials and evidence on record the trial Court found that the defendant Nos.7 and 45 were dead long before the institution of the Title Suit No.86 of 1975, and it also appears from the materials and evidence on record that defendant No. 7 Aswini Kumar of the aforesaid title suit died on 11-6-1944 and the defendant No.45 Khirode Sundari died on 14-4-46. Besides, it is also found by the trial Court that these two defendants were described in the cause title of the aforesaid title suit as residents of Kalibari PO Kalashgram but the summons was served at the permanent address and not at their present address and in view of that fact the learned trial Court arrived at a finding that the summons was not duly served on the defendants and summons was suppressed. After taking into consideration all the materials and evidence on record the trial Court came to a definite finding that the compromise decree was obtained by fraud and finally, the learned trial Court kept the issue open as to whether Prem Lata is the wife of Basanta Kumar Das or Lalit Fakir and observed that it would be decided at the trial of the suit by the trial Court.

7. Now let us see how far the submissions made by Mr Quayum, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff petitioners, are sustainable in law. His first submission that when a suit is decreed ex parte there are three remedies available to an aggrieved party namely, that the aggrieved party can prefer an appeal against the ex parte decree or can file an application under Order 47 rule 1 or file an application under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure and this proposition of law is not disputed by anybody. It is well settled now that in the event of an ex parte decree an aggrieved party can follow anyone of the aforesaid courses and simultaneously can file an appeal and also an application under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code. The next submission of Mr Quayum that where specific relief is available inherent power of the court under section 151 cannot be invoked is also beyond doubt and nobody questioned that proposition of law as has been laid down in the case reported in 29 DLR (SC) 185. The third submission of Mr Quayum is that section 151 of the Code does not create any new power nor does it confer any additional jurisdiction is also well settled and beyond doubt. But, in the instant case we are required to determine the scope and application of section 151 of the Code in a case where a party seeks to set aside ex parte decree on the ground of fraud. Mr Quayum while arguing the case relied on the decision reported in 43 CWN 969, wherein their Lordships of the Calcutta High Court observed that where there is an allegation of fraud committed on them the proper remedy is to file a regular suit and the aggrieved party cannot resort to section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure. It is now well settled that where a decree is sought to be set aside on the ground of fraud practised on a party the allegation of fraud can be gone into in a regular suit and not in summary proceedings because such an enquiry will not only be extraneous to the suit itself but also it would be hard on the losing party to be guilty of fraud in a summary proceeding under section 151 without having remedy by way of an appeal but where the decree has been obtained by practising fraud the court has not only the power but it is duty bound to set aside the decree even suomotu. The case relied on by Mr. Quayum as reported in 43 CWN 969 is not attracted in the instant case, inasmuch as in that case a consent decree was sought to be set aside on the ground of fraud by filing an application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure and in view of the facts and circumstances of that case it was observed that the proper course for having a consent decree set aside and vacated on the ground of fraud is by way of regular suit and not by an application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure which has no application, at least where the fraud is practised not upon the court but upon the party, e.g. where there was apparent consent but the consent, is said to have been obtained by fraud and misrepresentation. So, this case in fact does not help Mr Quayum, rather it helps the opposite party. Similarly, the case reported in 26 DLR 124 also does not help Mr Quayum, rather it helps the opposite party. It has been observed in that case by a Division Bench of this court that section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure does not create any new power for, nor does it confer an additional jurisdiction upon, a court; it merely furnishes legislative recognition to the well established principle that every court has inherent jurisdiction to act ex-debito justiciae to do that real and substantial justice for the administration of which alone it exists or to prevent abuse of process of the court. These powers are not to be trammelled or circumscribed by any procedural technicalities. Once the court is of the view that the cause of justice will be advanced or certain abuse of the process of the court will be prevented by a certain action on the part of the court, it will be the duty of the court to take such an action, notwithstanding anything to the contrary contained in the Code. The decision of the court cannot, however, be taken capriciously or arbitrarily. Since the powers, as recited in section 151 of the Code, are very wide and incapable of any precise definition, it requeres great care and circumspection on the part of the court in their exercise. From the aforesaid decision it is crystal clear that for ends of justice and to meet a substantial justice with regard to commission of fraud on the court, a court is empowered to invoke its inherent jurisdiction to set at naught any order which was obtained by a party by misleading the court itself.

8. While arguing the case Mr Quayum did not refer to the case reported in 10 DLR 79 but when this case was brought to his notice, the learned Advocate tried to distinguish the aforesaid case on the ground that in that case the application under section 151 was made in a pending suit. I think that we may profitably refer to the decision reported in 10 DLR 79, wherein it has been held that an application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure would lie seeking relief when the party alleging fraud was not a party to the order made by the court as a result of fraud practised upon the court. In that case it has been spelt out that when the allegation is that the decree was obtained by practising fraud on the court and the party complaining of fraud has been shown to be one of the parties to the solenama as agreeing to it, whereas he is completely ignorant about the solenama, the court has an inherent power, in fact, it is duty bound to set aside the solenama as an application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure. A case of this description is completely different from the class of cases where a person who is a party to a suit and assents to a consent decree which he subsequently seeks to impeach on the ground that his assent was obtained by fraud. In a case of this latter class, relief cannot be obtained by an application under section 151 of the Code, but a proper way of proceeding for setting aside the decree would be to institute a regular suit.

9. It, thus, clearly appears from 10 DLR case that when there is an allegation of fraud practised on the court, an application under section 151 of the Code lies but when the allegation of fraud is that fraud was practised on a party an application under section 151 would not lie and in that case the proper course would be to institute a regular suit. I, therefore, find that the cases relied on by Mr Quayum do not help him in the facts and circumstances of the present case, rather they support the case of the opposite party inasmuch as in the instant case it is the definite case of the opposite party that the decree dated 29-9-1975 was obtained by the plaintiff petitioner by practising fraud upon the court.

10. In this connection we may also take note of the case of Peary Chowdhury vs. Sanoo Das reported in 19 CM 419, wherein their Lordships observed:

We are of the opinion, however, that under the circumstances found by the learned District Judge the court had an inherent jurisdiction to set aside the decree. Not only has the court power, but it is its duty to set aside a decree obtained by fraud practised upon the court, when apprised of it. We agree with the following observations made in a case in the Bombay High Court in which a decree by consent was set aside in a summary manner upon an application by the defendant. What the defendant says is that there was a suit against him, and that the suit was declared to have ended by reason of a decree passed with his consent. He never consented, and the result has been that there has been fraud committed upon the court. The court was persuaded to sign a decree to which the defendant had never consented and that upon the representation that he had consented to it. Therefore, once the court is asked to go back upon its own procedure, it is not a question whether there is any section in the Civil Procedure Code to warrant the action of the court amending its proceedings. It is an inherent power of every court to correct its own proceedings where it has been misled".

Similarly, in the case reported in 24 DLR 116, it has been held that as to case where fraud is committed upon the court as well as the parties, a court has inherent jurisdiction to interfere in exercise of its power vested in section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure and in a case of fraud upon a party the only remedy is in a suit. Here we may also quote from an unreported decision of Single Bench of this court passed in Civil Revision No. 86 of 1962 decided by Ali J, on 30-4-65. On a consideration of a number of decisions his Lordship Ali, J, arrived at the following conclusion:

"On a careful perusal of these decisions as well as a number of the other authorities referred to therein I feel that it is firmly well settled that in case of fraud on a party the only remedy is in a suit. As to the cases where fraud is committed upon the court as well as the parties, the consensus of judicial opinion appears to be that the court has inherent jurisdiction to interfere in exercise of the powers vested in it under section 151. At any rate, no authority could be cited before me laying down categorically that in such cases the court has no inherent jurisdiction to interfere".

11. In another case reported in the same DLR ie24 DLR 133, it has been held that where further proceedings of a suit cannot be stayed under section 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure courts can, however, for ends of justice, stay such proceedings under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

12. Similarly, in the case reported in 35 DLR (AD) 42, it has been held that if in a particular case an application for temporary injunction does not come under the purview of Order 39 rules 1 and 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure a court is empowered to grant injunction by invoking section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure. It is also well settled that the court should not exercise inherent power under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure where there is alternative remedy in a case. Such power should be exercised to prevent abuse of process of the court and for ends of justice and for this proposition of law if any authority is required we may refer to the case reported in 24 DLR 133.

13. In this connection we may also refer to the case reported in 14 DLR 256 wherein an application under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure was allowed ex parte. Thereafter an application was filed under Order 47 rule 1 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the said order without moving the High Court Division under section 151 of the Code. It was contended in that case that such an application under section 151 of the Code is not maintainable inasmuch as there is express provision for revision against such an order. In that case the suit of the plaintiff was decreed on contest against defendant No. 1 and ex parte against defendant Nos. 2 and 3. Thereafter the defendant No. 3 filed an application under Order 9 rule 13 to set aside the ex parte decree passed against him. The application was allowed ex parte. Thereafter the plaintiff moved the court under Order 47 rule 1 read with section 151 to set aside the order passed ex parte on the application made under Order 9 rule 13 the Code of Civil Procedure but it was rejected by the Munsif as not being maintainable. In view of the facts and circumstances of the case it was held by the then Dhaka High Court that an application under section 151 of the Code lies and should not be thrown out in liminiin as much as a party has not precluded himself from seeking justice under section 151 of the Code to set aside an ex parte order passed in an application under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code for setting aside the ex parte decree, as the party did not take any step under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure though he was free to move the High Court under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

14. In this connection we may refer to the case of Abdul Aziz vs. Abani Mohan Mukharjee and others reported in 30 DLR (SC) 221. In that case an order of abatement of an appeal was obtained on production of false certificate of death. An application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure was subsequently made for setting aside the order on the ground of fraud practised upon the court. A question arose whether section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure can be invoked to set aside the order when there are other remedies open to the applicant. The High Court Division answered in the affirmative and set aside the order. On appeal the decision was affirmed. In course of judgment Ahsanuddin Chowdhury J, who delivered the judgment of the Appellate Division stated the legal position in the following terms:

"That the court has inherent power under section 151 of the Code to set aside its order passed under a misapprehension of facts when true facts are brought to light and that the court has also power under the aforesaid section 151 of the Code to vacate an order obtained by misleading the court and practising fraud upon it."

It may be noted that the provision of the Code are generally meant to serve the ends of justice but in their very nature they cannot read all possible circumstances. Consequently every court has an inherent power to make any order it considers necessary for the ends of justice. Reference on this point may be made to the following cases namely 19 CWN (Peary Chowdhury vs. Seno Das) 219; 45 CWN 392 (Akina Bibi vs. Mohammad Ali) AIR 1934 (All) 287 (Lachhman Rai vs. Jang Bahadur Rai AIR 1937 (Sind) 101 (Mohanial vs. Khushilini) 10 DLR 79 PLD 1958 (Dhaka) 295 (Ganesh Chandra Basu vs. Bashu Laskar).

15. What has been held in the above cases is that the court has inherent power under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure to set aside its order passed under a misapprehension of facts when true facts are brought to light and that the court has also power under the aforesaid section to set aside an order obtained by misleading the court and practising fraud upon it.

16. In this connection we may refer to the case reported in 31 DLR 109, wherein it has been held that if fraud has been committed upon the party as a result of which the court has been misled into passing certain orders, then it is a fraud upon the court and in such case, the court is entitled, under its inherent powers, to set aside any order passed upon a false representation. The court has inherent power to correct its own proceedings when it has been misled into passing an order by the fraud of any party to the suit.

17. There are cases where fraudulent decree were set aside in exercise of inherent powers of the court under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure. We may refer to the following cases namely, the case of Mofazzal Molla and another vs. Parul Bala Debi and others, 24 DLR 117, Md Amir Hossain Sarder vs. Sarat Chandra and others, 31 DLR 109, Mozaffar Ahmed and others vs. Moulvi Saleh Ahmed and others, 40 DLR 239.

18. Similar view is also expressed in the case reported in 1968 SCD 275, wherein it has been held that a court has inherent power to set aside an order obtained by practising fraud upon it at the instance of a party to the proceedings and there is no question of the court being functus officio. In the case reported in 13 BLD I, it has been held that as a general rule the powers of court under section 151 are not to be invoked where specific provision in the Code covers a particular case or there is alternative remedy. But the civil Court has ample reserve of its inherent powers to do what meets the ends of justice when fraud is committed on the court itself. A court commits an error of law in refusing to entertain an application for setting aside ex parte decree. It is fairly established that in cases of fraud upon the court, the court may exercise its inherent powers to set things right even though there are alternative remedies open.

19. I have already referred to some other decisions of the Indian jurisdiction as well as of Pakistani jurisdiction wherein it has been held that not only the court has such powers but it is duty bound to set aside the decree or order obtained by practising fraud upon the court itself.

<u>20. In view of legal position as discussed above it is found that there are authorities which laid down that even after the passing of the decree, the court can entertain an application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure in an appropriate case where fraud was practised upon the court and in such case the question of becoming functus officio after the pronouncement of judgment and signing a decree does not arise at all because fraud vitiates everything. If the court is found to be helpless in setting at naught its judgment and decree passed on being misled by a party then the court itself will remain party to the fraud which cannot be allowed to stand. In the instant case on a perusal of the materials and evidence on record we find that the trial Court has arrived at a positive finding that by practising fraud upon the court namely, by suppressing summons and instituting the suit against some dead persons, the plaintiff petitioners have obtained the ex parte decree and, as such, the trial Court rightly entertained the application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure by invoking its inherent jurisdiction and rightly interfered with the judgment and decree dated 29-9-75 and set aside the same. In view of the decisions cited above it is crystal clear that in the instant case the trial Court has rightly invoked its inherent jurisdiction and set aside the ex parte decree which was obtained from it by misleading the court.</u>

21. In that view of the facts and circumstances of the case there is no substance in this revisional application and the submissions made by Mr Quayum have no merits at all.

In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to cost.

End.

full_judgment: Md. Ismailuddin Sarker J: This appeal by leave by the appellant is from the judgment and order dated June 7, 1994 passed by the Administrative Appellate Tribunal in Appeal No. 75 of 1991. The appellant while acting as a Director of Fire Service, Civil Defence and Rescue Service was placed on suspension under Rule 11(1) of the Government Servants (Discipline and Appeal) Rules, 1985, herein after referred to as the said Rules, and later on January 27, 1986 a charge was framed against him under Rules 3(b) and 3(d) of the aforesaid Rules, for alleged corruption and misconduct by a Deputy Secretary, Ministry of Home Affairs, alleging that the appellant entered into service showing that he passed BA Examination, but, in fact, he did not pass the BA Examination. The appellant submitted written statement on February 4, 1986 denying the allegations and stating that he did not himself write his qualification as BA in the application for service nor in his annual confidential report which were done by others. The aforesaid Deputy Secretary, Ministry of Home Affairs also appointed a Joint Secretary, Ministry of Home Affairs as Inquiry Officer to enquire into the allegations against the appellant. The Inquiry Officer did not examine any witness in holding enquiry into the allegations and submitted a report finding that the allegations against the appellant were established. The authority then served a second show cause notice upon the appellant to which the appellant submitted a written reply on April 7, 1986 pleading not guilty of the charges. The Ministry of Home Affairs, however, without considering the reply of the appellant forwarded the case for opinion to the Public Service Commission which without examining the relevant papers gave consent to the proposed punishment The Secretary Ministry of Home Affairs thereafter issued the impugned order of compulsory retirement from service on June 1, 1986 and on the following day i.e June 2, 1986, issued a memo amending his order dated June 1, 1986 2. The appellant thereafter filed an application review on July 24, 1986 before the Hon'ble President of Bangladesh but he was informed on December 24, 1986 that the application was rejected by the Hon'ble President. The appellant then filed AT Case No. 67 of 1987 on March 28, 1987 before the Administrative Tribunal, Dhaka. The Secretary Ministry of Home Affairs contested the case on behalf of the Ministry filing a written statement contending, inter alia, that the appellant noted his qualification as BA in the relevant form, though, in fact, he failed to passed the BA examination. Although the Administrative Tribunal held that the proceeding and order of compulsory retirement was illegal and void being without jurisdiction, but dismissed the appellant's case by the judgment and order dated August 17, 1991 holding that the case was barred by limitation. The appellant thereafter filed an appeal before the Administrative Appellate Tribunal being appeal No. 75 of 1991 but the Administrative Appellate Tribunal by its Judgment and order dated June 15, 1992 dismissed the appeal affirming the finding of the Administrative Tribunal that the case was barred by limitation. 3. The appellant thereafter obtained leave to appeal from this Division and preferred Civil Appeal No. 82 of 1992 before this Court. This Division allowed the appeal by the judgment and order dated July 26, 1993 holding that the time spent on review before the President under the Government Servants (Discipline & Appeal) Rules. 1985 was to be excluded in the computation of the period of limitation and remanded the appeal to the Administrative Appellate Tribunal for disposal. After remand the Administrative Appellate Tribunal held that the ultimate order of compulsory retirement of the appellant was illegal and void inasmuch as the charge framed against the appellant by the Deputy Secretary, Ministry of Home Affairs was without jurisdiction, as according to the rules the Secretary, Ministry of Home Affairs was the designated officer to frame the charges against the appellant and further, the Deputy Secretary also appointed the Inquiry Officer whereas according to the Rules the himself was to appoint the inquiry officer. Accordingly, the Administrative Appellate Tribunal held that since the proceeding against the appellant was not initiated according to the Rules the same was without jurisdiction and the ultimate order of compulsory retirement of the appellant was illegal and void. But the Administrative Appellate Tribunal for dismissed the appeal on the ground of "estoppel" under section 115 of the Evidence Act as after passing of the order of compulsory retirement the applied appealed for LPR and accepted all financial benefits including monthly pension. 4. Being aggrieved by the impugned order passed by the Administrative Appellate Tribunal in Appeal No. 75 of 1991 the appellant preferred this appeal by leave to this Division. 5. It is contended by Mr. Abdur Rob Chowdhury, learned Counsel appearing on behalf of the appellant, that the appellant as a Government Servant did not go for voluntary retirement and he was given compulsory retirement from service as a measure of punishment and, as such, the principle of estoppel is not attracted in the facts and circumstances of the case inasmuch as the appellant under compelling circumstances had to accept the financial benefits from the Government. In support of his contention the learned Counsel has referred to the case of Hasina Mawla vs. Bangladesh Parjatan Corporation and another 45 DLR 112, the case of Akhlasur Rahman vs. Safarullan and others 42 DLR (AD) 189 and also the case of AC Jose vs. Sivan Pillai AIR 1984 (SC) 921. 6. Mr. B Hossain, learned Deputy Attorney General appearing on behalf of the respondents, on the other hand, tried to distinguish the case reported in 45 DLR 112 and also the case reported in 42 DLR (AD) 189 pointing out that the latter case arose out of a pre-emption proceeding in which the appellant waived his right by conduct. The learned Deputy Attorney-General submitted that the appellant accepted the retirement benefits by which he also waived his right and, as such, his case is also hit by section 115 of the Evidence Act. It may be pointed out in this connection that the point of estoppel was neither taken before the Administrative Appellate Tribunal nor before the Administrative Tribunal before filing of appeal by the appellant to this Division. After the judgment and order of remand by this Division the ground of estoppel was taken for the first time before the Administrative Appellate Tribunal which accept the same and dismissed the appeal, although on merit it held that the proceedings against the appellant and the order of his compulsory retirement from service was illegal and without jurisdiction. 7. In the case of Hasina Mawla 45 DLR 112 the learned Judges of the High Court Division held that the Parjatan Corporation failed to establish on the materials on record that she requested the Corporation to retire her from service owing to her ill health and also noticed that after receipt of gratuity benefits under compelling circumstances, she filed representation against her alleged retirement and, as such, the principle of estoppel was not applicable in her case. This Division dismissed the leave petition of the Bangladesh Parjatan Corporation in the aforesaid case of Hasina Mawla in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 66 of 1993. In the case reported in 42 DLR (AD) 189, a case on the right of pre-emption, this Division quoted with approval the following observation of Hamnodur Rahman J in the case of Ocean Industries Ltd. vs. Industrial Development Bank 18 DLR (SC) 354 which runs as follows : "To establish the case of waiver or estoppel it was necessary to clearly show that the party alleged to have waived its right had acted in such a manner as to lead the other side to. believe that such rights will not be enforced or will be kept in suspense or abeyance for some particular time. The "gist of the equity" as observed by Viscount Simonds in the case of Tool Metal Co. vs. Tungsten Electric Co., "lies in the fact that one party has by his conduct led the other to alter his position". Yet he cautioned that he would not have it supposed that in "commercial transaction mere acts of indulgence are apt to create rights. A mere gratuitous indulgence shown by not enforcing strictly one's legal rights for a brief period cannot, in our view, give rise to the inference that the rights have been abandoned for all times". 8. In the case reported in AIR 1984 (SC) 921 it was held that the principle of estoppel was not applicable if a voting process was not authorised by any law or Rule. Thus we are of the opinion that acceptance of pensionary benefits in the facts and circumstances of the present case cannot be accepted as estoppel within the meaning of section 115 of the Evidence Act. 9. In this connection reference may be made to the case of Bangladesh Parjatan Corporation vs. MiJfizur Rahman 46 DLR (AD) 46, wherein this Division discussed the principles of estoppel and acquiescence. ATM Afzal J (as his Lordship then was) after referring to the decisions of the Judicial Committee in the case of Sarat Chunder Dy. vs. Gopal Chunder Laha, Indian Appeals (1891-92) Vol. XIX, page 203 and the case of Ambur Nair vs. Kelu Nair, AIR 1933 (PC) 167 observed as follows "Having induced the Appellants to permit him to retire, the Respondent cannot be heard to say that the appellants had no power to relieve him from service. Even if the action of the appellants was not strictly sanctioned by law, the respondent was not the person to make any grievance of it, because he wanted a beneficial order in his favour and the appellants had only obliged him." 10. In that case the respondent who was an Officer of the Bangladesh Parjatan Corporation joined as a Director in the Directorate of Relief and Rehabilitation keeping lien of his service in the Corporation and after returning to the Corporation oh the expiry of his service in the Directorate of Relief and Rehabilitation he filed an application : praying for retirement from service which was ultimately allowed releasing him from service with all financial benefits; but after keeping quiet for more than a year the respondent challenged the order of his premature retirement and it was held by this Division that the respondent had acquiesced in the order of retirement and he was estopped from challenging the same, as the order of retirement was passed on his prayer. The present case before us is just the reverse. In the result, the appeal is allowed with costs. End.

lawyer:
Abdul Kuddus Mia, Advocate-----For the Petitioner Nos.1-4 
Abdus Salam Khan, Advocate------For Co-Petitioner No.5. 
Abdul Mannan Khan, with Abdul Mannan Bhuiyan, Advocates------For the opposite Party.
parties:
Mustafa Kamal Bhuiyan and others ----- Petitioner
Vs
Lutfunnahar Begum and 67 others ----- Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
This Rule arising out of an application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure is directed against the judgment and decree dated 22-2-93 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Third Court, Comilla (in-Charge) in Title Appeal No. 261 of 1990 allowing the said appeal and sending the suit back on remand to the trial Court for fresh decision on setting aside the judgment and decree dated 30-7-90 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Second Court, Comilla in Partition Suit No. 113 of 1982 dismissing the suit.

2. The short facts leading to the issuance of this Rule is set out below: The opposite party No. 1 as plaintiff instituted a suit No. 113 of 1982 in the Second Court of Subordinate Judge at Comilla for partition of the land of schedule 1 and 1(ka) and also the land of schedule Second, Third and Fourth-(ka) out of schedule 1 and 1(ka) and for a saham in the Fourth (ka) schedule land measuring 1.10 acres which was gifted by her husband, defendant No.10 by a registered Heba-bil-Ewaz deed dated 20-5-1982.

Aftabuddin, the father-in-law of the plaintiff out of his fund and interest purchased 2.27 acres of land in the benami of his father Abdul Gani Bhuiyan. Aftabuddin inherited 0.13 acres of land by way of inheritance from his father and thus became the owner of 2.40 acres of land, in schedule 1 and 0.225/11 acres in schedule 1 (ka) in all 2.625/11 acres of land in both schedule 1 and 1(ka). Aftabuddin died leaving behind wife Anwarernessa, two sons defendant Nos. 9 and 10 and daughter defendant No. 11. Thereafter Anwarernessa died leaving behind two sons defendant Nos. 9 and 10 and daughter defendant No. 11. The defendant No. 10 inherited 1.5921/55 acres of land from his father Aftabuddin and mother Anwarernessa. Defendant No.1O gifted 1.10 acres of land by way of registered Heba-bil-Ewaz deed dated 20-5-82 in favour of the plaintiff. The suit property having been in ejmaJi possession of the co-sharers, the plaintiff faced inconvenience in ejmali possession and her demand for amicable partition having been refused thus suit for partition had been filed by her.

3. The defendant Nos. 1-3 contested the suit by filing joint written statement. The defendant Nos. 12 and 40 also contested the suit by filing another set of written statement. In both the sets of written statement, the defendants denied all the material allegations made in the plaint and stated that Abdul Gani Bhuiyan had not been the benamder of his son Aftabuddin and he purchased 2.27 acres of land out of his fund and own interest. Claim of the plaintiff of the defendant No. 10's inheriting 1.59-21/55 acres of land from his father and mother is absolutely false. Defendant also described the Hcba-bill-Ewaz deed in favour of the plaintiff as fraudulent transaction and asserted that the plaintiff did not acquire any right, title and possession over the said gifted land.

4. The defendant Nos. 9, 10 and 11 prayed for a Shaham of their respective shares.

5. The learned Trial Judge dismissed the suit on contest against defendant Nos. 1-3 and 12-14 and ex parte against other defendants in holding that the plaintiff signally failed to prove her case of benami transaction and the suit is bad on the point of hotchpotch.

6. The appeal preferred by the plaintiff was heard by the learned Additional District Judge, Third Court, Comilla (in-Charge) who allowed the appeal, set aside the judgment and decree passed by the learned Subordinate Judge and sent the suit back on remand to the trial Court for a fresh decision.

7. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid judgment of remand the defendant Nos. 1-3 and 14 carried a Civil Revisional application to this Court under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained this present Rule.

8. The plaintiff-opposite-party opposes the Rule by filing an affidavit-in-opposition.

9. The opposite-party No.10 who was defendant No.12 in the suit was transposed as co-petitioner No.5 in the Rule by this Court's order dated 21-8-96.

10. Mr. Abdus Salam Khan, the learned Advocate for the transposed co-petitioner No. 5 appearing in support of the Rule contended that the order of remand passed by the lower appellate Court is not well founded on law and the same suffers from gross illegality. The learned Advocate placed before me the provisions contained in order 41 rule 23, 24 and 25 and also section 107 of the Code of Civil Procedure and argued that the order of remand is neither covered nor sanctioned by the provisions of Order 41 rule 23 and 25 read with section 107 of the Code of Civil Procedure. In advancing his argument the learned Advocate further contended that the whole evidence and materials were before the lower appellate Court and it having got all the powers of a trial Court could dispose of the appeal itself instead of remanding the suit back to the trial Court and caused unnecessary harassment to both the parties and the lower appellate Court thus shirked its responsibility.

11. Mr. Abdul Quddus Mia the learned Advocate for the petitioner Nos. 1-4 adapted the arguments advanced by Mr. Abdus Salam Khan, the learned Advocate for the transposed co-petitioner No. 5.

12. Mr. Abdul Mannan Khan, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff-opposite-party on the other hand submitted that though the order of remand is not sanctioned by the provisions contained in Order 41 rule 23 and 25 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the court for the ends of justice can take resort to its inherent power under section 151 of the Code and in the exercise of its inherent power the appellate Court was quite within its competence and jurisdiction to pass any order which it felt necessary and the lower appellate Court exercised that power and, as such, the order of remand does not warrant any interference by this Court in Revisional jurisdiction under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

13. Perused the Revisional application, Affidavit-in-opposition filed by the plaintiff-opposite-party, judgments of the courts below and also considered the submissions advanced from both the sides.

14.To appreciate the question involved in this Rule the provisions of Order 41 rule 23, 24 and 25 and section 107 of the Code of Civil Procedure which deal with the remand of a case by the appellate Court may be extracted here:

"23. Where the Court from whose decree an appeal is preferred has disposed of the suit upon a preliminary point and the decree is reversed in appeal, the Appellate Court may, if it thinks fit, by order remand the case, and may further direct what issue or issues shall be tried in the case so remanded, and shall send a copy of its judgment and order to the Court from whose decree the appeal is preferred, with directions to re-admit the suit under its original number in the register of civil suits, and proceed to determine the suit; and the evidence (if any) recorded during the original trial shall, subject to all just exceptions, be evidence during the trial after remand.

24. Where the evidence upon the record is sufficient to enable the Appellate Court to pronounce judgment, the Appellate Court may, after resettling the issues, if necessary, finally determine the suit, notwithstanding that the judgment of the Court from whose decree the appeal is preferred has proceeded wholly upon some ground other than that on which the Appellate Court proceeds.

25. Where the Court from whose decree the appeal is preferred has omitted to frame or try any issue, or to determine any question of fact, which appears to the Appellate Court essential to the right decision of the suit upon the merits, the Appellate Court may, if necessary, frame issues, and refer the same for trial to the Court from whose decree the appeal is preferred, and in such case shall direct -such Court to take the additional evidence required;"

Section 107 of the Code runs as follows:

"107.-(1) Subject to such conditions and limitations as may be prescribed, an Appellate Court shall have power-

(a) to determine a case finally; (b) to remand a case;

(c) to frame issues and refer them for trial:

(d) to take additional evidence or to require such evidence to be taken.

(2) Subject as aforesaid, the appellate Court shall have the same powers and shall perform as nearly as may be the same duties as are conferred and imposed by this Code on Courts of original jurisdiction in respect of suits instituted therein".

15. From a plain reading of the above staed Provisions of law it clear that under Order 41 rule 23 of the Code there can be no remand unless the following conditions exist:

(a) that the entire suit and not a portion of it has been disposed of by the trial Court.

(b) that the disposal must be on a preliminary point.

(c) and that the preliminary point on which the suit is decided has been reversed by the appellate Court.

16. Order 41 rule 24 of the Code enjoins that where the evidences on record are sufficient the appellate Court is competent to determine the suit finally and there is no need for remand.

17. Order 41 rule 25 of the Code lays down that only specific issues can be sent to the trial Court for findings and not for re-trial of the entire suit and the appeal is to be heard under Order 41 rules 26 of the Code.

18. Under section 107 of the Code the appellate Court is vested with the power to determine a case finally and also to remand case. Sub-section 2 of section 107 of the Code lays down that the appellate Court shall have the same powers and shall perform as nearly as may be the same duties as are conferred and imposed by this Code on Courts of original jurisdiction in respect of suits instituted therein.

19. The question now falls for determination is whether the lower appellate Court was justified in remanding the suit to the trial Court for fresh decision. Record of the suit was called for by this Court at the time of issuance of the Rule. The lower appellate Court in remanding the suit to the trial Court observed that though the original title deeds of the benami transaction matter had been filed by the defendant Nos. 9-11, the plaintiff at least was required to file the certified copies of those title deeds. On perusal of the record it appears that the title deeds of the benami transaction had been filed by the defendant No. 10 and those two documents were of the year 1914 and 1917 i.e. 30 years old documents. The said two documents were exhibited as Exhibit Nos. D(1) and D(3). The defendant No. 10 is no other than the son of Aftabuddin and husband of the plaintiff and it is the positive case of the plaintiff that her husband defendant No. 10 gifted the divisible 1.10 acres of land to her by registered Heba-bil-Ewaz deed and it was natural that the custody of those two documents would be with the defendant No. 10. The said two documents were filed in the court from the custody of defendant No. 10. Thus it appears that the lower appellate Court misdirected itself in its approach on the question of non-filing of the certified copies of the deeds of benami transaction and the order remanding the suit to trial Court for a decision on this point suffers from a gross error of law.

20. The lower appellate Court found fault with the trial Court in not framing any issue on the question of benami character of the said two deeds. The appellate Court found that the plaintiff did not pray for a declaration of title of the benami character of the kabala deeds. The plaintiff though filed an application for amendment of the plaint in the appellate Court seeking the relief of declaration of title of benami character of the said two deeds the appellate Court did not decide the amendment matter and left the matter for decision by the trial Court. The plaintiff suit being a suit for partition, the question of benami character of the two deeds could be gone into and well decided by the appellate Court and a separate relief of declaration of title on the question of benami character of the deeds was not required and even if there was an application filed by the painful-petitioner for amendment of the plaint incorporating the relief of declaration of title and that application also could be disposed of by the appellate Court and appellate Court was quite competent enough to dispose of the said amendment matter. The order of remand passed by the appellate Court on this score is also unwarranted.

21. The lower appellate Court had every right to accept or reject the findings of the trial Court and come to its own finding on the basis of the evidence and materials on record. Under the provisions of section 107 of the Code, the appellate Court having got all the powers of a trial Court was competent enough to dispose of the suit finally but instead of doing so the appellate Court remanded the suit for fresh decision. Having gone through the judgments I can't help feeling that the appellate Court shirked its responsibility in not deciding the suit when the evidences on record were sufficient to enable it to determine the suit finally. Order 41 rule 24 of the Code is a clear and standing bar in cases like the present one before me.

22. The appellate Court directed the trial Court to consider the question of hotchpotch. This question also could be decided by the appellate Court and for that reason there was no necessity for sending the suit back on remand to the trial Court.

<u>23. Now let me consider the contention contended by the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-opposite-party that to secure the ends of justice the court in the exercise of the inherent power under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure was within its competence to pass an order of remand. The learned Advocate in support of his contention could not cite any authority. It is true that the order of remand can be passed by the appellate Court when it is clearly apparent that the appellate Court cannot itself dispose of the suit taking resort to the specific provisions contained in Order 41 rule 23, 24 and 25 of the Code. The inherent power is the last reserve in the hands of the Code and cannot be used to remand the case unless there is some violence to the sense of justice which cannot be remedied otherwise than by an order of remand. Reference may be made in this connection to a Full Bench decision of the Calcutta High Court decided in the case of Gaznabi vs. Allahabad Bank Limited reported in 21 CWN 877 (FB) and also to a Single Bench decision by Ibrahim J (his Lordship there was) in the case of Abdur Rashid vs. Sm Joydharenhessa and others reported in 6 DLR 33.</u>

24. On perusal of the record of the case it appears that in this instant case all the evidences and materials were before the lower appellate court and the lower appellate Court itself could have disposed of the appeal finally. My considered view is that this is not a case where the court could exercise inherent power under section 151 of the Code in remanding the suit to the trial Court for fresh decision. The contention of the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-opposite-party is without any substance and the same thus fails.

<u>25. It is settled principles of law that unnecessary order of remand entails hardship, agony of fresh hearing and additional expenditure and the same is to be deprecated and discouraged as it tends to delay the administration of justice far from advancing its course.</u>

26. The Pakistan Supreme Court and the Appellate Division of our Supreme Court decided the question of the order of remand in a good number of cases notable among others are the cases of Pramotha Nath Chowdhury and seventeen others vs. Kamir Mondal and others reported in 17 DLR (SC) 392, Probodh Ranjan Shome vs. Md. Easinreported in 1980 BSCR 457, Abdul Awal Khan vs. Md. Sadu Mia and others reported in 1986 BLD (AD) 156 and Abdul Mannan and others vs. Akram Ali and others reported in 43 DLR (AD) 125.

27. The Supreme Court of Pakistan in the case of Pramotha Nath Chowdhury and seventeen others vs. Kamir Mandal and others 17 DLR (SC) 392 held:

"a remand cannot be likely ordered if the evidences on record is sufficient for the appellate Court to decide the question itself. There can be no bar to the court doing so."

28. The Appellate Division in the case of Probodh Ranjan Shome vs. Md. Easin 1980 BSCR 457 observed that:

"It is well-settled that remand orders are not to be made as a matter of course. When there is sufficient evidence on record, remand of a case to the trial Court for fresh hearing is not called for."

29. In the case of Dr. Razia Khatun vs. Banu Guha and another 1986 BW (AD) 156 it was observed by the Appellate Division:

"The long line of judicial decisions is to the effect that the remand order should be avoided as far as possible and even the Privy Council in some cases observed that indiscriminate order of remand tantamounts to shirking the responsibility."

30. In the case of Abdul Awal Khan vs. Md. Sadu Mia and others reported in 1986 BLD (AD) 156 the Appellate Division held:

"when evidences on all materials points are there on record, the revisional court is not justified in sending the case back to the court below for reconsidering the matter".

<u>31. In the case of Abdul Mannan and others vs. Akram Ali and others 43 DLR (AD) 124 it was held by the Appellate Division:</u>

<u>"both oral and documentary evidence having been available on record there was no necessity for the remand as ordered by the High Court Division".</u>

32. In view of the discussions made above and the preponderant judicial views emerging out of the authorities referred to above I am of this view that the lower appellate Court was fully competent to decide the case by itself as the evidence and other materials on record were sufficient to enable it to come to a final decision without entailing the parties unnecessary trouble and expenses and the appellate court shirked its responsibility and thus committed an error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning a failure of justice in remanding the suit to the trial Court for fresh decision. I am further of this opinion that the ends of justice will be met if the matter is remitted to the appellate Court below for final disposal of the matter.

33. In the result, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to costs. The impugned judgment and order dated 22-2-1993 passed in Title Appeal No. 261 of 1990 is hereby set aside and the case is sent back on remand to the lower appellate Court [or disposal of the same touching all points. The appellate Court is also directed to dispose of the appeal preferably within 3(Three) months from the date of the receipt of the record.

34. Stay granted by this Court stands vacated. Send down the LC Records at once.

End.

lawyer:
Kazi Shahadat Hossain, Advocate ------ For the Petitioner. 
Mahmudul Islam, Advocate ------ For the Opposite Parties
parties:
Syed Monirul Huda Chowdhury ------ Petitioner
vs
Fouzia Chowdhury and others ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment: Abu Sayeed Ahammed J: The defendants are revisionist. Fray is among the collateral relations of the same family. We are called upon to consider whether in a suit for ejectment of licencees, a prayer for declaration of plaintiffs title in the suit holding can be allowed by amending the plaint under Order 6 rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure which has been worded as follows; "The Court may at any stage of the proceedings allow either party to alter or amend his pleadings in such manner and on such terms as may be just and all such amendments shall be as may be necessary for the purpose of determining the real question in controversy between the parties." Subordinate Judge, 4th Court, Dhaka allowed the amendment by its impugned order dated 1.9.93 permitting the defendants to file additional written statement if any, in Title Suit 56 of 1993, filed by the opposite parties 1-4. Plaintiffs had obtained an ex parte decree in the said suit for ejectment of the petitioners as licencees, since they failed to file written statements. On an application under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure after setting aside the ex parte decree, the suit was restored. Thereafter, on filing a written statement the defendants denied plaintiffs' title and claimed their own title in the suit holding. In this backdrop, plaintiffs filed application under Order 6 rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure to amend the plaint to add the prayer for declaration of their title in the suit holding prefacing the earlier prayer for ejectment of the defendants as licencecs. 2. Mr. Kazi Shahadat Hossain the learned Counsel representing the petitioner focuses his arguments that the amendment has changed the nature and character of the suit, it has brought a new cause of action and it has caused prejudice to the defendants. Mr. Hossain, relied on the decision in the case of Radha Krishna vs. Dwarka Das, 36 DLR (AD) 253. 3. Mr. Mahmudul Islam, the learned Counsel appearing on behalf of the opposite parties, advanced his arguments that since the defendants denied the plaintiffs title in the suit property the amendment of the plaint with an additional prayer for declaration of title of the plaintiffs became very pertinent, it has not at all changed the nature and character of the suit, it will help the parties to avoid multiplicity of litigations, there is no scope for cropping up of a new cause of action. He further submits that since the trial Court permitted to file additional written statement if any, the defendants have not been prejudiced. 4. Mr. Islam also relied on the decision of 36 DLR (AD) 253. In that case originally suit was filed for declaration of rights and accounts by a partner of a partnership business and subsequently amendment was prayed for dissolution of the farm as well. High Court Division disallowed, Appellate Division allowed, holding, inter alia, that amendment of plaint should be allowed when it is necessary to avoid multiplicity of proceedings, hardships to the parties and for complete adjudication of the dispute and determination of the real question in controversy. 5. Mr. Islam also cited the decision in the case of Ma Shwe Mya vs. Maung Mo Hsaung AIR 1922 (PC) 249. In that case in a suit for Specific Performance of Contract on the basis of oral agreement, amendment was sought for claiming damages for breach of contract. Their Lordships of the Privy Council held as under:- "All rules of court are nothing but provisions intended to secure the proper administration of justice, and it is therefore essential that they should be made to serve and be subordinate to that purpose, so that full powers of amendment must be enjoyed and should always be liberally exercised, but nonetheless no power has yet been given to enable one distinct cause of action to be substituted for another, nor to change by means of amendment of the subject matter of the suit." 6. Mr. Islam lastly cited the case of Managing Committee NMC Model High School and others vs. Obaidur Rahman Chowdhury and others 31 DLR (AD) 133. In that case in a suit for permanent injunction, at a later stage amendment was sought for declaration of title and recovery of possession. Their Lordships held as under: "It is now well-settled that the amendment of the pleadings could be allowed at any stage of the proceeding for the purpose of determining the real question of controversy between the parties, but it could not be allowed if it changed the nature and character of the suit, or if the prayer for amendment had become barred by lapse of time and a right had accrued to the other side. But the latter principle can be departed, if there are circumstances which outweigh the hardship and cause of prejudice to the appellant." 7. In the case of Keramat Ali vs. Mohammed Yunus Hazi, 15 DLR (SC) 120 in pars 28 it has been held: "The Judicial Committee of the Privy Council consistently maintained that it had undoubtedly full power to allow such amendment even where a legal right had accrued by lapse of time if the special circumstances of the case outweighed such consideration." 8. We have coddled and meticulously checked up the revision petition, the impugned order, counter affidavit of the parties and heard the learned Counsels of both parties at a reasonable length. We have carefully consulted the following decisions in making this judgment. Charan Das vs. Amir Khan AIR 1921 (PC) 50; Radha Krishna vs. Dwarka Das 36 DLR (AD) 253; Kashi Nath Das vs. Sadasbiv Pat Naik 209 11,R (Cal) 805; EKS Chetyar Firm vs. Mating Min AIR 1933 (Rang) 247; Ma Shoe Mya vs. Maung Mo Hsaung AIR 1922 (PC) 249; Gotam Hafiz Mia vs. Khadam Ali Alia 29 DLR (SC) 311; Keramat Ali vs. Md. Yunus Hazi 15 DLR (SC) 120; Md. Zahoor Ali Khan vs. Mst. Thakoorune 11 MPR 468; Abdul Razzak vs. Nashuruddin Ahamed 63 CWN-766; Nurun Nahar vs. Md. Fazio, Rahman 1979 BSCR 135; Managing Committee vs. Obaidur Rahman Chowdhury 31 DLR (AD) 133; Kanda and others vs. Waghu AIR 1950 (PC) 68. 9. In the instant case we do not find that the plaintiff tried to bring any new averments in the plaint about the subject matter by way of amendment or to substitute one cause of action for another, nor the amendment as proposed invites any new cause of action. Nevertheless, in a suit for ejectment of licencees the prayer for declaration of plaintiffs’ title is rather necessary to constitute the suit in a complete legal form and for final adjudication of the matter in dispute. 10. We hold that obviously the amendment is required to avoid multiplicity of litigation between the parties and it shall not prejudice the defendants in any way as the trial Court permitted the defendants to file additional written statements, if any. In our view the amendment in the instant case does not change the nature and character of the suit which must refer to the foundation on which a suit is based and not the prayer in the plaint that determines its fundamental character. The amendment in question is merely an additional relief for re-arrangement of the facts in the plaint to their proper perspective and necessary for appropriate relief. The impugned order is not explicit but it is impliedly very clear and in accordance with law. 11. In the aforesaid premises the arguments of Mr. Kazi Shahadat Hossain does not inspire any confidence in us and are struck down. On the contrary the arguments of Mr. Islam having legal force are accepted. The revision is thus devoid of any merit. The result, therefore, is that the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs. End.

caseno: Appeal from Original Order No. 247 of 1995 with Civil Rule No. 387 (FM) of 1995.
lawyer:
Joynal Abedin, Advocate -----For the Appellant. 
Md. Amirul Islam with Tania Amir, Advocates ----- For the Respondent No.1.
parties:
Sarhind Garments Ltd ----- Appellant
Vs
Glory Truth Industries Ltd and another ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
Syed Amirul Islam J: This First Miscellaneous Appeal at the instance of the plaintiff appellant is directed against the Judgment and order dated 28-11-1995 passed by the 5th Subordinate Judge, Dhaka. in Title Suit No. 143 of 1995 refusing to grant an order of temporary injunction restraining the defendant respondent Nos. 1 and 2 from demanding payment and paying the amount as contemplated in the back to back LC No. 01-00281-95 dated 9-3-1995.

2. The plaintiff appellant is a private limited company incorporation under the Companies Act, 1994. The defendant respondent No. 1 is also a private limited company incorporated in Hong Kong.

3. The defendant respondent No. 1 opened an irrevocable Master Letter of Credit (LC) FKB 950138 dated 14-2-95 through Hong Kong and Shanghai Banking Corporation Ltd. Hong Kong in favour of the plaintiff for supply of 54,000 pieces of Men's 100% Cotton Woven Sports Shirt to Walmart Stores Inc. USA for US Dollar 358020.00. In terms of the said Master LC the plaintiff-appellant was required to make shipment of the said finished garments between 31st March and 15th April, 1995. The defendant respondent No. 1 opened the said Master LC in favour of the plaintiff-appellant on 14-2-1995 on condition that the plaintiff-appellant would buy fabrics and accessories from the defendant-respondent No. 1 by opening back to back LC and accordingly, the plaintiff-appellant on receipt of the said Master LC had drawn back to back LC. No. 01-00281-95 dated 9-3-1995 through their bank namely, National Bank Limited i.e. defendant-respondent No. 2 of the instant appeal for importing fabrics and accessories of US Dollar 2,47,316.48 equivalent to Taka 99,68,239.10 as per proforma Invoice Nos. P-032/94 P-038/94 and P-0041/94 of the defendant respondent No. 1. After the said back to back LC dated 9-3-1995 was opened by the plaintiff appellant in favour of the defendant-respondent No. 1 for supply of fabrics and accessories the defendant-respondent No. 1 over telephone and by a letter dated 10-3-1995 requested the plaintiff-appellant to take delivery of fabrics and accessories already sent by them on account of their party in Bangladesh under bill of lading dated 16-1-1995 by fraudulent representation that the said consignments of fabrics and accessories were in order and would conform to the contract specifications mentioned in the aforesaid back to back LC, knowing fully well that the said consignments were defective and accordingly, these were rejected by the third party. The plaintiff appellant relying on such assurances and representations agreed to take delivery of the same from the port by paying necessary customs and port duties. Since the said consignments of fabrics and accessories were sent to a third party by the defendant respondent No. 1 it took a long time for the plaintiff appellant to clear the said consignments from the port. The plaintiff appellant ultimately succeeded in taking delivery of the said consignments in the first part of April, 1995 and the plaintiff-appellant received the consignments at its factory premises on 12-4-1995. Before the said consignments were cleared from the port and received at the factory premises the defendant respondent No. 1 by fax dated 11-3-1995 gave an undertaking to the plaintiff appellant that if the said consignments of the fabrics and accessories were found to be bad or defective the defendant respondent No. 1 would remain responsible and liable for the same. The plaintiff-appellant immediately after arrival of the said consignments at the factory premises vide their letter dated 12-4-1995 informed the local agent of the defendant respondent No. 1 that inspection of the said consignments will be held immediately and requested their local agent namely, M/S Rasel International to send their representative at the time of inspection and the inspection of the said consignments was done on 14-4-1995 and it was found that the goods were defective because of colour shading, weaving defects in every yard of the fabric and also cut pieces and it is asserted that this inspection took place in presence of one Mr. Pooni who is said to be representative of Walmart in Bangladesh. The representative of M/S Rasel International was also present. After the said inspection the defendant respondent No. 1 was duly informed of the said defects in the fabrics both by the local agent of the defendant respondent No. 1 as well as the plaintiff appellant. The plaintiff appellant by a letter dated 18-4-1995 while informing about the defective fabrics also requested the defendant respondent No. 1 to accept the finished garments made with the defective fabrics by extending the period of shipment by amending the Master LC. The local agent of the defendant respondent No. 1 also assured the plaintiff appellant by fax dated 15-4-1995 and 11-5-1995 that the defendant-respondent No. 1 would arrange for resale of the said fabrics to some other party so that the plaintiff appellant do notsuffer any loss. Ultimately, they did nothing in that respect. The further case of the plaintiff appellant is that in this background of the matter, the plaintiff appellant carried out another inspection of the said fabrics by SGS (Bangladesh) Ltd. and obtained a report dated 4-7-1995 which also revealed that the said fabrics were defective because of the colour shading and cut pieces.
