<u>9. Now let us examine the relevant laws in view of the conflicting submissions made by the learned Advocates for the plaintiff appellant and the defendant respondent No. 1 in the instant case. It is asserted by Mrs. Tania Amir that the suit itself is not maintainable under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act inasmuch as the LC in question is neither property as contemplated in section 42 of the Specific Relief Act nor the opening of the LC in question by the plaintiff appellant in favour of the defendant respondent No. 1 has conferred a legal character on the plaintiff appellant and in that view of the matter the plaint is liable to be rejected in limineunder Order 7 rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure. It has been decided in the case reported in 26 DLR 10, that while disposing of an interlocutory matter the court is competent to enter into the question of maintainability of the suit and adjudicate upon that point but later on a Division Bench of this Court has deprecated that practice and observed that in an interlocutory matter the court should not enter into the merits of the case and decide the question of maintainability of the suit. In that view of the matter we propose not to give any opinion on this question because we are of the opinion that without adverting to that question we can effectively dispose of the appeal. Similarly, the learned Advocate drew our attention to the provisions of Order 39 rule 1(a) and (b) and urged before us that the instant application for injunction does not come within the ambit of Order 39 rules 1 and 2. It is now well settled that in an appropriate case even if an application for injunction does not come within the ambit of Order 39 rules 1 and 2, the court in the interest of justice can invoke inherent jurisdiction and grant an injunction under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure. If any authority for that proposition of law is required we may refer to the case reported in 35 DLR (AD) 42 and in that view of the matter we also propose not to enter into the controversy as to whether in the instant case the application for temporary injunction satisfies the requirements of Order 39 rules 1 and 2. We may keep it out of our consideration and dispose of the matter on merits.</u>

10. It is now well settled that be it under Order 39 rules 1 and 2 or under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure, an applicant for temporary injunction must satisfy the court that he has good prima facie arguable case for injunction. Of course, apart from that, in order to obtain an order of temporary injunction there are two other important requirements, namely, the balance of convenience and inconvenience and the question of irreparable loss that may be sustained by the applicant in the case of non-granting of temporary injunction. The above principles governing temporary injunctions have been well settled in the case of Uttara Bank vs. Macneil and Kilburn Ltd. and observed as follows:

Injunctions are granted when the court is satisfied (1) that the applicant has a prima facie case to go to trial; (2) that protection is necessary from irreparable injury before his legal right can be established; (3) the mischief or inconvenience likely to arise from withholding injunction will be greater than which is likely to arise from granting it. It is well settled that there can be no injunction for actionable wrongs for which damages are proper remedy.

In the case of SR Gupta & Co. vs. Sadananda Ghose and others reported in 11 DLR 370, it has been observed in more detail by their Lordships as follows:

"In the case of a temporary injunction (a) an applicant must show a fair prima facie case in support of the right claimed (b) an actual or threatened violation of the right (c ) productive of irreparable or at least serious damage (d) his conduct must be such as not to disentitle him to assistance but it should be fair and honest and in particular there must be no acquiescence or delay, (3) there must be a greater convenience in granting than refusing the injunction and (d) equally efficacious relief must not be obtainable by other usual mode or proceeding.

11. The meaning of prima facie case in relation to an application for temporary injunction has been spelt out in the case of Miah Mohammad Latif vs. Province of West Pakistan, reported in 22 DLR (SC) 98, wherein it has been observed:

"In a case where temporary injunction is claimed, the plaintiff has only to make out that he has a good prima facie case, meaning thereby that an important question of law is to be tried in the suit and that in the event of success if the injunction is not issued he will suffer irreparable injury."

<u>12. Mere presence of a prima facie case or arguability thereof will not by itself be a ground for issuing temporary injunction conditions, viz. the existence of a prima facie case, the irreparability of loss and balance of convenience must co-exist before temporary injunction could be allowed in the matter. The applicant must show further that irreparable injury will occur to him if the injunction is not granted. "Irreparable injury" means only that the injury must be one that cannot be adequately compensated for in damages. Loss measurable in terms of money is not irreparable loss. It is also well settled that the balance of convenience rule has no place where the applicant's right is doubtful, or where he can be compensated by damages in money, or where the wrong might have been redressed if the applicant had been sufficiently vigilant.</u>

13. Now let us examine the materials on record and see if the plaintiff appellant in the instant case has been able to make out a prima facie case. In the instant case there is no dispute as to the opening of the Master LC dated 14-2-1995 and back to back LC dated 9-3-1995 and on a perusal of the back to back LC it appears that it has been specifically stipulated in the back to back LC that the alleged claim is subject of UCP 1993 Revision LC publication N 500. It thus appears that the Uniform Customs and Practice for Documentary Credits, 1993 has been incorporated as terms of the said back to back LC and the law with regard to the LC is by now well established. The judicial pronouncements of the superior courts of this sub-continent and the superior courts in the English jurisdiction and American superior courts are of one opinion that, LC although ancillary to an agreement is yet independent of a parent contract between the buyer and the seller. If we examine the nature and character of international trade we find that in an international trade between two parties, in fact, there are 4 contracts. Firstly, the buyer enters into an agreement with the seller which is the parent contract. Secondly, in pursuance of that contract the buyer enters into an agreement with a local bank to open an irrevocable letter of credit in favour of the seller and the LC. is the product of that contract between the buyer and the bank which is known as issuing of originating bank. The third contract is between the seller and his local bank known as correspondent or negotiating bank. By opening the LC the issuing bank enters into a contract with the negotiating bank to make payment under the LC on receipt of the document contemplated in the LC and in the event of any discrepancy in the documents the negotiating bank has no authority whatsoever to receive the payment. Similarly, the negotiating bank also enters into a contract with the seller and undertakes an obligation to make payment to the seller when the necessary documents are presented to it and the seller is not a party to the LC created by the issuing bank nor the buyer has any privity to that agreement. It is an independent agreement between the two banks. Credits, by their nature, are separate transactions from the sales or other contracts on which they may be based and banks are in no way concerned with or bound by such contract, even if any reference whatsoever to such contracts is included in the credit. Consequently, the undertaking of a bank to pay, accept and pay drafts or negotiate and/or to fulfil any other obligation under the credit is not subject to claims or defences by the applicant resulting from relationships with the issuing bank or the beneficiary. A beneficiary can in no case avail himself of the contractual relationships existing between the banks or between the applicant and issuing bank.

14. Now let us see if the plaintiff appellants have been able to make out a prima facie case in support of their contention. The Appellate Division in the Uttara Bank's case reported in 33 DLR (AD) 393; 1981 BLD (AD) 230 considered the nature and character of the obligations created under the LC in connection with international transactions. After considering various decisions of different jurisdictions the Appellate Division observed.

"That the courts are very reluctant to interfere with commercial transactions which have been entered into by the parties in business transactions through performance guarantee or letter of guarantee which are involved in the commercial dealings. The decisions show that the court will not interfere by granting an injunction for performing or discharging the contractual obligations.The only dispute is as to the performance of contract and this dispute can be resolved by taking resort to appropriate actions and the plaintiff if successful would be entitled to damages but certainly not through an order of injunction which would interfere with the normal banking transaction and also the contractual obligation of the bank. The balance of convenience is also against the grant of injunction."

15. In arriving at the aforesaid conclusion their Lordships of the Appellate Division relied on the observation made by the Court of Appeal in the case of Howe Richardson Scale Co. Ltd. vs Polimex Cokop and National Westminster Bank 1978(Lloyd's Law Reports) 166, wherein it has been observed:

"1. The bank was, in principle, in a position not identical with but very similar to the position of a bank which had opened a confirmed irrevocable letter of credit. The obligation of the bank was to perform that which it was required to perform' by the particular contract and that obligation did not depend on the correct resolution of a dispute and as to the sufficiency of performance by the seller to the buyer or the buyer to the seller as the case might be under the contract.

2. It would be quite wrong for the court to interfere with Polimex's apparent right under the guarantee to seek payment from the bank because to do so would involve putting upon the bank an obligation to inquire whether or not there had been timeous performance of the seller's obligation under the sale contract and in accordance with the principles laid down in American Cyanamid vs. Thircon(1975) AC 396 the balance of convenience was against the grant of an injunction."

Their Lordships further relied on the observations make by Lord Justice Roskill who observed.

"Whether the obligation arises under a letter of credit or under a guarantee the obligation of the bank is to perform that which it is required to perform by the particular contract and that obligation does not in the ordinary way depend on the correct resolution of a dispute as to the sufficiency of performance by the seller to the buyer or by the buyer to the seller as the case may be. Under the sale and purchase contract the bank here simply is concerned to see whether the event has happened upon which its obligation to pay has arisen."

Their Lordships also relied on the observations made by Lord Denning MR in the case of Edward Owe n Engineering Ltd. vs Barclays Bank International Ltd. and Umama Bank reported in 1978 Lloyd's Law Reports Vol-1 page 166, wherein it has been observed.

"It is not concerned in the least with the relations between the supplier and the customer nor with the question whether the supplier has performed his contracted obligation or not nor with the question whether the supplier is in default or not. The bank must pay according to its guarantee on demand, if so stipulated, without proof of conditions. The only exception is when there is a clear fraud of which the bank has notice."

Similarly, their Lordships also relied on the observations made by Indian Supreme Court in the case Tarapore and Co. Madras vs. Tractor export, Moscow, reported in AIR 1970 (SC) 891, wheren it has been observed by the Indian Supreme Court that an irrevocable letter of credit has a definite international implication. In that case in pursuance of a contract with a Russian firm for supply of machinery, an Indian firm opened a confirmed irrevocable letter of credit with a bank in favour of the Russian firm. The Indian firm brought a suit alleging that machinery supplied was not upto the contract. In that suit the only substantive relief asked for was that the bank of India and as well as the Russian firm should be restrained from taking any further steps in pursuance of the letter of credit opened by the Indian firm in favour of the Russian firm. A further prayer was made for restraining the Russian firm from enforcing it. The Russian firm opposed those applications but the trial Court granted the temporary injunction asked for. The High Court reversed the decision and the matter was ultimately taken to the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court quoted from Halsbury's Laws of England as under.

"It is often made a condition of a Mercantile contract that the buyer shall pay for the goods by means of a confirmed credit, and it is then the duty of the buyer to procure his bank, known as the issuing or originating bank, to issue an irrevocable credit, in favour of the seller by which the bank undertakes to the seller, either directly or through another bank in the seller's country known as the correspondent or negotiating bank, to accept drafts drawn upon it for the price of the goods, against tender by the seller of the shipping documents. The contractual relationship between the issuing bank and the buyer is defined by the terms of the agreement between them under which the letter opening the credit is issued, and as between the seller and the bank, the issue of the credit duly notified to the seller creates a new contractual nexus and renders the bank directly liable to the seller to pay the purchase price or to accept the bill of exchange upon tender of the documents. The contract thus created between the seller and the bank is separate from, although ancillary to, the original contract between the buyer and the seller, by reason of the bank's undertaking to the seller, which is absolute. Thus, the bank is not entitled to rely upon terms of the contract between the buyer and the seller which might permit the buyer to reject the goods and to refuse payment therefor and, conversely, the buyer is not entitled to an injunction restraining the seller from dealing with the letter of credit if the goods are defective."

It was further observed.

"An irrevocable letter of credit has a definite implication. It is a mechanism of great importance in international trade. Any interference with that mechanism is bound to have serious repercussions on the international trade of this country. Except under very exceptional circumstances, the courts should not interfere with that mechanism.

Credit was given in this case by the plaintiffs appellant and the defendants respondent No. 1 has placed it for encashment of the letter of credit. The bank is only obliged to comply with the demand made by the defendant respondent No.1. The only dispute is as to the performance of contract and this dispute can be resolved by taking resort to appropriate actions and the plaintiff, if successful, would be entitled to damages and in that view of the matter an order of injunction cannot be made which would interfere with the normal banking transaction and also the contractual obligation of the bank.

16. Similar question came up for consideration before a Division Bench of the High Court Division in the Uttara Bank's case which is reported in 40 DLR 70. In that case the High Court Division refused to attach the LC before judgment in a money suit filed by the buyer. In that case it was an admitted fact that the seller had supplied to the buyer the goods as contracted. The only dispute was as to their quality. It has been observed by the Division Bench that in the instant case it is not a matter of commercial transaction between two citizens in a local market where goods are received in one hand and the price is paid by the other hand over the counter completing the transactions. In matters like this which covers two companies in two different countries prices are paid by this kind of LC and once goods are shipped on board the ship as per specification and as per terms and conditions of credit by the seller the sale, so far the seller is concerned, is complete and he is to be paid.

17. In that case it was contended by the plaintiff that the terms of the credit had been violated in that there was a condition in the indent that the seller will provide for installation within 7 days yet nothing was done and some of the machineries were not of Japanese origin but of Taiwan origin so no money could be paid. The Division Bench replied to the same in the following terms:

"There is no substance in it. In such credit system Banks are not concerned with the quality of the goods shipped nor with the non-fulfillment of other conditions of the contract but only with the credit document and fulfillment of its terms. Such as the submission of bill of lading, insurance and other shipping documents, etc. When no fraud appears on the face of it, of which the Bank has no obvious previous knowledge."

It has been further observed.

"Fraud vitiates everything and in most cases it originates when a commercial party contracting with a rogue. But in international documentary credit papers are mostly acted upon in good faith and Banks cannot police it. In fact, banks cannot be made to sit as a policeman to see whether proper goods are shipped and original goods are, in fact, shipped or whether after shipment the boat had not been diverted in midway to another port and real goods are unloaded and fake goods loaded. Acts 3 and 4 of the Uniform Customs clearly negatives this role of the Banks as a policeman or as a court of law deciding disputes arising out of contract between the parties."

In giving those findings their Lordships relied on an observation made by Jenkins, LJ in delivering the judgment in the case of Males and another 1's. British Industries Ltd. reported in 1958 All ER (Court of Appeal) 262. Jenkins, LJ observed."

We were referred to several authorities, and it seems to be plain that the opening of the confirmed letter of credit constitutes a bargain between the banker and the vendor of the goods which imposes on the banker an absolute obligations to pay, irrespective of any dispute which there may be between the parties on the question whether the goods are upto contract or not An elaborate commercial system has been built up on the footing that bankers confirmed credits are of that character, and in any judgments it would be wrong for this court in the present case to interfere with that established practice. It is also to be remembered that vendor of goods selling against a confirmed letter of credit is selling under the assurance that nothing will prevent him from receiving the price. That is no mean advantage when goods manufactured in one country are being sold in another. Similarly, their Lordships also put reliance on another observation made by Lord Diplock in the case of United City Merchants (Investment) Ltd. and others vs. Royal Bank of Canada and others, reported in 1982 (2) All ER 720. Lord Diplock in delivering the judgment for House of Lords observed:

"The First, which we will call the documentary credit point, relates to the mutual rights and obligations of the confirming bank and the beneficiary under a documentary credit. It is of importance to all those engaged in the conduct and financing of International Trade for it is the basic principle of documentary credit operation that banks that are parties to them deal in documents only, not in the goods to which those documents purported to relate."

18. Thus it appears that only in two exceptional circumstances an issuing bank can absolve its responsibility of not honoring the obligation created by it under a letter of credit. Firstly, if it is proved that there is a clear fraud of which it has knowledge the bank may refuse to pay and secondly, if the case is of such a nature that there is very special circumstance which warrants an interference by the court. In the instant case it is submitted by Mr. Joynal Abedin, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff appellant, that they opened the LC in question on 9-3-1995 and asserted that they had no knowledge that the consignment in question had been shipped on 16-1-1995 and it had been lying in the Chittagong port. it is for the first time through a letter of the defendant respondent No. 1 dated 10-3-199 5 they came to learn for the first time that the goods had been shipped on 16-1-1995 and were lying in the Chittagong port and from letter dated 18-5-1995 of the defendant respondent No. 1 it becomes apparent that earlier these materials were shipped to Angel Corporation in Bangladesh and they have refused to accept the goods and those were not upto the mark and thereby it was practised on them by fraudulent misrepresentation and false assurance given by the defendant respondent No. 1 as to the quality and specification of the goods shipped on 16-1-95. As against that the submission of Ms Tania Amir is that it is not correct to say that they had the knowledge about the consignment earlier rather it was brought to their notice long before the opening of Master LC as well as back to back LC. Mr. Larry Ting, the Managing Director of the defendant respondent No.1, was in Dhaka from 3-2-95 to 13-2-1995 and he personally negotiated the matter with the plaintiff appellant and everything was known to them. To substantiate her submission a supplementary counter affidavit was filed wherein certain documents were annexed from which it appears that the plaintiffs were in the know of the affairs before the opening of the back to back LC. An affidavit-in-reply to the supplementary affidavit has been filed by the plaintiff appellant wherein they have asserted that the papers annexed at pages 5, 7, 9 and 11 of the supplementary counter affidavit are spurious and manufactured documents created for the purpose of this case and the same were never sent to them and received by the plaintiff appellant at any point of time and further asserted that they are not aware of the other documents as well. In reply to that Ms. Tania Amir submits that they did not file these documents at the trial Court as the plaintiff appellant did not make out a specific case of fraud. It is only before this court they have made an attempt to bring their case within the ambit of fraud and, as such, to meet their allegation they have annexed these documents. Since the genuineness of these documents have been questioned by the plaintiff appellant and since we can dispose of the matter without relying on these documents we would not like to enter into the controversy as to whether the documents annexed at pages 5, 7, 9 and 11 of the supplementary counter affidavit are genuine or not and, as such, keeping these documents out of out consideration we shall decide the matter on the basis of other materials available on record. Here it may be mentioned that Ms. Tania Amir also submitted that an allegation of fraud must be specifically pleaded and proved but in the instant case the plaintiff did not make out any specific case of fraud either in the plaint or in their application for injunction. She further submitted that the alleged story of defective quality is proved to be false by their own paper namely, the survey report submitted by SG (Bangladesh vide Annexure-G.

19. Before we advert to the necessary materials we would like to discuss the law on the point. There are 4 English decisions which have dealt with the issue of fraud.

Hamzeh Milas and Sons. V British Imex Industries (1958) 92 QBD 127, (2) RD Harbottle  (Mercantle) Ltd. and anr. vs. National Westminster Bank Ltd. (1977)(2) All ER 862. (3) Edward Owen Engineering Lid.vs. Barclays Bank International Ltd (1981) (1) All ER 1976) and (4) CCM (Investment) vs. Royal Bank of lndis (1982(2) All ER 720). The last case is of the House of Lords where Lord Diplock in his speech said (at page 725).

"The whole commercial purpose for which the system of confirmed irrevocable documentary credits has been developed in international trade is to give to the seller an assured right to be paid before he parts with control of the goods and that does not permit of any dispute with the buyer as to the performance of the contract of sale being used as a ground for non-payment or reduction or deferment of payment.

To this general statement of principle as to the contractual obligation of the confirming bank to the seller, there is one established exception, that is, where the seller, for the purpose of drawing on the credit, fraudulently presents to the confirming bank documents that contain, expressly or by implication, material representations of fact that to his knowledge are untrue,. Although there does not appear among the English authorities any case in which this exception has been applied, it is well established in the American cases, of which the leading or landmark case in Sztein Henry Schgoder Banking Corporation (1941) 31 NYS 2d 631. This judgment of the New York Court of Appeals was referred to with approval by the English Court of Appeal in Edward Owen Engineering Ltd. vs. Barclays Bank International Ltd. (1987) 1 All ER 979 QB 159, though this was actually a case about a performance bond under which a bank assumes obligations to buyer analogous to those assumed by a confirming bank to the seller under a documentary credit. The exception of fraud on the part of the beneficiary seeking to avail himself of the credit is a clear application to the maxim exturpicaus a non oritureactio or, if plain English is to be preferred, fraud unravels all. The courts will not allow their process to be used by dishonest person to carry out a fraud.”

<u>20. In Bangladesh there is no statutory law which governs the letters of credit whereas there is statutory law relating to guarantees. However, as is clear from the various Judgments, the same principles of English law were also followed in the subcontinent in connection with the cases relating to irrevocable letters of credit.</u>

21. Trade has crossed national frontiers and now we talk in terms of international trade and one has to consider the services rendered by banks in the matter of providing finance of the international trade and creating an atmosphere in which the international trade transaction can take place and this is done with the machinery of letter of credit. Denning MR has stated in the case of Edward Owen Engineering Ltd. vs. Barclays Bank International Ltd. 1977 (3) WLR 764 as follows:

"That the performance guarantee stands on a similar footing to a letter of credit. A bank which give a performance guarantee must honour that guarantee according to its terms. It is not concerned in the least with the relations between the supplier and customers, nor with the question whether the supplier has performed his contracted obligations or not; nor with the question whether the supplier is in default or not. The bank must pay according to its guarantee, on demand, if so stipulated, without proof or conditions. The only exception is when there is a clear fraud of which the bank has notice."

Kerr, J. in RD Harbottle (Mercantile) Ltd. and another vs. National Westminster Bank Ltd. and others, (1977) 2 AER 862, observed.

"It is only in exceptional cases that the courts will interfere with the machinery of irrevocable obligations assumed by bank. They are the lifeblood of international commerce. Such obligations are regarded as collateral to the underlying rights and obligations between the merchants at either end of the banking chain. Except possibly in clear case of fraud of which the banks have notice, the courts will leave the merchants to settle their disputes under the contracts by litigation or arbitration as available to them or stipulated in the contracts. The courts are not concerned with their difficulties to enforce such claims; these are risks which the merchants take....The machinery and commitments of banks are on a different level. They must be allowed to be honored, free from interference by the courts otherwise trust in international commerce could be irreparably damaged."

In United Commercial Bank vs. Hanuman Synthetics Ltd. and others (1987) 61 Comp. Case. 245 (Cal) the Calcutta High Court followed the above decision of the Supreme Court. The court also held that in order to come within the exception of fraud, it is not enough to allege fraud but the buyer must clearly establish that the documents that were presented by the beneficiary were forged or fraudulent. In this case the buyer agreed to purchase "viscose staple fibre" but the Customs authoritities were of the view that the goods imported were "polyester fibre" and not viscose staple fibre. The buyer wanted to prevent the bank from paying contending that there was a fraud. The court held that this was only an allegation of Customs Department and the fraud has not been established in any way. Hence the bank cannot be prevented.

22. The exception to the strict rule is of very limited scope. In order to come within the exception, it has to be shown (1) the documents were being presented by the beneficiary himself and (ii) the bank knows when the documents are presented that they are forged or fraudulent. The case of Discount Records Ltd. vs. Barclays Bank Ltd. (1975) 1 All ER 1071 was referred to by Browne LJ to illustrate the point that it was not enough to allege fraud, but fraud must be clearly established.

23. In the case of Discount Records Ltd. Mcgarry J refused to grant the prayer of injunction and observed at page 1074 of (1975) 1 All ER that.

"During the argument on this point before me, the familiar English phrase "Fraud unravels all' was lso discussed, However, it is important to notice that in the Sztein's case (1941) 31 NYS 2d 631 the proceedings consisted of a motion to dismiss the formal complaint on the ground that it disclosed no cause of action. That being so the court had to assume that the facts stated in the complaint were true. The complaint alleged fraud, and so the court was dealing with case of established fraud. I should also add that on the facts required to be assumed in Sztein's case (1941) 31 NYS 2d 631, the collecting bank there was not a holder in due course who would not be defeated by the fraud, but was merely an agent for the fraudulent seller."

The court further held that it has to be noted that under Article 9 of the Uniform Customs and Practice for Documentary Credit, the banks do not assume any liability or responsibility, inter alia, for "the description, quality, weight, quantity, condition, packing, delivery, value or existence of the goods represented thereby."

24. Mr. Joynal Abedin relied on Annexure-'I' annexed to the injunction application to bring home the allegation of fraud in the instant case. It appears from Annexure-'I' that the respondent No. 1 originally shipped the goods to Angel group and they refused to accept the goods. As a result they sold goods/fabrics to the plaintiff appellant but this annexure does not disclose that these fabrics and accessories were refused by the Angel Corporation on the ground of defective quality or for non-compliance of the contracted specification. So, from this document prima facie it does not appear that the goods were really refused by the Angel Corporation on the ground that these were sub-standard fabrics and not fit for stitching. If we refer to Annexure-A' which is a letter dated 10-3-1995 written by the defendant respondent No.1 to the plaintiff appellant it appears that there also the defendant respondent No. 1 mentioned that earlier on 16-1-1995 they shipped these goods to Angel Corporation Ltd. and from the contents of this letter it appears that this fact was disclosed to the plaintiff appellant by the seller i.e. the defendant respondent No.1 earlier to 4-3-1995. We are therefore, of the opinion that from this document, which is an undisputed document, it appears that the plaintiff appellant had knowledge long before 9-3-1995 that these goods were shipped to Angel Corporation. These goods originally were shipped to Angel Corporation and on their refusal to accept the same these were offered to the plaintiff appellant and after due conversations and negotiations they have agreed to take these goods and after opening of master LC on 14-2-1995, the plaintiff appellant opened back to back L/C dated 9-3-1995. So the allegation of the plaintiff appellant that the defendant respondent No. 1 defrauded them by misrepresentation as to the quality and specification of the fabrics and accessories appears to be groundless and this submission is not borne out by the materials on record. In this connecting we may profitably quote the observations made by their Lordships in the case reported in 40 DLR 72, in para 51 at page 81 that

"Fraud vitiated everything and in most cases it originates when a commercial party contracting with a rogue. But in international documentary credit papers are mostly acted upon in good faith and banks cannot police it. In fact banks cannot be made to act as a policeman to see whether proper goods are shipped and original goods are in fact shipped or whether after shipment the boat had not been diverted in midway to another port and real goods are unloaded and fake goods loaded. Articles 3 and 4 of the Uniform Customs clearly negatives this role of the banks as a policemen or as a court of law deciding dispute arising out of a contract between the parties."

In the instant case only ground to substantiate the allegation of fraud is that they had no knowledge on 9-3-1995 when they opened the back to back LC. But we have already referred to Annexure-'A' which negatives this contention of the plaintiff appellant. On top of that it appears that their grievance is in effect about the quality of the goods and even if it be so that the goods are not as per specifications as . contemplated in the letter of intent and the concerned LC then also it does not amount to fraud and in fact if the goods are really defective or substandard the plaintiff appellant is at liberty either to reject the goods as not in conformity with the contracted specification or in the alternative can bring an action for damages for supplying defective goods. But in the instant case the plaintiff appellant neither rejected the goods nor brought an action for damages against the defendant respondent No. 1 for reasons best known to them and this circumstances speaks volume, against the plaintiff appellant and, in our opinion, demolish the allegation of fraud. Mr. Joynal Abedin the learned Advocate for the plaintiff appellant, tried to bring his case within the ambit of exception as spelt out in the decision reported in 33 DLR (AD) 298 wherein their Lordships of the Appellate Division quoted an observation of the Indian Supreme Court reported in AIR 1970 (SC) 891, wherein the Indian Supreme Court held that only in exceptional circumstances a court may interfere with the mechanism of LC.

25. Mr. Joynal Abedin submitted that there are some very special circumstances in the instant case such as the respondent No. 1 is a foreign company which has no properties and assets in Bangladesh and in that view of the matter even if the appellants bring an action for damages and get decree, they would not be in a position to execute the same in Bangladesh nor in Hong Kong as Bangladesh has no reciprocal arrangement with Hong Kong. On top of that the ligation may take 18/20 years to reach its finality and after lapse of such period his client will be left with practically no remedy. He also submitted that if no injunction is granted the suit itself will become infructuous. He also asserted that if payment is made Bangladesh will lose hard earned foreign exchange. In reply to his submissions on this point here we may profitably note that the same arguments were advanced before the Indian Supreme Court in the Tarapore's case that the Russian firm has no assets in India and therefore any decree that may be obtained against the Russian firm cannot be executed. Hence they must be restrained from further dealing with the LC which promised to pay and the bank for not honoring it, The Indian Supreme Court repelled the submission and held that.

"The allegation that Russian Firm has no assets in this country was not made in the pleading. That apart in the circumstances of this case that allegation has no relevance. An irrevocable letter of credit has a definite implication in international trade. Any interference with that mechanism is bound to have serious repercussions on the international trade of this country. Except under very exceptional circumstances the courts shall not interfere with that mechanism."

And that observation of the Indian Supreme Court has been approvingly quoted by our Appellate Division in the case reported in 33 DR (AD) 298. The same question also came up for consideration before a Division Bench of this court in the case of Janata Bank. In that case also the same sort of arguments were put forward but the contentions were rejected by the Division Bench of this Division holding that the Janata Bank cannot be restrained by an order of attachment before judgment of that amount from being reimbursed in favour of Bank of Tokyo as guarantee by the LC as that would go against all norms and customs of international banking and also as promised and contracted for by the Janata Bank with the foreign Bank and, in fact, this sort of interference by the court with international commercial contracts would seriously affect our international trade."

<u>26. It is thus crystal clear that no prohibitive order can be passed by courts to interfere with the normal Banking transaction and also the contractual obligation of the Bank when the only dispute is as to the performance of contract and that dispute can be resolved by bringing an appropriate action for damages. We have already found that the appellant have failed to substantiate their allegation of fraud. They have also failed to bring their case within the ambit of "very exceptional" circumstances to warrant an order of injunction. We, therefore, hold that the appellant have failed to make out a prima facie case in support of their prayer for injunction.</u>

27. Now let us advert to second requirement for temporary injunction. i.e. whether the injury or threatened injury would cause irreparable loss to the plaintiff appellant or not. It is crystal clear from the averments made by the plaintiff appellant both in the plaint as well as in the application under Order 30 rules 1 and 2 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure that in facts they have suffered huge loss in terms of money because of defective quality of the imported fabrics and the loss suffered by them is nothing but pecuniary loss which can be compensated by monetary damages. A loss which can be compensated by money payment is not irreparable loss and for such loss or injury injunction cannot be granted. If any authority is required we may refer to the decisions reported in 29 DLR (SC) 86 and 156. In that view of the matter we find that in the instant case the alleged injury that would be suffered by the plaintiff appellant if the payment is made by the defendant respondent No. 2 bank is nothing but a pecuniary loss and that can be compensated by damages. This view finds support from the Uttara Bank case 33 DLR (AD) 298 wherein their Lordships observed that no injunction can be granted for non compliance with the contractual obligation or to interfere with the normal banking transaction. In that view of the matter also we find that in the instant case the plaintiff appellant has failed to show that if no injunction is granted they would suffer any irreparable loss.

<u>28. Now let us see where lies the balance of convenience and inconvenience. We have seen that by opening a LC the issuing Bank undertakes an absolute obligation to make the payment under the LC. The contract thus created between the seller and the bank is an independent contract although ancillary to the contract between the buyer and seller. The issuing bank is under a legal obligation to make payment provided there is no discrepancy in the documents. So long the documents conform to the requirement of the LC issuing bank has no other alternative but to make the payment and the buyer has no privy to that contract. A letter of credit has an autonomy of its own and it need be negotiated without reference to the very contract out of which the credit arises. The LC is independent and never qualified by the original contract of sale or by any underlying transaction or dispute between the buyer and seller. LC is a mechanism of great importance in international trade. Any interference with LC is bound to have serious repercussions on the international trade of country. Therefore, it must be presumed that the convenience is always in favour of the LC.</u>

29. From our aforesaid discussions it appears that the plaintiff appellants have miserably failed to bring their case within the legal requirements for getting an order of injunction in their favour and the trial Court, in our opinion, has rightly refused to grant injunction in the instant case and rejected the application for temporary injunction.

30. In view of our aforesaid discussion we do not find any merits in this appeal which must be dismissed.

<u>31. Tania Amir, the learned Advocate for the defendant respondent No.1, strenuously argued that in the instant case a cost should be awarded against the plaintiff appellant because they have brough this case upto this level on false and flimsy grounds. It should be remembered that this appeal is preferred against an interlocutory order and the main suit is awaiting trial and from our earlier discussion also it is crystal clear thatwe have refrained ourselves from entering into the merits of the case at this stage and in that view of the matter it would not be proper to award any cost in the instant appeal.</u>

<u>32. Tania Amir filed an application on the last day of hearing to direct the defendant respondent No. 2 Bank to make payment under the LC. We have already found the impugned judgment and order to be in accordance with law and we are going to dismiss the appeal and the law will take its own course. Besides, in this case the respondent No. 2 bank is defendant No. 2 in the suit and they have not gone to court praying for any relief. It is the plaintiff appellant who has filed the suit and, as such, there is no scope for us for giving any direction to the respondent No. 2 Bank for making the payment under the LC. We think that it is beyond the scope of the suit. In that view of the matter the application filed by the defendant respondent No. 1 for giving a direction to the defendant respondent No. 2 bank to make payment is rejected.</u>

33. In the result the appeal is dismissed without any order as to cost.

In view of the fact that the appeal is dismissed the connected Rule is also discharged accordingly.

End.

full_judgment: These two Second Appeals being Second Appeal No. 306 of 1976 and Second Appeal No. 307 of 1976 arise out of the same and one judgment dated 20th April, 1976 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Faridpur disposing of the two appeals namely, Title Appeal No. 94 of 1975 and Title Appeal No. 95 of 1975 by reversing the decisions of the trial Court dated 26.4.1975 passed in TS No. 108 of 1974 and TS No. 221 of 1973. 2. Both the appeals have been heard together and, as such, those are being disposed of by the following one judgment. 3. The trial Court decreed both the suits in part but the lower appellate Court decreed the suit of the present plaintiff-respondent in full allowing specific performance of the contract and dismissing the other suit of the present appellant for declaration of title and recovery of possession of the suit land. 4. The present appellant Santosh Kumar Paul as plaintiff instituted Title Suit No. 221 of 1973 for declaration of his title in respect of 0.78 decimals of the suit-land as detailed in the schedule of the plaint against the present respondent who was defendant in the above suit and also for recovery of possession of the same by evicting the said defendant with removal of his huts therefrom. 5. The case of the plaintiff-appellant Santosh Kumar Paul was, that he purchased the suit-land from one Umesh Chandra Saha by two Kabalas dated 12.2.62 and 13.7.62 vide Exts. A. and A (1) respectively and since the time of his purchase, he was in possession of the suit-land by erecting huts in some part and by maintaining a panboraj and garden in the remaining part of the land. His further case was that he was a photographer and the defendant No. 1 Nuruddin Ansari was a disciple (Murid) of the Pirshabeb of Medinipur situated within West Bengal. That defendant No. 1 the present respondent, used to visit the shop of the plaintiff for obtaining photographs in order to procure passport for visiting his Pirshabeb at Medinipur and in this way some intimacy developed between the plaintiff and the defendant and ultimately the plaintiff, the present appellant also became a murid of the said Pirshaheb and thus the plaintiff started to rely on and believe the defendant. 6. During the liberation war of Bangladesh when the Pak Army advanced to Rajbari on 21.7.71 and the Beharis started looting and arson here and there the plaintiff-appellant left his house at Laxmi Kon Village within Rajbari PS and moved here and there at different places for their safety; that in the 1st part of Bhadra, 1377 BS the defendant-respondent had occasion to see him in the rice-patti of Rajbari Bazar when he was asked to meet him as he had a secret talk with him. The plaintiff-appellant believing the defendant-respondent in good faith went to see him at the shop of one Tafazzal Mia of the rice-patti where the defendant respondent asked the plaintiff to put his signature in two blank stamp- papers but the plaintiff-appellant was hesitating when the defendant-respondent drew his attention to a non-Bengali (Behari) who was kept standing thereby. The plaintiff-appellant thereon being afraid put his signatures on the blank papers to save his life, as the non-Bangalees (Beharis) used to kill people at that time. Further case of the plaintiff was that due to the threat of defendant No. 1, the plaintiff-appellant along with the members of his family roamed over different places and after the liberation of Bangladesh, he took shelter in the Sarker's house of Laksmikul Village and therefrom he went to visit the suit-land and found that the defendant i.e. the plaintiff of Suit No. 108 of 1974 the present respondent was residing there by erecting two huts. The plaintiff asked the defendant-respondent to vacate the suit premises but he refused to do so on different pleas and at this the plaintiff-appellant brought the matter to the notice of the local SDO by filing a petition who then referred the same to the Chairman of the Arbitration Council of the locality but the Chairman did not take any step in the matter. The plaintiff was therefore obliged to file the present suit being Title Suit No. 221 of 1973 as stated above. It was further stated in the plaint that it was the apprehension of the plaintiff that the defendant might' create antedated and collusive documents in the blank stamp-papers in which he obtained the signatures of the plaintiff by undue influence and threat. It was further alleged that the plaintiff-appellant did not enter into any contract to sell out his suit-land to the defendant-respondent on receipt of any consideration money and if there was any such document, that must be false, fraudulent, illegal, void and without any consideration, 7. The defendant No. 1 Nuruddin Ansari the present respondent contested the Title Suit of the plaintiff by filing a written statement contending, inter alia, that the suit was not maintainable in the present form and the same was barred by limitation, the principles of estoppel, waiver and acquiescence and it was further contended that the allegations made in the plaint were false and fabricated. 8. The defendant's case was, in short, that the plaintiff appellant being hard pressed for money voluntarily entered into an agreement with the defendant to sell out the suit land to the defendant-respondent for a consideration of Rs. 1201.00 and accordingly, executed a bainapatra on the 16th Paush, 1377 BS corresponding to 1.1.71 vide Ext. B. on receipt of a sum of Rs. 901.00 as earnest money in part payment. The plaintiff-appellant promised to execute and register the kabala deed in favour of the defendant on the basis of the agreement after obtaining income tax-clearance certificate and necessary permission from the competent authority. But as civil disturbance started in the country all on a sudden the plaintiff-appellant could not procure the income tax-clearance certificate and permission and he being pressed for money further approached the defendant-respondent to pay the balance of the consideration money. But as the defendant respondent was not willing to give the entire consideration money without registration of the deed the plaintiff then managed to procure a titled house at the cost and expense of the defendant-respondent and himself took initiative in erecting a tiled hut on the suit-land with the help of some labourers and put the defendant-respondent in actual possession of the same and thus obtained a further sum of money from the defendant. The defendant- respondent later on made some other constructions of his house in the suit-land and started residing therein. He also planted some saplings of fruit- bearing trees there in the homeland. The defendant respondent requested the plaintiff-appellant repeatedly to execute and register the kabala deed in his favour for the suit-land on receipt of remaining sum of money but he (the plaintiff) did not do so on different pretexts and now being ill advised he brought the false and frivolous suit against the defendant-respondent for declaration of his title and recovery of possession in the suit-land which is liable to be dismissed with costs. 9. The defendant-respondent however as plaintiff brought subsequently Title Suit No. 108 of 1974 in the same court in respect of the self same land for specific performance of contract against the present appellant Santosh Kumar Paul i.e. the plaintiff in title Suit No. 221 of 1973. The averments made in the written statement by the defendant No.1 Nuruddin Ansari in Title Suit No. 221 of 1973 were however repeated in the plaint of Title Suit No. 108 of 1974 and the statements made in the plaint of the first suit i.e. Title Suit No. 221 of 1973 were repeated in the written statement filed by the present appellant as defendant in the 2nd suit denying the story of contract vide bainapatra Ext. B for sale of the suitland on receipt of a consideration of Rs. 901.00 in the manner as stated above. 10. Both the suits were heard together by the learned Munsif. The present appellant Santosh Kumar Paul examined himself as PW 1 in his suit and no other witness was examined on his behalf but the present respondent i.e. plaintiff in Title Suit No. 108 of 1974 and defendant in TS No. 221 of 1973 however examined 8 witnesses including himself as DW 1 and other witnesses of the Bainapatra Ext. B and also some labourers who were engaged in the construction of his huts on the suitland at his expense in the presence of and with the co-operation of the present appellant Santosh Kumar Paul. 11. The learned Munsif found that admittedly the suit land belonged to the plaintiff-Santosh Kumar Paul and he used to reside there in some part of the suit land by erecting huts and both the plaintiff and the defendant were very intimate and also disciples or murids of the Pirshaheb of Medinipur. Hence, formulated the following main issues for consideration: 1) Whether the plaintiff Santosh Kumar Paul of Title Suit No. 221 of 1973 entred into an agreement with the defendant i.e. the present respondent Nuruddin Ansari for sale of the suitland and whether he executed the Bainapatra (agreement) on receipt of Rs. 901.00 from the defendant and whether subsequently he received a further sum of Taka 200.00 and put the defendant into possession of the suit-land? 2) To what relief, if any, the plaintiffs of both the suits were entitled? 12. The learned Munsif on consideration of the materials on record decreed both the suits in part by one judgment and observed in the same that Santosh Kumar Paul, the plaintiff of the first suit received Rs. 901.00 from the defendant Nuruddin Ansari and that Santosh Kumar Paul might have contracted to sell out the suit-land to Nuruddin Ansari by executing the bainanama Ext. B. His further observation was the Nuruddin Ansari, the plaintiff of the 2nd suit, was not entitled to get a decree for specific performance of contract, even if the story of the contract was true, in view of the hardships on the part of the defendant Santosh Kumar Paul of the 2nd suit. He therefore decreed the first suit in part with an embargo that the decree could not be executed until and unless the plaintiff Santosh Kumar re-paid Rs. 901.00 to the defendant Nuruddin Ansari. The learned Munsif thus disposed of both the suits by a single judgment dated 26th April, 1975. Being aggrieved by the same the present Respondent Nuruddin Ansari defendant of Title Suit No. 221 of 1973 and plaintiff of TS No. 108 of 1974 preferred 2 Appeals namely, Title Appeal Nos. 94 and 95 of 1976 before the learned District Judge, Faridpur which were transferred to the court of the learned Additional District Judge, Faridpur for hearing and disposal. The learned Additional District Judge heard both the appeals together as because the same arose out of the same single judgment covering both the suits. He formulated only one point for determination as to whether the decision of the learned Munsif was correct? The learned Additional District Judge heard the arguments of both the parties and on consideration of the submissions and the materials on record, came to a finding that the contract i.e. the Bainapatra Ext. B. was genuine and the same was executed by the present appellant Santosh Kumar Paul on receipt of sum of Taka 901.00 from the plaintiff of the 2nd suit who was put into possession of the suitland by the defendant No.1 Santosh Kumar Paul himself i.e. the present appellant and further found on consideration of the evidence on record that it would be unjust to deny a decree for specific performance of contract to the appellant (the plaintiff of the 2nd suit) on the ground of alleged hardship of the respondent (the defendant of the 2nd suit) and he therefore found that the learned Munsif was not justified in denying a decree for specific performance of contract to the plaintiff, the present respondent. Accordingly, he was pleased to allow both the appeals on contest with costs and set aside impugned judgment and decree passed by the learned Munsif and decreed Title Suit No. 108 of 1974 on contest with cost against the contesting defendant (the present appellant) and ex parte against defendant No. 2 and dismissed Title Suit No. 221 of 1973 with cost against the contesting defendant and ex parte against the defendant No. 2. It was further declared that the plaintiff of Title Suit No. 108 of 1974 was entitled to get a kabala executed and registered by Santosh Kumar Paul with respect to the suit land by way of specific performance of contract, on payment of the balance sum of the consideration money of Taka 300.00 to the said defendant Santosh Kumar Paul and the said defendant was directed to execute and register the kabala deed within 30 days from the date of receipt of notice of deposit of the above balance amount of the consideration money in court by the plaintiff (present respondent,) in default, the plaintiff Nuruddin Ansari would be free to get the kabala executed and registered through court and accordingly, passed the judgment on 20.4.76 which was followed by decrees. 13. Being aggrieved by the said judgment and decree passed by the learned Additional District Judge, the plaintiff of the first suit and defendant of the 2nd suit Santosh Kumar Paul preferred the present two Second Appeals being Nos. 306 and 307 of 1976 before this court. It may be mentioned that the present appellant after passing of the judgment in both the suits by the trial Court filed 2 cross-objections before the court of appeal below but for reasons unknown he ultimately did not pursue the same. 14. Mr. Miah Abdul Gafur, the learned Advocate with Mr. NK Saha and Mr. Abbasuddin Ahmed, the learned Advocates appeared for the appellant and Mr. Nurul Hoque with Mr. AKM Shahidul Huq and Mrs. Tania Siddique, Advocates appeared for the respondent. 15. Mr. Md. Abdul Gafur, the learned Advocate for the appellant Santosh Kumar Paul, has firstly taken me through both the impugned judgments of the courts below and thereafter he argues that the impugned judgment of the Court of appeal below are not at all proper judgments of reversal and the learned Additional District Judge without sufficiently adverting to the reasonings of the trial Court reversed the findings and decisions of the said court and held that the Bainanama Ext. B. was a genuine document of agreement executed by the defendant appellant and accordingly, he allowed both the appeals on contest with cost and set aside the impugned judgments and decree of the trial Court and thereafter decreed Title Suit No. 108 of 1974 on contest with costs against the contesting defendant and ex parte against defendant No.2 and dismissed Title Suit No. 221 of 1973 on contest with costs against the contesting defendant and ex parte against defendant No. 2 and thus allowed the specific performance of contract subject to payment of the balance consideration money of Taka 300.00 to defendant Santosh Kumar Paul by the plaintiff Nuruddin Ansari. The learned Advocate for the appellant argued that the trial Court correctly considered the evidence on record and observed that the date in the schedule of land in the Bainapatra Ext. B appeared to have been inserted later on though the signature of the executant Santosh Kumar Paul in the said Bainapatra appeared to be genuine in spite of the fact that the signature of plaintiff Santosh Kumar Paul of the 1st suit was found to be with a different ink, The trial Court however expressed doubt as to the genuineness of the Bainapatra Ext. B. and hence the learned Munsif was pleased to decree the suit being TS No. 221 of 1973 in part subject to payment of the sum of Taka 901.00 to the contesting defendant Nuruddin Ansari by the plaintiff Santosh Kumar. Accordingly the other suit being TS No. 108 of 1974 was decreed in part. Now, it is the contention of the learned Advocate for the appellant that the lower appellant Court has not properly considered the evidence on record and wrongly found that the Bainapatra Ext. B was a genuine document and the same was voluntarily executed by the defendant Santosh Kumar Paul and accordingly decreed in full the suit being TS No. 108/1974 of the present plaintiff respondent for specific performance of contract subject to payment of the balance amount of Taka 300.00 to the contesting defendant Santosh Kumar Paul who was also directed to execute and register the necessary kabala deed within 30 days from date of receipt of notice of the deposit of the above balance consideration money in court by the plaintiff, in default the plaintiff i.e. the present respondent Nuruddin Ansari be free to get the kabala deed executed and registered through the court in his favour. The learned Advocate for the appellant has drawn my attention to the impugned Bainapatra Ext. B and tried to show that there were some gaps here and there in some parts of the same and also absence of some figures of the consideration money and writings of the date, and the figures therein and that the Bainapatra appears to have been written by the contesting defendant with a different ink showing subsequent writings. The learned Advocate for the appellant therefore, contends that the learned Additional District Judge without noticing the above defects in the alleged Bainapatra (Ext. 1) B. wrongly believed the case of the plaintiff Nuruddin Ansari and found the Bainapatra Ext. B to have been genuinely executed by the contesting defendant Santosh Kumar Paul, on receipt of some earnest money from the plaintiff Nuruddin and illegally found the Bainapatra (Ext. B) as genuine one and wrongly decreed the suit for specific performance of contract subject to payment of the remaining consideration money and illegally dismissed the suit of the appellant Santosh Kumar Paul i.e. Title Suit No. 221/1973. It is further contended by the learned Advocate for the appellant that the learned court of appeal below failed to see that the signature of the defendant Santosh Kumar Paul appearing in the Bainapatra Ext. B. might be genuine but the same was obtained through undue influence and intimidation and, as such, the said Bainapatra ought to to have been held to be not genuine and the suit of the respondent Nuruddin Ansari ought to have been dismissed. In reply to the above submissions of the learned Advocate for the appellants, Mr. Nurul Haque, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-respondent however argued that the submissions made by the learned Advocate for the appellant relates mainly to the question of facts as to whether the Bainapatra was genuine or not. He further submits that the allegations made by the learned Advocate for the appellant that the dates, days, years and some figures of the schedule of lands were introduced on different dates by a different hand and different ink are not correct. The learned Additional District Judge, on scrutiny of the said document Ext. B. the figures, dates and other writings therein along with the evidence on record came to the findings that the defendant Santosh Kumar Paul voluntarily executed the Bainapatra (Ext. B) by putting his signature on receipt of the earnest money and the same was a genuine one. The learned Advocate for the respondent further contends that this court of Second Appeal is bound by the finding of fact of the court of appeal below if such finding of course is not a perverse one. He further contends that this court in Second Appeal cannot go to disturb any finding of fact if arrived at on due consideration of the evidence on record. In this connection he has referred to section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure and relied on a decision in the case of Abdul Mannaf Khan and others vs. Bangladesh and another reported in 38 DLR (AD) 201 wherein it been observed "As far back as 1880 AD in the case of Durga Choudin vs. Jawher Singh 17 Indian Appeal 122 (PC) the Privy Council emphatically declared under section 584 of the earlier Code which corresponds to section 100 of the present Code, there is no jurisdiction to entertain a second appeal on the ground of erroneous finding of fact, however gross or inexcusable the error may seem to be; and they added a note of warning, that no court in India has power to add or enlarge the grounds specified in section 100. The learned Advocate for the respondent therefore contends that both the courts below found the signature of the executant Santosh Kumar Paul in the Bainapatra Ext. B to be voluntary and genuine on his acceptance of the earnest money of Taka 901.00 from Nuruddin Ansari. Hence the basic facts for the proof of genuineness of the agreement i.e. Bainapatra Ext. B have been concurrently found to be proved by both the courts below and ultimately Ext. B, has been found to be genuine, hence there was no scope for interference by this court in second appeal in the above concurrent finding of facts of the court below. Of course as to the voluntariness of the execution of the said Ext. B, the trial Court appears to have expressed some doubt but in the long run it did not come to any specific finding to the effect that the agreement Ext. B. was false or fraudulent due to subsequent writing of date or figures by any different ink in the agreement. However this aspect of the matter has been thoroughly scrutinised and considered by the lower appellate Court vis-a-vis the evidence on record and ultimately, it came to a conclusive finding that the said Bainapatra was written in the same sitting as per instructions of the executant Santosh Kumar Paul on receipt of the earnest money of Rs. 901.00 and hence Ext. B was a genuine contract for sale of the suit-land of the executant Santosh Kumar Paul. 16. Now, the genuineness of a document is a question of fact and it is contended by the learned Advocate for the respondent that this court in second appeal should not and cannot interfere with such question of fact. 17. I have heard the learned Advocate of both the sides and carefully considered their submissions vis-a-vis evidence on record and the relevant laws and I find much force in the above submissions of the learned Advocate for the respondent Nuruddin Ansari and hold that the agreement Ext. B. is a genuine one voluntarily executed by Appellant Santosh Kumar Paul. 18. Nextly, it is contended by the learned Advocate for the appellant that relief for specific performance of contract under section 22 of the Specific Relief Act is a discretionary one and even if the agreement or Bainapatra was found to be a genuine one, still then in the facts and circumstances of this case, the court of appeal below should have exercised the discretion in favour of the executant defendant by refusing the prayer for specific performance of contract, if necessary by giving some reasonable compensation as solacium to the plaintiff of the second suit by the defendant who is a member of the minority community and appears to have executed the Bainapatra Ext. B on the 16th of Bhadra, 1377 BS corresponding to 1.1.71 just prior to the serious turn of the liberation war of Bangladesh when there was serious tension amongst the members of the minority community in Bangladesh and who subsequently fell in untold miseries and hardships. 19. In the light of the above, it is further contended by the learned Advocate for the appellant that through the execution of the aforesaid document Ext. B, the plaintiff tried to have an unfair advantage over the defendant i.e. the plaintiff of the 1st suit. It has been alleged that the present appellant having returned to his village Laxmikona after the war of liberation, he could not have any house to live in and he had to take shelter in the house of the Sarkers and therefrom he started residing in a rented house and thus he has been put to serious hardships which he could not foresee at the time of execution of the agreement Ext. B. He therefore, badly requires the suit-land for his own purpose if necessary by payment of reasonable compensation to the respondent Nuruddin Ansari in addition to the money he received from him as the earnest money. 20. The learned Advocate for the respondent, on the other hand, contends that in the instant case, the plaintiff-respondent on the basis of the agreement Ext. B was put into possession of the suit land and he subsequently developed the homestead and constructed huts therein by spending enough of money and also had grown valuable trees and he has been residing in the suit premises for more than 23 years with his family and the homestead has now fallen within the Rajbari pourasabha and as a result of which the price of the said property has gone up several times. If he is to vacate the premises, he will be shelterless with his family and to procure suitable land inside Municipality and to construct house for his residence, a good amount of money will be necessary which he has no means to procure at this stage. It is therefore contended that hardships of the respondent will be greater than that of the defendant-appellant. 21. The learned Advocate for the respondent further submits that the value of the suit premises will be about Taka 5 lacs at the moment and hence it is not a case of hardship only on the part of the parties but is a question of fairness and natural justice also. 22. Now, the relief under section 22 of the Specific Relief Act is no doubt discretionary, but the discretion must be exercised judicially in the facts and circumstances of 'ne case. The learned Advocate therefore contends and if the prayer of the respondent for specific relief is refused at all, then the amount of solacium should be reasonably considered in the light of the facts and circumstances of the case and the present valuation of the suit premises. Before considering the above submissions of the learned Advocates of both the sides, let me have a look into section 22 of the Specific Relief Act which reads as follows: "22. Discretion as to Decreeing Specific Performance," The jurisdiction to decree specific performance is discretionary, and the Court is not bound to grant such relief merely because it is lawful to do so; but the discretion of the Court is not arbitrary but sound and reasonable, guided by judicial principles and capable of correction by a Court of appeal. The following are cases in which the Court may properly exercise a discretion not to decree specific performance: I. Where the circumstances under which the contract is made are such as to give the plaintiff an unfair advantage over the defendant, though there may be no fraud or misrepresentation on the plaintiffs’ part. II. Where the performance of the contract would involve some harship on the defendant which he did not foresee, whereas its non-performance would involve no such hardship on the plaintiff. The following is a case in which the Court may properly exercise a discretion to decree specific performance: III. Where the plaintiff has done substantial acts or suffered losses in consequence of a contract capable of specific performance." 23. This section has been interpreted in a number of decisions by this Court and in this connection, Mr. Gafur, the learned Advocate for the appellant, has relied on a decision in the case of Administrator of Waqfs and another vs. Musammat Sahera Begum Chowdhurani and others reported in 28 DLR 238 wherein it has been observed: "Section 22 of the Specific Relief Act does no doubt provide that the jurisdiction of the court to pass a decree for specific performance of a contract is discretionary, but this discretionary power is not arbitrary." 24. It has been also observed "Having regard to the facts and circumstances of the case, there is no manner of doubt that this is a fit case in which the discretionary power of the court to refuse specific performance of contract should be exercised, even though it may be argued that this hardship arises out of events subsequent to the date of contract." 25. Mr. Nurul Huque, the learned Advocate for the respondent in order to show the principles regarding compensation or solacium, referred to some other decisions, one in the case of Lutfur Rahman and others vs. Golam Ahmed Shah and others reported in 1986 BCR (AD) 138 and another in the case of Jugesh Chandra Das and others vs. Farida Hasan reported in 1984 BCR (AD) 127 and still another in the case of Tobarak Ullah vs. Ram Gupta reported in 43 DLR (AD) 100. In all the above decisions, one thing is very clear, that granting or refusing of relief for specific performance of contract is discretionary with the court and even on payment of reasonable compensation or solacium, the court concerned reserves the right of refusing specific performance of a contract. Of course, no exact guideline has been specified in the above sub-sections 1, 2 and 3 of section 22 of the Specific Relief Act in respect of the quantum or the mode of payment of compensation or solacium. But from the above decisions of our Court and some decisions of the Indian Jurisdiction we get some light on the exercise of discretion as to compensation or solacium to the party concerned by the court. In the case of ML Devender Singh and others vs. Syed Khaja, reported in AIR (SC) 2457, it has been observed: "The rules contemplate an exercise of the arbitrium, not arbitrariness of Judges. A capricious exercise of discretion in fact becomes indiscretion. The discretion is not to be exercised arbitrarily, but on sound and reasonable grounds guided by judicial principles according to the circumstances of each case." and again, in the case of Satya Narayana vs. Yelloji reported in AIR 1965 (SC) 1405, it has been observed as follows: The discretion has to be exercised on sound principles of justice, equity and good conscience having regard to the circumstances of the case, the conduct of the parties and respective interest of the parties to the contract. The discretion is neither absolute nor arbitrary or fanciful; neither does it run on fixed iron rails." 26. Now, the question of hardship comes under sub-section 2 of section 22 of the Specific Relief Act. But there is another provision in sub-section 1 of section 22 which relates to the advantage of the plaintiff over the defendant by execution of the contract. But in the instant case it appears that aspect of the matter has not been considered by the lower Appellate Court. Of course the learned Additional District Judge appears to have taken into consideration the question of hardship that may be caused to the plaintiff-respondent in case of non-performance of the specific relief according to the contract as prayed for in this suit and also the long possession of the plaintiff in the suit-land in pursuance of the contract Ext. B and further construction of his huts thereon and development of the homestead. The trial Court, however appears to have considered the hardship of the defendant i.e. Santosh Kumar Paul and decided to refuse specific performance of contract and dismiss the suit on contention that the contesting defendant i.e. the present appellant shall pay back the sum of Taka 901.00 received from the plaintiff at the time of execution of agreement Ext. B. From the above, it appears to me that both the courts failed to consider and appreciate the provisions of sub-sections 1, 2 and 3 of section 22 of the Specific Relief Act in their proper perspective. Sub-sections 1 and 2 of section 22 of the Specific Relief Act relate to exercise of court's discretion in refusing to decree the suit for Specific Performance of Contract, but sub-section 3 of the said section 22 of the Specific Relief Act relates to a case in which the court may properly exercise the discretion to pass a decree for the Specific Performance of a contract. But as I have observed that relief under section 22 of the Specific Relief Act is, after all, discretionary with the court which discretion has to be exercised judicially and not arbitrarily in the facts and circumstances of each case according to the sound judicial principles as have been laid down in the aforesaid decisions. Hence, I would like to consider this case from both the above points. Undoubtedly the agreement Ext. B was executed on 1.1.71 when there was already some disturbances in the country towards the liberation movement giving rise to some sort of hardship to the parties. In the instant case, both the parties were faced with hardships and this hardship did not appear to have occurred to one particular party alone. However, it may be noticed that after execution of the agreement Ext. B, the plaintiff-respondent entered into possession of the suit-land and he constructed some huts in the homestead and made some developments of the same and grew a number of trees and he has been still living in the homestead with his entire family. If the plaintiff is to vacate the suit premises he will be put to serious hardships and sufferings. Now, the defendant is no less sufferer than the plaintiff. In the critical situation during the liberation war as stated above he had to leave his homestead and subsequently hide himself from place to place with his family for safety and in an abnormal situation he had to enter into the contract for sale (Ext. B) of the suit-land for a small consideration of money and on his return after the liberation of Bangladesh he could not take shelter in his own house or place but in the house of one Sarkar and now is living in a small rened house having no land to construct his own house. Thus his hardships also does not appear to be less than those of the plaintiff Nuruddin Ansari. 27. In the above facts and circumstances I am of the view that for the ends of justice, the discretion in the instant case should be exercised in favour of the defendant-appellant by refusing the prayer of the plaintiff-respondent for specific performance of the contract subject to payment of a reasonable compensation i.e. solacium by him i.e. the defendant to the plaintiff-respondent. As discussed above, the lower Appellate Court does not appear to have applied its mind properly to the provisions of section 22 of Specific Relief Act, particularly its sub-sections and has failed to properly exercise its discretion on a sound and reasonable basis in the facts and circumstances of the case and has wrongly decreed the suit for specific performance of contract and allowed the appeal being TA No. 94 of 1975. In my considered view, this is a fit and proper case where the prayer for specific performance of contract should be refused in the interest of justice with the grant of reasonable solacium to the plaintiff to be paid by the defendant. 28. Now, remains the question of quantum of solacium that should be granted to the plaintiff, while refusing the prayer for specific performance of the contract. I have heard the submissions of the learned Advocates of both the sides and taken into consideration the same along with materials on record and the facts and circumstance of the case and I am of the view that the ends of justice and equity will be sufficiently met, if the quantum of solacium is assessed at Taka 1,50,000.00 (taka one lac and fifty thousand only) to be paid by the defendant-appellant Sontosh Kumar Paul to the plaintiff-respondent Nuruddin Ansari at a time, apart from the return of the consideration money of Taka 901.00. For the reasons stated above, the appeal being Second Appeal No. 306 of 1976 is allowed in part.
