Reading Article 3 of the Order it is apparent that conferral of citizenship on a person by Article 2 of the Order is never absolute. It is always conditional and thus liable to be defeated if the conditions mentioned in Article 2 are not fulfilled. It will be worthwhile now to refer to the impugned notification dated 18.4.73 so far it relates to Prof. Golam Azam. The notification speaks that the respondent was staying abroad since before the liberation of Bangladesh and by his conduct he cannot be deemed to be a citizen of Bangladesh and the said person (Professor Golam Azam) has continued to be a citizen of Pakistan. It can be mentioned here that staying abroad since before the liberation of Bangladesh and the conduct have been considered as disqualifications under Article 3 of the Order and consequently, the Government declares under Article 3 that the respondent did not qualify himself to be a citizen of Bangladesh. This is the decision given by the Government under Article 3 of the Order whereby the respondent was not qualified to be deemed to be a citizen of Bangladesh. I may point out here that staying abroad since before the liberation of Bangladesh and the conduct by themselves are not at all material considerations, as clause (1) of Article 2 does not contemplate such considerations at all. Thus, it appears that in passing the impugned Notification under Article 3 some irrelevant facts were taken into consideration, not strictly relevant to resolve the doubt as to whether a person is qualified to be deemed to be a citizen of Bangladesh under Article 2 of this Order.</u>

186. It is on record that the respondent was absent from Bangladesh from 22.11.71 and he returned to Bangladesh on 11.7.78. Admittedly during this period the respondent remained outside Bangladesh. So the vital question for consideration is, whether his continued stay outside Bangladesh from 22.11.71 upto the date of promulgation of President's Order No. 149 of 1972 renders him to be disqualified to be deemed to be a citizen of Bangladesh and whether he ceased to continue to be a permanent resident of Bangladesh. The question whether a person has ceased to be a permanent resident of Bangladesh for his temporary absence from the country is a question of fact and this has to be determined on the facts and circumstances of each particular case. Further, this question is to be answered squarely within the context of this Order and not beyond Article 2(1) of the Order. The expression is used as permanent resident and this we are to interpret as to what is meant by permanent resident. Unless and until the term 'permanent resident' could be clearly understood with reference to its connotation as meant in determination of citizenship, the question of one's citizenship can never be lawfully and strictly determined. In 'the order' permanent resident' and also the word 'resident' in Bangladesh have been used. So these two expressions must be clearly understood and spelt out in determining the citizenship of a person in Bangladesh. In Black's Law Dictionary, 5th Edition, 'permanent abode' means—

"A domicile or fixed home, which the party may leave as his interest or whim may dictate, but which he has no present intention of abandoning".

In this Order, the expression used is 'permanent resident' which is akin to domicile. Domicile has been defined in Black's Law Dictionary like this—

"Domicile. "That place where a man has his true, fixed, and permanent home and principal establishment, and to which whenever he is absent he has the intention of returning. The permanent residence of a person or the place to which he intends to return even though he may actually reside elsewhere. A person may have more than one residence but only one domicile. The legal domicile of a person is important since it, rather than the actual residence, often controls the jurisdiction of the taxing authorities and determines where a person may exercise the privilege of voting and other legal rights and privileges. The established, fixed, permanent, or ordinary dwelling place or place of residence of a person as distinguished from his temporary and transient, though actual, place of residence. It is his legal residence, as distinguished from the temporary place of abode; or his home, as distinguished from a place to which business or pleasure may temporarily call him."

'Resident' has been defined in Black's Law Dictionary meaning thereby;

"Resident. Any person who occupies a dwelling within the State, has a present intent to remain within the State for a period of time, and manifests the genuineness of that intent by establishing an ongoing physical presence within the State together with indicia that his presence within the State is something other than merely transitory in nature. The word "resident" when used as a noun, means a dweller, habitant or occupant; one who resides or dwells in a place for a period of more, or less, duration; it signifies one having a residence, or one who resides or abides."

The citizens of a country are members of a political community to which they belong and they compose State and they establish the Government for the promotion of their general welfare and for the protection of their individual as well as their collective rights in the State. The citizen of a State enjoy full fundamental, civil and political rights. The term Citizenship refers to the relationship of an individual with State from the internal aspect and 'nationality' refers to similar relationship from international aspect. From the international standpoint, the nationality is the status and quality of belonging to particular nations or States. All nationals of a State are not citizens though citizens must be nationals. A national of a State may not possess full civil or political rights, but a citizen must possess full civil and political rights.

187. President's Order No. 149 of 1972, only declares certain categories of persons who shall be citizens of Bangladesh at the commencement of this Order i.e. on 15.12.72. Clauses (1) and (2) of Article 2 of the Order only give tentative qualifications for acquisition of Bangladeshi citizenship at the commencement of the Order. A little reflection would, however, show that the provisions of Article 2 deal with ad hoc situation, where rights of citizenship were conferred on persons at the commencement of the Order with certain qualifications and reservations.

<u>188.  It is to be kept in mind that the Pakistan Citizenship Act, 1951, briefly, called the 'Act', is very much in existence today in our country as a valid law by The Bangladesh (Adaptation of Existing Bangladesh Laws) Order, 1972, effective from the 26th day of March, 1971. This Act provides for the mode of acquisition and deprivation of citizenship in Bangladesh subsequent to the commencement of 'The Order'. It appears that from the 26th day of March, 1971, both 'The Order' and 'The Act' are governing the field of citizenship of Bangladesh. The Act of 1951, was promulgated on 13th April, 1951 and section 3 of the Act speaks of citizenship at the date of commencement of this Act. After the Division of British-India, Pakistan was created on the 14th day of August, 1947 and the necessity of promulgating this Act was felt to provide for Pakistan Citizenship. Like clauses (1) and (2) of President's Order 149 of 1972, this Act also provided for conferring citizenship to certain categories of persons at the commencement of this Act. Section 4 of the Act speaks of citizenship by birth and the same is referable to person born after the commencement of this Act. In this Act, section 16 speaks of deprivation of citizenship in case the citizenship has been obtained by a person by certificate of domicile or certificate of naturalization under the Naturalization Act, 1926 by means of fraud, false representations or the concealment of some material fact. The power of depriving citizenship to such a person is left entirely with the Government. This power of deprivation of citizenship as contemplated in section 16 of the Act has got nothing to do with depriving the citizenship of a person who is deemed to be a citizen by Article 2(1) of the Order. A reference to President's Order 149 of 1972 (with upto date amendments) shows that a person who is deemed to be a citizen of Bangladesh under Article 2(1) of the Order can be disqualified to be a citizen of Bangladesh either under Article 3 or under Article 2B, as the case may be. If the respondent does not possess the qualifications as mentioned in sub-article (1) of Article 2 of the Order he can be disqualified to be a citizen of Bangladesh with retrospective effect or its non-accrual at any point of time. But in the case of the respondent, the question of determination under the Act does not arise. Deprivation presumes that at some point of time a person was a citizen of Bangladesh, but the respondent's case is to be looked at as if he shall be deemed to be a citizen of Bangladesh under this Order or he never could claim to be a citizen under the Order at any point of time. Thus the provisions of the Order and the Act supplement each other and have to be read together to disqualify or deprive a citizen of Bangladesh either under Articles 3 and 2B of the Order or under section 16 of the Act as the case may be. The provisions of the Act and the Order are to be read together to get a complete picture of the law of Citizenship in Bangladesh.</u>

<u>I may refer in this connection that the citizenship of India is governed by Part-II of the Constitution of India (Article 5 to Article 11) and by the Citizenship Act, 1955. Unlike the Constitution of our constitution there is and corresponding provisions contained in Part-II (Citizenship) of the Constitution of India. Citizenship is entirely left to be determined by legislation-as contained in Article 6 (1) of our Constitution.</u>

<u>189. It must be stated here that the case made out by respondent No. 1 in his Writ Petition has not been controverted by specific denial by the government appellant. As a matter of fact no material could be bright on record by the appellant to show that the respondent really intended to leave his permanent residence and voluntarily acquired citizenship of Pakistan by any positive act and thereby he ceased to be a permanent resident of Bangladesh. The intention must be an intention to reside permanently or for an indefinite period: If a Person goes to a country for employment; business, or to stay there for some other purposes he will retain his permanent residence his domicile of origin. The domicile of origin is thus a concept of law and Clings to a man till he abandons it but if it can be shown that the person has permanently settled down in a country and has established his permanent home and residence with his family and Children then, of course, the matter will be different. By mere place of residence itself without any animus to acquire a permanent home or residence the permanent residence or domicile is never lost. For example, if the respondent would have purchased a house in Pakistan or estate coupled with long residence therein and non-retention of any home in his birth place it might be sufficient to prove the .intention to acquire a new permanent home. It is on record that the respondent's wife and children are continuously living in Bangladesh since before and after liberation of Bangladesh. Every person acquires his domicile of Origin, (Permanent residence) at his birth, which continues until he has Validly acquired domicile of choice thus even though a person leaves the country of his origin with intention 'of 'never returning to it, his domicile of Origin in that country is -never lost, until he has actually settled in another country with the intention of making that country his permanent Ionic. In other words, the domicile of origin is not lost by mere temporary abandonment Domicile of origin acquired subsists until it is replaced by a fresh domicile of choice. Hence residence in foreign country; going 'to imprisonment as a political. refugee or as invalid for change of climate or for service or diplomatic missions, studies and/or for business is not sufficient for acquisition of permanent residence. The permanent residence continues until a person has voluntarily relinquished and acquired a permanent residence in any country. The appellant could not place, any material whatsoever to show that the citizenship acquired by respondent No. 1 by birth and by operation of law has been voluntarily relinquished or abandoned at any point of time. There being nothing on record to show that respondent No. 1 voluntarily renounced or abandoned his permanent residence, and took up citizenship of Pakistan he is deemed to be a Citizen Of Bangladesh as continues to be permanent resident in Bangladesh under clause (1) of the Order. In this connection I will refer to two English decisions. In the case of Ramsay Vs. Liverpool Royal Infirmary, 1930 (AC) .588, the fact relevant is that, one George Bowie was .born in Glasgow in 1845 and therefore with a Scottish domicile of origin. From there he moved his resident to Liverpool (UK) in 1892, lived, there and died there in 1927. George Bowie lived in England for the last 36 years of his life. During this time he occasionally went outside England. He was proud to be a Glasgow man and resolutely, refused on several occasions to return to Scotland, even for the purpose of attending his mother's funeral. George. Bowie left a will that was valid if his domicile at death was Scottish, but invalid it was English. In that case the House of Lords unanimously held, that George died domiciled in Scotland, though he lived for 36 years, in Liverpool and died at Liverpool and was buried there. Their Lordships were of the view that prolonged residence did not disclose an intention to choose England as his, permanent home. It that case Their Lordships answered the question in the following terms:</u>

<u>"The real question in the cases whether this prolonged residence in England was accompanied by an intention on the part of the deceased to choose. England as his permanent home in preference to the country of his birth. The law requires evidence of volition to change. Prolonged actual residence is an important item of evidence of such volition, but it must be supplemented by other facts and circumstances indicative of intention. The residence, must answer a qualitative as well as a quantitative test."</u>

<u>The case of Witans Vs. AG, (1904) AC. 287, relates to the dormice of On Witans who was born in 1823 in USA From 1850-59  he went to Russia and within employment there. He married a British subject and came after two years in UK due to his ill health on the advice of his doctor. He took lease of two houses in UK at the time of his death. From 1860-70, he lived for four months of the winter at his residence in UK and remaining eight months in Russia. Subsequently before his death he lived from 1893 to 1897 entirely in England. Winans had two objects in life, first, to construct in Baltimore (USA) gar large fleet or Spindle-Shaped vessels and, secondly, to develop a large property of 200 acres in Baltimore. The fact that he resided in England for 37 years of his life raised a strong presumption in favour of an English domicile., but. Their Lordships held, that the domicile of origin in New Jersey had not been lost. Lord Macnagthen held as follows:</u>

<u>"On the whole I am unable to come to the conclusion that Mr. Witans ever formed a fixed and settled purpose of abandoning his American domicile and settling finally in England. I Think up to the very last he had an expectation or hope of returning to America and seeing his 'grand schemes inaugurated."</u>

<u>190. Learned Attorney-General argued that the respondent's possessing the Passport of Pakistan is a positive proof that he is a Citizen of Pakistan and he is a permanent resident of Pakistan and Thereby his not qualified to be a citizen of Bangladesh. In this regard he referred to section 9 of the Indian Citizenship Act, 1955 and Rule 30 framed thereunder. Section 9 speaks of termination of citizenship: According to section 9(2) if a person possesses a foreign passport, a determination by the Central. Government under section 9(2) cannot be dispensed with. Rule 30(3) speaks that obtaining a passport from any other country shall be conclusive proof of voluntarily acquiring citizenship of that country. In our law there in no such provision like Indian Citizenship Act, 1955, and hence this argument is not relevant in this case. Further, the possession of a passport does not necessarily imply that he is a citizen of that country, but it may only mean that he is a national of that country. Under The Bangladesh Passport Order, 1973 (President's Order 9 of 1973), passport is primarily a travel document of a citizen of Bangladesh and other persons for the, purpose, of departure from Bangladesh. In the passport of Bangladesh, issued by the Government of Bangladesh, nowhere it is written as citizen of Bangladesh, but as national of Bangladesh.</u>

191. From the judgment of the High Court Division it appears that the 26th day of Marco, 1971 was taken to be the commencing day of President's order 149 of 1972. Commencement means the time at which the Act comes in to operation. Presidents order 149 of 1972 was promulgated on 15th December 1972 and came into force on that date thought it was made effective from the 26th day of March 1971. Hence legally speaking the commencement day of this order is the 15th December, 1972 and we are to see whether upto this date a person qualifies the tests as contained in clause (1) of Article 2 of the order. Clause (1) of Article 2 of the Order only speaker of permanent residence on 25th day of March, 1971 and nowhere it has been mentioned that one is to be physically present at/any point of time after 25th day of March, 1971. From the 26th day of March, 1971 upto 15.12.72 the investigation will be whether a person continues to be so permanently resident is Bangladesh upto the date of commencement of the order. In other words, Article 2 of the Order does not provide any mode for acquisition of citizenship of Bangladesh subsequent to the commencement of the Order.

192. A discussion has been made with regard to proviso of Article 2 of the Order by the two learned Judges of the High Court Division. But to me it appears that the proviso has got no relevance in the facts of the present case. The present case is one of temporary absence from the permanent residence and this has got nothing to do with studies or employment in Pakistan as mentioned in the Proviso to Article 2 of the Order. In the case of Peoples Republic of Bangladesh Vs. Abdul Haque, 1982, BLD (AD) 143, it appears that respondent Abdul Haque was born in Satkhira within the territory of Bangladesh. In November 1971 he had gone to Pakistan in connection with his business. In 1975 he came to Bangladesh with Pakistan passport. He surrendered his passport to the Government and applied for citizenship of Bangladesh. Government did not grant him citizenship and asked him to leave the country under Foreigners Act, 1946. Before the High Court Division the respondent in his writ petition stated that he never abandoned his permanent residence in Bangladesh while his wife and children are continuously living in Bangladesh. In that decision it was held that the citizenship by birth is not lost by temporary absence from the country of origin. The learned Judges after considering Article 2 of President's Order 149 of 1972 held that in the eye of law, the respondent remains a resident of Bangladesh. The fact and law of this case apply with all force to the present case.

<u>193. The appellant's case is that the respondent was never deemed to be a citizen of Bangladesh .under President's Order No. 149 of 1972. Respondent's case is that he is a citizen of Bangladesh by birth, he was physically present in Bangladesh on 25th day of March, 1971 and even when he was temporarily absent from his permanent residence from 21.11.71 he continues to be a permanent resident of Bangladesh. The appellant alleges that the respondent was never a citizen of Bangladesh and that he is a citizen of Pakistan. In the present .case the onus of proving that the respondent has lost his citizenship from the country of his permanent residence is on the appellant who seeks to deprive the respondent of his rights as a citizen and for discharging the onus the appellant could not place any objective material before us other than mentioning about the conduct and mental attitude of the respondent. The test of citizenship, so far it relates to the order as it originally stood, is to be determined by objective tests and not by conduct and subjective satisfactions. In the order, the concept of citizenship is that of permanent residence (domicile) and it does not evaporate with the passing of time and it clings to a person wherever he may go. I may unhesitatingly say that in Article 2 of the Order "permanent residence" is made one of the basic conditions for treating a person to be deemed to be a citizen of Bangladesh. The appellant has totally failed to show that the respondent has voluntarily renounced his original citizenship or is guilty of some conduct as not being qualified to be ‘deemed citizen of Bangladesh’ under the Order.</u>

194. Lot of decisions have been cited by the learned Advocate for the respondent to show that the principle of natural justice has not been followed in this case before issuing the impugned notification under Article 3 of the Order. Without going into any decision, it can be safely said that citizenship involves a determination of a very vital issue concerning an individual by which his fundamental, political and civil rights arc affected and consequently, the Government is called upon to dispose of the issue of citizenship in a quasi-judicial manner and the ends of justice demands a fair hearing in the matter. It has been argued by the learned Attorney-General that in the facts of the present case it was not possible to serve any notice on respondent No. 1. From the record it appears that there was no bonafide attempt on the part of the appellant to issue any show cause notice to the respondent when the respondent's permanent addresses at Brahmanbaria and Dhaka were known to the appellant before issuance of the impugned notification. Thus the two learned Judges were correct in holding that the principle of natural justice has been violated in this case.

195. From the two judgments of the High Court Division it appears that on a detailed discussion of the materials on record, the two learned Judges have observed that the delay has been sufficiently explained. Further, the appellant-State having also contributed to the delay the question of delay is of no prime importance in this case, when a very valuable right of the respondent is adversely affected.

Before parting with the case, I want to mention that in President's Order No. 149 of 1972. Article 28 was inserted on 22.6.73, by an amendment which speaks of oath of affirmation, allegiance and conduct. The exercise of power by the Government not being under Article 2B of the Order and the learned Attorney-General having accepted the position, I refrain from saying anything on this score.

End.

Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed with Dr. M Zahir and SM Munir, Advocates ----- For the Petitioners 
Md. Khalilur Rahman, Advocate ----- For the Respondent No.2. 
AF Hasan Arif, Deputy Attorney-General ----- For the Respondent Nos.1 and 3
parties:
Ariff A Shekha and others ------ Petitioners

full_judgment:
Habibur Rahman Khan J: At the instance of Ariff A. Shekha and 9 others a Rule Nisi was issued by this court on 19.7.87 calling upon the respondents to show cause why the order communicated vide Memo No. Shilpa/Dairy No. 937/DT-2/87/3028 dated 27.5.87 (Annexure-H) should not be declared to have been made and issued illegally and without lawful, authority and why direction should not be issued upon the respondents to forthwith release the Company Eastern Tubes Ltd. and its assets to the petitioners or such other or further order or orders passed as to this court may seem fit and proper. Subsequently in course of hearing of the Rule on an application filed and moved by the petitioners another Rule Nisi was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the Notification bearing No. 186-81 dated 31.12.71 issued in respect of Eastern Tubes Ltd. Tejgaon Industrial Area under Group No. F (i) (8)- Tejgaon Industrial Area, published in the Bangladesh Gazette Extraordinary dated 3rd January, 1972 (Annexure-A) to the writ petition should not be declared to have been made and published illegally and without lawful authority and why a direction should not be issued upon the respondents to withdraw/cancel/rescind the same forthwith or such other or further order or order passed as to this court may seem fit and proper.

2. The petitioners' case as stated in the application is as follows:

The petitioners are the share-holders of the Company, Eastern Tubes Limited, which is a private limited company incorporated under the Companies Act, 1913 in the former East Pakistan and registered with the Registrar of Joint Stock Companies at Dhaka on 26.6.94. The petitioners are the shareholders of the company having their respective shares and all of them together held 1,04,265 shares out of total 1,70,000 shares, and 19,240 shares are held by Bangladesh Shilpa Rin Shangsta. These constitute 72.65% of the share-holding of the said company. The company was running its industry manufacturing fluorescent tube lights at Tejgaon Industrial Area through their appointed directors, managers, officers and other executive’s at all relevant times. The Government of Bangladesh under the Acting President's Order No. SEC-X1/1M-35/71/17 dated 30.12.1971 by Notification No. 186-S1 dated 31.12.71 placed the same under the Management Board and subsequently placed it under the Engineering and Ship Building Corporation vide Notification No. P/E-1/ 1855 dated 17.5.1972 for the management of the aforesaid business. The said management also continued under Abandoned Property (Control, Management and Disposal) Order 1971 (President's Order No. 16 of 1972). The taking over of the Company and its assets was challenged by the share-holders vide letters dated 20.1.72, 15.2.72 and 4.6.72. On many occasions share-holders pressed for the release of the business of the company but the Government did not respond. The petitioner Ariff A. Shekha received letter for the first time on 22.2.78 whereby the prayer for the release of the company to the share-holders was rejected. On receipt of Mr. Ariff's letter dated 23-2-78 and 18-7-78 the Ministry asked for the documents and proof of nationality of the share-holders vide its Memo No. IND/DC-1/SSC-29 77-787 dated 21.10.78 and Memo No. IND/ DC-1/SSC-29/77-537 dated 31.8.79. Further case of the petitioner is that in the meantime Bella Artifitex Industries Limited and some other sister enterprises of the said company in which major shares were held by the same group of persons was released to the shareholders by the Government being satisfied as to genuineness of the claim of the shareholders. Suddenly the petitioner No. 1 received Memo No. Shilpa/Dairy No. 937/Dt-2/87/3028 dated 27.5.87 which was addressed to Mr. Md. Ashraf Daud, Executive Director of Bella Artifitex Industries Limited intimating that Eastern Tubes Limited and another company would not be released to its share-holders like Bella Artifitex Industries Ltd. as the Government has decided to disinvest these two industrial units by giving 51% and 49% shares of the said two companies to the Corporation and the general public respectively. On receipt of the Memo dated 27.5.87 containing the decision of the Government as regards Eastern Tubes Ltd. the petitioners sent a notice demanding justice by registered post on 21.6.87 to the respondent Nos. 1 and 2 but no reply having been received by the petitioners it is presumed that justice has been denied to them. The petitioners thereafter having moved this application before this Court obtained the instant Rule.

3. Mr. Khondaker Mahbubuddin Ahmed and at a later stage Dr. M. Zahir, the learned Counsels appearing for the petitioners, made their submission in support of the Rule which was opposed by Mr. AF Hasan Arif, the learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing for the respondent Nos. 1 and 3 and the learned Counsel Mr. Asrarul Hossain along with learned Advocate Mr. Md. Khalilur Rahman appeared for the respondent No. 2.

4. From the facts stated in the case it appears that the Company National Tubes Ltd, which was an industrial enterprise, was taken over for the management and operation either directly or through the appointment of Administrator vide Notification No. IM-35/71-13 dated 26.12.71 (shortly known as Acting President's Order No. 1 of 1971) by the Ministry of Industries in exercise of the authority given by the Acting President's Notification No. Sec. Xl/IM-35/71/30 dated 30.12.71 and by subsequent notification dated 3rd January, 1972 under Bangladesh (Taking over of Control and Management of Industrial and Commercial Concerns) Order, 1972, shortly known as Acting President's Order No. 1 of 1972 published on 3rd January. 1972 by which provision was made that the Government of Bangladesh by notification in Official Gazette may take over the control and management of the industrial and commercial concerns where the owners or directors or managers or majority of the owners have left Bangladesh or are not available in Bangladesh to control and manage the commercial concern and where in the opinion of the Government of Bangladesh the owners or directors of any industrial or commercial concern cannot be allowed to control and manage the enterprise for some reason or the other. The Acting President's Order No. IM-35/71-13 dated 26.12.71 stood repealed but in spite of the repeal all orders passed under the Acting President's Order No. 1 of 1971 were deemed to have been issued by the Acting President's Order No. 1 of 1972.

5. It appears that from the very beginning the petitioners were making representations against the taking over of their company and its assets and shares with a prayer for the release and restoration of the same to them and consequently they were asked to submit documents so as to facilitate the payment of compensation money.

6. After taking us through the writ petition and the annexures thereto Md. Khondaker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, the learned Counsel appearing for the petitioner, submitted that the very order of taking over of the company and its assets and shares by notification dated 31.12.71 while the business of the company was being run and conducted by its officers, directors, manager and the staff, purported to have been made under the Acting President's Order dated 26.12.71 was illegal and has been made without lawful authority. Mr. Ahmed, in support of his contention, cited the case of Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Industries Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh. and others in CA No. 31 of 1991, Bangladesh Steel and Engineering Corporation represented by its Secretary vs. Dhaka Steel Works Ltd. and others in CA No. 40 of 1991 reported in 45 DLK (AD) 69. In the said case the company was taken over on 7.3.72 in exercise of the repealed. Acting President's Order vide Notification No. Sec-XI/1M-35/71/17 dated 30.12.71 and therefore, the question arose as to whether the property could be taken over under the repealed Acting President's Order and on that score the taking over of the property by the Government was found to be not properly done. In the instant case the company was taken over in exercise of the Acting President's Order dated 26.12.71 while it was subsisting and, therefore, the point raised by the learned Counsel for the petitioners in this regard is not exactly the same or similar. Acting President's Order dated 26.12.71 with the amendment thereof remained in force till 3rd January, 1972 when it was repealed by the Acting President's Order No. 1 of 1972 which provides that1) where the owners, directors or managers of any industrial or commercial concern have left Bangladesh or 2) they are not available to control or manage the concern or 3) in the opinion of the Government, the owners, directors of such concern cannot be allowed to control and manage the same the Government may, notwithstanding anything to the contrary, take over its control and management by Article 6 of the Acting Presidents Order No. 1 of 1972. Though the Acting President's Order dated 26.12.71 was repealed all notifications issued earlier under it was deemed to have been issued under the relevant provision of the Acting President's Order No. 1 of 1972. Neither Acting President's Order dated 26.12.71 nor Acting President's Order No. 1 of 1972 specifically provide for taking over any industrial and commercial concern describing the same as abandoned property. The concept of abandoned property appeared for the first time in the Bangladesh Abandoned Property (Control, Management and Disposal) Order, 1972 (president's Order No.16 of 1972) which came into force with effect from 28.2.1972 when the Acting President's Order dated 26.12.71 was not subsisting as it was repealed with the promulgation of Acting President's Order No.1 of 1972 on 3.1.72. Though the Acting President's Order dated 26.12.71 was repealed all actions taken under the said order was validated by the Acting President's Order No.1 of 1972 and thus the taking over of the enterprise remained in force and continued as such. In the meantime President's Order No. 16 of 1972 was promulgated on 28.2.72. Now the question arises whether the company along with its assets and shares which was taken over under the Acting President's Order dated 26.12.71 and continued as such under Acting President's Order No. 1 of 1972 could vest under the President's Order No. 16 of 1972 after it came into operation. From the averments made in paragraph 3 of the affidavit-in-opposition filed on behalf of the respondent No. 2 it appears that the taking over of the Industrial Units in question as Abandoned Property under the President's Order No. 16 of 1972 has been admitted stating that after taking over the Industrial Unit in question as abandoned property the petitioners cannot claim the shares of the property or the industrial unit itself as the property has been lawfully vested in the Government. The facts of taking over of the concerned industry by the Government as an abandoned property is also admitted by the respondent No. 2 in his affidavit-in-opposition. Because of the inconsistent stand taken by the Government as well as by the respondent No. 2 we are unable to accept the submission of the learned Deputy Attorney-General that the company which was taken over under the Acting President's Order dated 26.12.71 and for that matter under Acting President's Order No. 1 of 1972 was not vested and treated as abandoned property under President's Order No. 16 of 1972 as well. Thus we find that from 26.12.71 to 26.2.72 there were three Presidential Orders which provided for taking over properties including the industrial and commercial enterprises. These were Acting President's Order dated 26.12.71, Acting President Orders 1 of 1972 dated 3.1.72 and President's Order No. 16 of 1972 dated 26.2.72. Mr. Khondaker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, the learned Counsel for the petitioners, submitted that the company was taken over initially under the Acting President's Order No. 1 dated 26.12.71 and thereafter deemed to have been taken under Acting President's Order No. 1 of 1972 and then with the promulgation of President's Order No. 16 of 1972 on 26.2.72 was admittedly treated as abandoned property by the respondents and, as such, vesting of the said company and the shares thereof under the President's Order No. 27 of 1972 dated 17.5.92 was not proper and, therefore the impugned order dated 27.5.87 vide Annexure-H refusing the prayer of the petitioners for the release and restoration of the shares to the owners on the ground that there is no scope for restoration of the company and shares thereof is without any lawful authority and is of no legal effect. Mr. Khondaker Mahbubuddin Ahmed argued that Acting President's Order No. 1 of 1972 which seems to have replaced Acting President's Order No.1 dated 26.12.71 also became extinct on its repeal on 7.3.72 and more so when in the meantime President's Order No. 16 of 1972 came into operation on 26.2.72 and the company was treated to have vested as Abandoned Property. Mr. AF Hasan Arif, the learned Deputy Attorney-General, argued that as the enterprise was taken over under Acting President's Order No.1 dated 26.12.71 and subsequently validated under Acting President's Order No. 1 of 1972 which was a continuous legislation, the placement of the same under President's Order No. 27 of 1972 independent of its abandoned character is quite valid in law and hence the question as to whether it was rightly vested an abandoned property or not is not relevant. This argument of Mr. AF Hasan Arif is of no avail because of the admission of the respondents that the company was also treated as abandoned company after the promulgation of President's Order No. 16 of 1972. The learned Deputy Attorney-General also argued that Acting President's Order No. 1 of 1972 was not expressly repealed by President's Order No. 16 of 1972 and therefore, the taking over of the company under the Acting President's Order dated 26.12.71 having been merged under Acting President's Order No. 1 of 1972 which came into force on 3.1.72 continued. It is argued that by President's Order No. 151 of 1972, Acting President's Order No. 1 of 1972 was amended with retrospective effect and the impact of the said amendment was that no specific notification was necessary for taking over any company under Acting President's Order No. 1 of 1972. The property was taken over under Acting President's Order No. 1 of 1972 and while it was kept as such under the management and control of the Government, abandoned character was attributed to it with the promulgation of President's Order No. 16 of 1972 and therefore it is argued that the taking over of the company and vesting of the shares with the Government under President's Order No. 27 of 1972 is independent of the fact that it was taken over as an abandoned property. By way of adding claues (2A) after Article 2 of Acting President's Order No. 1 of 1972 by President's Order No. 151 of 1972 a separate list of Industrial and Commercial concern was required to be kept and published for the public but in the instant case the learned Deputy Attorney-General could not produce any such list showing that the company was taken over under Acting President's Order No.1 of 1972 and remained as such till it was vested under President's Order No. 27 of 1972. The list produced later on in the court does not contain the name of the enterprise in question.

7. Though Acting President's Order No. 1 of 1972 was not expressly repealed and the doctrine of implied repeal cannot be invoked by applying the rule of exhaustion the effect remains that the company along with its shares was also taken over treating the same as abandoned company under President's Order No. 16 of 1972 which is a comprehensive law regarding the abandoned property having been promulgated on 26.2.72. Mr. Khondaker Mahbubuddin Ahmed and along with him Dr. M Zahir appearing for the petitioners submitted that under clause(1) of Article 2 of President's Order No. 16 of 1972 an abandoned property' means any property owned by any person who is not in Bangladesh or that whose whereabouts are not known, or who has ceased to occupy, supervise or manage in person his property including any property taken over under the Bangladesh (Taking over of Control and Management of Industrial and Commercial Concerns) Order, 1972 (Acting President's Order No. 1 of 1972) but under sub- clause (a) of clauses (i) (ii) does not include any property the owners of which are residing outside Bangladesh for any purpose which, in the opinion of the Government, is not prejudicial to the interest of Bangladesh. The explanation to the Article 2 of President's Order No. 16 of 1972 reads as "Person who is not present in Bangladesh" includes anybody of persons or company constituted or incorporated in the territory or under the laws of a State which at any time after the 25th day of March, 1971, was at war with or engaged in military operations against the People's Republic of Bangladesh. In the instant case the property was taken over on 26.12.71 by an order of Acting President before Acting President's Order No. 1 of 1972 came into force on 3.1.72 and such taking over continued till it was vested with the promulgation of President's Order 16 of 1972. The learned Counsel argued that the company having been incorporated with its head office in Bangladesh cannot be declared as abandoned and its share only could be declared as abandoned according to the provision of President's Order No. 16 of 1972.

8. It is argued on behalf of the petitioners that while the company with its share and assets held by the petitioners was declared as abandoned under President's Order No. 16 of 1972 by the authority without applying its mind as to whether the owner and the shareholders are not present in Bangladesh or whose whereabouts are not known or who has ceased to occupy or supervise or manage in person the property or were residing outside Bangladesh for the purpose which in its opinion is prejudicial to the interest of Bangladesh or that they were residing as a citizen in any country outside Bangladesh which after 25th day of March, 1971, was at war with or engaged in military operations against Bangladesh.

9. Mr. Asrarul Hossain, the learned Counsel appearing with learned Advocate Mr. Md. Khalilur Rhaman for the respondent No. 2, submitted that the industrial enterprise was placed under the Corporation invoking its general power of placement under Acting President's Order dated 26.12.71 and it continued as such after the promulgation of Acting President's Order No. 1 of 1972 on 28.2.72 and hence the taking over of the charge for the purpose of the management and control of the concern by the Government under President's Order No. 27 of 1972 cannot be challenged and the petitioners are not entitled to get back the company and its share.

10. Besides the law relating to taking over of the property and the industrial and commercial concern invoking the aid of Acting President's Order No. 1 dated 26.12.71, Acting President's Order No. 1 of 1972 and after vesting of the property under President's Order No. 16 of 1972, President's Order No. 27 of 1972 under the heading Bangladesh Industrial Enterprise (Nationalisation) Order, 1972 was promulgated on 26th day of March, 1972 to provide for the nationalisation of certain industrial enterprises, establishments or Corporations in Bangladesh for the purpose of control, supervision and coordination of the nationalised and some other enterprises and for the establishment and development of new industrial enterprises and the matters connected therewith or incidental thereto. Article 4 (1) of President's Order No. 27 of 1972 provides that all such shares and other proprietory interests in each of the scheduled industrial enterprises placed under a Corporation by, or by an order under clause (1) of Article 10 and all shares and proprietary and other interests, as have not already vested in the Government by or under any law for the time being in force, shall by virtue of this Article and without any further proceeding or formality, stand vested in, and allotted to the Government free of any trust, mortgage, charge, lien, interest or other encumbrances whatsoever and on such placement the Government shall be the sole shareholder in or owner of such industrial enterprises. Thus on the commencement of the said order certain establishment like Bangladesh Jute Mills Corporation, Bangladesh Textile Mills Corporation and Bangladesh Sugar and Food Industries Corporation, Bangladesh Steel Mills and Engineering Corporation and Bangladesh Chemical Industries Corporation were established. It is further provided under Article 10 (IA) that "notwithstanding anything contained in any other law, an industrial enterprise, placed under any Corporation shall be deemed to have always vested in the Government and no such order of placement shall be challenged on the ground that the industrial enterprise or the shares or interest therein had not vested in the Government, or that the industrial enterprise or any share or interest therein was not liable to be vested in the Government." Mr. AF Hasan Arif, the learned Deputy Attorney-General and also the learned Advocate for the respondent No. 2, submitted that regardless of the question whether the company and its properties and assets were abandoned or not, the vesting of its share in the Government is complete after its placement under the corporation and the vesting is unchallengable. In support of his contention the learned Deputy Attorney General quoted the new clause (IA) which was added to clause (i) of Article 10 by way of amendment of President's Order No. 27 of 1972 by President's Order 153 of 1972 which provides as follows:

"(IA) Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law, an industrial enterprise, placed under any corporation by an order notified in the official Gazette under sub-clause (d) of clause (i) of Article 10 and all shares or other proprietory interest in such industrial enterprise shall be deemed to have always vested in the Government and no such order shall be challenged on the ground that the industrial enterprise or the shares and interest therein had not vested in the Government.er that the industrial enterprise, or any share and interest, therein, was not liable to be vested in the Government."

11. The learned Deputy Attorney-General also has drawn our attention to the subsequent amendment made in Article 4 of President's Order No. 27 of 1972 by Ordinance XXV of 1976 and submitted that in addition to Article 10(1A) under the amended Article 4(1) also the shares and other proprietary interests of the company, if not already vested in the Government, stand vested in and allotted to the Government free from any trust, mortgage, etc, without any further proceeding or formality stand vested in, and allotted to, the Government free from any trust, mortgage, charge, lien, interest or other encumbrances whatsoever. Let us now quote below the provision of Article 10(I)(d) which runs as follows:

"Bangladesh Steel Mills and Engineering Corporation and Bangladesh Chemical Industries Corporation in each of which shall have and exercise the powers of the corporation under this order in respect of such industrial enterprise including enterprises owned wholly or partly by the Government under the Bangladesh Abandoned Property (Control, Management and Disposal) Order 1972 (President's Order No. 16 of 1972) or owned or managed by any statutory corporation, as may by order published in the official Gazette, place under it,"

The learned Deputy Attorney-General argued that since an industrial enterprise established under Article 10(1) (a) to (d) can be placed by the Government under a Corporation it is immaterial as to whether the Company is an abandoned property or not. Once it is placed under a Corporation the vesting of its shares or other proprietory interests in the Government is complete and its abandoned character is a question of the past. It is submitted that the placing took place under the Government's general power of placement of all kinds of industrial enterprises and the resultant vesting is immune from any attack or challenge. Even if the industrial enterprise was not taken over under Acting President's Order No.1 of 1972 or under President's Order 16/72 the vesting of its shares or other proprietory interests taken place for the first time under President's Order No. 27 of 1972 is not invalid unless it could be shown that the placement is prompted by any malafide intention but under such circumstances the question of payment of compensation to the former share-holders will arise. Since it is claimed that an industrial enterprise was placed under the Corporation because it was taken over under Acting President's Order No.1 of 1972 then vested under President's Order No. 16 of 1972 and treated as an abandoned property as such, the placement was made not because it was just an industrial enterprise left uncared for by the owners or shareholders but because it was earlier declared and treated as an abandoned property. While analysing the scope of application of Acting President's Order No. 1 of 1972 and the President's Order No. 16 of 1972 we have seen that Acting President's Order No. 1 of 1972 applies in three situations 1) where the owners, directors or managers, or the majority of them, or any industrial or commercial concern have left Bangladesh, or 2) are not available to control and manage the concern, or 3) where, in the opinion of the Government of Bangladesh, the owners or directors of any industrial or commercial concern cannot be allowed, in the public interest, to control and manage the concern. To determine whether the company and its shares were placed under the Corporation under President's Order No. 27 of 1972 legally and properly, it is to be seen whether the vesting of the property as abandoned property under President's Order No. 16 of 1972 was legal and valid. It is submitted by the Deputy Attorney- General appearing on behalf of the respondent Nos. 1 and 3 that the industrial enterprise and commercial concern were taken over and placed under the Corporation by operation of Article 4 of Nationalisation Order, 1972 and vested in the Government under its general power of placement and no such order of placement can be challenged on the ground that the industrial enterprise had not vested in the Government, or that the industrial enterprise was not liable to be vested in the Government. It is submitted by the learned Advocate for the petitioners that in the instant case the company and its assets and shares having been taken over and placed not under the general power of the authority but for the reason that it was taken over under Acting President's Order dated 26.12.71, regularised under Acting President's Order No. 1 of 1972 and then vested as abandoned property under President's Order No. 16 of 1972, such taking over and placement is not immune from challenge. It has been found by the Supreme Court in the case reported in 45 DLR (AD) 69 that placement is the cause and the vesting is the result and therefore the placement of the property before it is taken over and vesting the same under President's Order No. 27 of 1972 is not proper. The basis of challenge is that the industrial enterprise on its being treated as abandoned property could not be placed under the corporation under Article 10(1) of President's Order No. 27 of 1972 and that being the basis of challenge is available to the petitioners in spite of the bar of Article 10(1A) and Article 4(1) as introduced in President's Order No. 27 of 1972 by Ordinance XXV of 1976. The question arises as to whether the company which owned the industrial enterprise was taken over under Acting President's Order No. 1 of 1972 and declared as abandoned property and, as such, its shares and proprietory interests have vested in the Government under the Industrial Enterprises (Nationalisation) Order, 1972 (president's Order No. 27 of 1972) and placed under the Corporation. The company was declared as abandoned industrial unit in terms of President's Order No. 16 of 1972 and thereafter the Government took over the management and control of the same. It is to be seen whether the company and its shares could be declared as abandoned property. If the application of President's Order No. 16 of 1972 is found to be unauthorized subsequent action taken on the basis of unauthorized decision were also unauthorized. Mr. Khondaker Mahbubuddin Ahmed submitted that the company was incorporated in the country before 25th March, 1971 and all the share-holders, directors, managers and staffs were present at that time and hence the question of taking over of the property under Acting President's Order dated 26.12.71 did not arise and furthermore, the company has not also fallen within the mischief of the definition of Article 2(1) of President's Order No. 16 of 1972 which runs as follows:

"2(1) "abandoned property" means any property owned by any person who is' not present in Bangladesh or whose whereabouts are not known or who has ceased to occupy, supervise or manage in person his property, including

(i) any property owned by any person who is a citizen of a State which at any time after the 25th day of March, 1971, was at war with or engaged in military operations against the People's Republic of Bangladesh:"

12. Though under sub-article 2(1) (ii) any property taken over under the Bangladesh (Taking over of Control and Management of Industrial and Commercial Concerns) Order, 1972 (Acting President's Order No.1) are included within the definition of the abandoned property but under Article 2(1) (i) (ii) (a) any property the owner of which is residing outside Bangladesh for any purpose which, in the opinion of the Government, is not prejudicial to the interest of Bangladesh are excluded. The question whether the property could be taken over initially under the Acting President's Order dated 26.12.71 was also raised in the case of Helal Jute Press Ltd. vs. Govt. of Bangladesh reported in 27 DLR 551 wherein it was held:

"The owners of the properties in question were the petitioner No.1, i.e. Helal Jute Press Limited, and this Company being incorporated in the then East Pakistan and having its registered office in Dacca, could not be considered at the point of time to be absentee owners who were not otherwise available in Bangladesh. "

In was also held:

"The provisions of Article 2(1) including clause (11) (a) of President's Order No. 16 of 1972 read together, would reasonably mean that the mischief of this law shall not be applicable to such persons who were away from Bangladesh for a temporary period not prejudicial to the interest of Bangladesh."

13. The learned Advocate for the petitioners argued that in the present case notwithstanding the fact that the company was incorporated within the territory now comprising Bangladesh the major share-holders of the company in question themselves may not be present in the country at the relevant time but they were not engaged in war on any occasion as they were British and Malaysian nationals and two of the shareholders were Bangladeshi nationals and the managers and top executives of the company were available in Bangladesh to manage and control the company. In the case reported in 27 DLR 1551 it was further held:

"Even if the major share-holder being its top management as Managing Director was away from Bangladesh for a temporary period, such absence could not be ascribed by the Government as prejudicial to the interest of Bangladesh particularly when the said person lived during his temporary absence in a country which was most friendly to Bangladesh at the relevant time and returned to Bangladesh as citizen of Bangladesh with the elearance of the Government of Bangladesh."

14. In support of his contention, the learned Advocate for the petitioners has taken us through the statements made in paragraph 2 of the writ application wherein it has been specifically asserted that the petitioner No. 1 Ariff A. Shekha and petitioner No. 10 are Bangladeshi nationals and petitioner Nos. 2-8 were British Nationals at the relevant time.

15. In the affidavit-in-opposition filed on behalf of respondent No. 1 on 14.12.87 and affidavit- in-opposition filed on behalf of the respondent No. 2 on 10.7.89 no specific denial has been made with regard to the nationality of the petitioner as stated in the writ application. At a later stage the respondent No. 2 in the affidavit-in-opposition raised doubt about the nationality of the petitioners No. 3, 4, 5 and 9 on the ground that their nationalities could not be verified by the Bangladesh Mission in UK for their alleged non-appearance. From the letter addressed to the petitioner N01 by the Ministry of Home Affairs, Immigration Branch-VI (Annexure-Xl) and two letters addressed to petitioner No. 1 Ariff A. Shekha on 25.1.82 and 12.2.82 (Annexure-XI) it appears that on verification of the nationality of the petitioners it was found that they acquired British Citizenship on different dates before 1971. From the certificate issued by the British Consulate General Karachi-6 on 4th August, 1976 it appears that the petitioner Ahmed Ismail Bhaimiah and his wife Mrs. Amina Bibi Patail were British subjects being holders of British passport on 16th December, 1970. Mr. Asrarul Hossain the learned Counsel for the respondent No. 2 appearing with Mr. Md. Khalilur Rahman, submitted that during Pakistani period dual citizenship was not allowed under Pakistani Citizenship Act of 1951. Dr. M. Zahir submitted that whether dual citizenship was permissible or not the fact remains that the petitioner once acquiring British nationality did not cease to be the British national at the relevant time. Section 14 of the Pakistan Citizenship Act 1951 (Act No. 11 of 1951 provides as follows:

"14. Dual Citizenship or nationality not permitted. (1) Subject to the provisions of this section if any person is a citizen of Pakistan under the provisions of this Act, and is at the same time a citizen or national of any other country, he shall, unless he makes a declaration according to the laws of that other country renouncing his status as citizen or national thereof, cease to be a citizen of Pakistan."

<u>16. Whether or not the petitioners had the dual nationality at the relevant time the fact remains that they were also the national of the country which was not at war with Bangladesh in 1971. Now the question arises as to whether the company and its share was rightly taken over and vested as abandoned company and, as such, placed under the corporation. It is found that the share-holders were either Bangladeshi or they were nationals of the country which were not at war with Bangladesh, the vesting of the company and its share under President's Order No. 16 of 1972 becomes unauthorized and for that matter the vesting of the said company and its share for the 2nd time under Articles 4(1) and 10(1A) of President's Order No. 27 of 1972 placing the same under the corporation which is resultant on the vesting of the company as abandone, in our view, is not immune from challenge.</u>

17. In the case of Government of Bangladesh vs. Messers ATJ Industries Ltd. and others reported in 28 DLR (AD) 120 the question regarding the interpretation of Articles 2(2) and 4 of the Bangladesh Abandoned Property (Control, Management and Disposal) Order was raised and it has been held that:

"It has first defined with denotation and connotation the words 'abandoned property' and then has employed an inclusive definition, and then an exclusion clause. It has also added an explanation. Interpretation of the definition clause no doubt creates some complexity. The best way to interpret it is to give a harmonious meaning to all the clauses of Article 2(1) so that each clause gets its own meaning and at the same time harmonises with the meaning of the whole. The defining part denotes property owned by a person who is either not present in Bangladesh, or whose whereabouts are not known, or who has ceased to occupy, supervise or manage in person his property. A question may arise whether the three sub-clauses are disjunctive or conjunctive. We think they have been used disjunctively and there is no need to construe them conjunctively".

It was also found:

"Then comes the inclusive definition. In the inclusive definition is included two categories of property, first is the property owned by a person who is a citizen of a State which after 25th day of March, 1971 either is at war or engaged in military operation against Bangladesh; the second is the property taken over by the Government under Acting President's Order No.1 of 1971. So far as the inclusion clause is concerned both the categories of properties come within the meaning of the definition of 'abandoned property. "

Then is the exclusion clause. The first question which arises is whether the exclusion clause also qualifies the inclusion clause. Except for the fact that the exclusion clause follows the inclusion cause, there is nothing in the grammatical construction of the whole clause to indicate that it qualifies the inclusion clause. Exclusion clause contemplates two categories of property. The first is the property the owner of which is residing outside Bangladesh for any purpose which in the opinion of the Government is not prejudicial to the interest of Bangladesh. The second is the property which is in possession or under the control of the Government under any law in force for the time

being."

18. Thus from the principle laid down in the case cited above, it is found that the construction of Article 2(1) is implicit in the determination of a property as an abandoned property. Therefore preliminary formation of the opinion of the Government is necessary. In this connection the case of Government of Bangladesh vs. Mirza Shahab lspahani reported in 40 DLR (AD) 116 may also be referred. In the said case the question of dual nationality was raised and it was contended by the Appellant-Government that the respondent cannot be deemed to be citizen of Bangladesh within the meaning of the provisions of Articles 2 and 2A of the President's Order No. 149 of 1972 and, therefore, the property fell within the definition of abandoned property under Article 2(1) (i) of President's Order of 16 of 1972. The respondent contended that his property is not an abandoned property as he never ceased to look after his property after liberation in 1971 and he also made representation to the Government but the Government refused to consider the same. The Appellate Division re-iterated the earlier decision in which it was held that:

"The law of abandoned property is a stringent law no doubt, but as has been noticed in 28 DLR and 30 DLR (SC) the definition contains the clause on exclusion and inclusion. One thing is very well settled that no person shall be deprived of his life and property unless it comes within the clear provisions of law itself. He cannot be deprived of his property by fallacious approach nor by provisions of enactment which merely by side wind points a finger to such property. To be taken away of any property it must be shown that his property has come within the mischief of law clearly."

In the said case it was also held:

"Citizen is distinct from nationality. Citizenship is solely a creature of domestic law. It refers to right which a state sees fit to confer upon certain individuals who are also its nationals. Citizens are those persons who have full political rights as distinguished from nationals who may not enjoy full political rights and are still domiciled in that country."

19. In the said case the property was released on the claim of the respondent Mirza Shahab Ispahani though he obtained the British nationality and was staying outside Bangladesh.

It is also held in the case:

"When there is no satisfactory evidence as to the respondent's permanent residence in this country on 25.3.71 and there is no averment that he relinquished his Pakistani Citizenship and the respondent's refusal to give satisfactory answer to the appellant's queries, it only deepens the appellant's doubt that he was on 25.3.71 and from that time on till 6.4.1972 a resident of the UK as a Pakistani citizen. Article 3 of President's Order No. 149 of 1972 provides that in case of doubt as to whether a person is qualified to be a citizen of Bangladesh under Article 2 of the said order, the question shall be decided by the Government, which decision shall be final."

20. The learned Deputy Attorney-General, Mr. AF Hasan Arif also questioned the locus standi of the petitioners to avail the scope to invoke the aid of the writ jurisdiction. The learned Deputy Attorney- General submitted that the petitioners' claim of shares in the company being a disputed question of fact they should have chosen the alternative forum for the establishment of their claim of share first before invoking the aid of writ jurisdiction. It is also submitted that the petitioners should have come before this court with the basic share-holding documents in the absence of which their claim cannot be entertained. Mr. Khondaker Mahbubuddin Ahmed and also at a later stage Dr. M Zahir referred to Annexure-M series which shows the acknowledgement of the receipt of the application for compensation in respect of the company 'Eastern Tubes Ltd.' along with the share certificates from the Ministry of Industries. In the supplementary affidavit filed on 9.3.94 summary of share capital and list of share-holders made up to 30th December, 1970 in respect of Eastern Tubes Limited as received from the office of the Registrar, Joint Stock Company, Dhaka, have been annexed as Annexure-O. No specific denial has been made challenging these documents which came from the Registrar, Joint Stock Company and Ministry of Industries and furthermore the respondents have not discharged their burden by way of producing their original share registers to controvert the position as it stood on 31st December, 1970. Thus there remained no controversy with regard to the holding of shares by the petitioners in the company. Furthermore, Bela Artifitex Industries Limited, which was found to have been released in favour of the petitioners, shows that the share-holding position and status of the petitioners were fully verified earlier. It has been stated in paragraph 8 of the writ petition that in respect of Bela Artifitex Industries Limited the Government being satisfied as to the nationality of the petitioners and with regard to the genuineness of the claim of those share-holders after holding enquiry through the Ministry of Home Affairs and the High Commissioner of Bangladesh in United Kingdom, released the said industry in favour of the owners and share-holders who are also the petitioners in the present case holding major shares in the company in question. It has been then argued on behalf of the respondents that the majority of the shares belonged to Latif Bawany Jute Mills Ltd. being 1,70,000 shares and the petitioners have not been able to show the transfer of the said shares from the Latif Bawany Jute Mills Ltd. to the petitioners. In reply, it is submitted in the supplementary affidavit filed on behalf or the petitioners that Latif Bawany Jute Mills Ltd. was the principal share-holder but not holder of 1,69,960 shares as alleged. Latif Bawany Jute Mills Ltd. owned 50,000 shares in 1966-67 and Taka 10,40,618.00 as due from Eastern Tubes Ltd. Latif Bawany Jute Mills Ltd. decided to convert this (share plus amount due up to Taka 10,00,000 into equity capital, i.e. shares of Eastern Tubes Ltd. and distributed the same as bonus shares in lieu of dividend to the share-holders of Latif Bawany Jute Mills Ltd. It is submitted that the petitioners are not in possession of the documents showing transfer of shares as the share-holders register are maintained by the Registrar Joint Stock Companies under section 31 of the Companies Act and furthermore, the respondents once admitted the claim of the petitioners for the payment of compensation. It is also submitted that since the respondents were in control of the books and records of the company it is required by the company to submit those in the court to show the correctness or otherwise of the share-holding position of the company. On perusal of paragraph 3(f) of the letter written by the Bangladesh Steel and Engineering Corporation on 30.12.81 annexed with the supplementary affidavit as Annexure-X by the petitioners it appears that share-holding list as verified on 30.12.70 was received by the petitioners from the Registrar of Joint Stock Company. It is said therein that" On verification of the share list as on 30.12.70 received from the Registrar of Joint Stock Company it is found that 1,00,345 shares are held by the above 10(ten) shareholders instead of 1,04,265 Nos. out of which claim for 91,099 shares were verified and accepted for payment of compensation and submitted to the Ministry of Industries for payment. It is understood that no payment has yet been made by the Government. The position may be confirmed by compensation wing of Ministry of Industries. "It also stated in paragraph 34 "in order to verify the share-holding position of the Enterprise we requested the Registrar of Joint Stock Company to send us the list of share-holder as in 1971 and subsequent changes, if any. We have since received the share-holding position as on 30.12.69 and 30.12.70."

21. Mr. Asrarul Hossain, the learned Counsel, submitted that a share-holder of a company has no direct interest in the property of the company. The learned Counsel cited the case of Punjab Ali Pramanik and others vs. Mohd, Mokarram Hossain reported in 39 DLR (SC) 185. The learned Counsel has also cited the case of EBM Company Ltd. vs. Dominion Bank reported in 1937 (PC) 279 wherein it was observed "Their Lordships were unable to support the decision in favour of the Bank upon the grounds suggested by Riddell, JA. They believe it to be of supreme importance that the distinction should be clearly marked, observed and maintained between an incorporated company's legal entity and its actions, assets, rights and liabilities on the one hand, and the individual shareholders and their actions, assets, rights, and liabilities on the other hand."

<u>22. The principles laid down in the cited case are not relevant and helpful for the purpose of coming to a decision in the instant case. From the facts and circumstances and the submissions made by the learned counsels of the respective parties it is found that this company along with its assets and shares was first taken over under Acting President's Order dated 30th December, 1971 then regularized under Acting President's Order No.1 of 1972 and with the promulgation of President's Order No. 16 of 1972 the company along with its shares and assets were treated as abandoned property on the alleged ground that the shareholders and the officers were not found available in Bangladesh to take control and management of the company. At the time of taking over the company as abandoned the formation of the opinion of the Government as to its abandoned character was necessary. It is submitted by Mr. Khalilur Rahman, the learned Advocate for the respondent No.2, that the shares of the company Artifitex Ltd. were not released but sold to the previous share-holders. Under sub-clause (a) of clause (i) of Article 2 of President's Order No. 16 of 1972 the property of the person who is away from the country for a temporary period being not prejudicial to the interest of Bangladesh and under sub-clause (b) of the said Article 2(1) (ii) of President's Order No; 16 of 1972 the property or industrial concern though taken over under the possession and control of the Government under the Action President's Order No. 1 of 1972 are excluded from being declared and treated as abandoned property. Furthermore, before declaring a company as abandoned Government is to form opinion that the owners and share-holders were absent from the country and were not found to control and manage the company and or that they were residing in a country which was at war or engaged in military operation with Bangladesh after 25th day of March, 1971 . This view gets support from the case reported in 30 DLR (SC) 101 and 40 DLR (AD) 116. The control and management of the enterprises in question having been taken over under Acting President's Order No. 1 of 1972 it falls within the exclusive clause of Article 2 of President Order No. 16 of 1972 and, therefore, we are of the view that the vesting of the company and shares thereof bringing it within the mischief of President's Order No. 16 of 1972 and on that ground placing and vesting of the same to the corporation under President's Order No. 16 of 1972 by the Government without applying its mind so as to hold that the absence of the share-holders were prejudicial to the interest of Bangladesh, cannot be accepted. As the definition of the abandoned property were not attracted in the instant case, the company and all its assets could not be said to have vested in the Government and consequently the taking over of the company along with its assets and shares and placing the same for the management and control of the Corporation on the ground that it was treated as abandoned cannot also be said to have been validly done. In the instant case separate Rule was issued on the prayer of the petitioners by this court on 23.1.91 calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the notification bearing No.186-SI dated 31.12.71 in respect of the company and subsequently regularized by the Acting President's Order No. 1 of 1971 published in the Bangladesh Gazette Extraordinary of January, 3, 1972 should not be declared to have been made and published illegally and without lawful authority. From the notification it appears that the company was taken over along with all its property's assets located in Bangladesh for appointing management board to operate and conduct the affairs of the enterprise. This is not a case that under President's Order No. 27 of 1972 the industrial enterprise were taken over and vested in the Government applying Articles 4 and 10(1A) regardless and also independent of the vesting of the property under President's Order No. 16 of 1972. Had it been so then it would have been necessary for us to see whether the placement of the company and its share thereof under Acting President's Order No. 1 of 1972 was lawful or not As the company and its shares have been vested under President's Order No. 27 of 1972 on the ground that it was vested in the Government as abandoned property, under President's Order 16 of 1972 if it is found. that the company and shares thereof does not carry abandoned character then the shares of the petitioners who were found to have been away from the country and have been residing as its national in any country which was not at war with Bangladesh could not be treated as abandoned shares and for that matter could remain vested with the Government. Furthermore, it will not be out of place here to mention that the Ministry of Industries acknowledged the share certificates submitted by the petitioners for the purpose of compensation in respect of Eastern Tubes Limited and Annexure-X series to the supplementary affidavit filed on behalf of the petitioners and Annexure-J filed by the respondent Nos. 1 and 3 along with the affidavit- in-reply filed by the petitioners and the supplementary affidavit-in-opposition filed by the respondent Nos. 1-3 show the share-holding position of the petitioners in company in question and contain the statements of verification of shares by the Bangladesh Steel and Engineering Corporation for the purpose of payment of compensation to the share-holders of Eastern Tubes Limited.</u>

23. From the facts and circumstances and materials placed before us and the reasons stated above, we find that more than 50% shares of the industrial concern Eastern Tubes Limited which was incorporated in Bangladesh and more than 51 % shares were held by the petitioners who were found to have been absent from the country but could not be found by the Government that they were national of a country which were at war with Bangladesh at the relevant time and, therefore, their shares are not liable to be treated as abandoned. In view of the above we hold that the decision as communicated vide letter dated 27.5.87 (Annexure-II) for retention on 51 % shares with the Corporation has been taken without any lawful authority and is of no legal effect and, as such, the same is liable to be released in favour of the petitioners after ascertaining the shares on proper verification. This order of ours relates to shares of the petitioners in respect or Eastern Tubes Limited only.

In the result, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to costs.

End.
