parties:
Amena Khatun and ors ------ Petitioner
vs.  
Md Afsaruddin being dead his heirs 1 (ka) Maleka Khatun and ors ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
This application by the defendant petitioners is directed against the judgment and decree dated 16- 7 -92 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 1st Court, Dhaka in T A No.185 of 1968 affirming those dated 30-3-1968 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 5th Court, Dhaka in TS No.22 of 1967. 

2. The opposite party No.1 Md Afsaruddin (now dead) as plaintiff filed Title Suit No.22 of 1967 against the predecessor of present petitioner and opposite party Nos. 2-19 for partition and recovery of khas possession after assertaining the plaintiffs' title to the suit land which is an undivided dwelling house. 

3. The plaintiffs', case, in short, is that one Abdul Gafur was the original owner of the suit plot and he sold the same to defendant Nos. 1 to 4 who were brothers on 31-10-32. Defendants No.4 Kalimuddin while in joint possession of the same property transferred his 4 annas share to his wife Safatunnessa by registered Heba bil Ewaz deed dated 22-7-42. Thereafter Safatunnessa possessed the land till 22-1-53 and then sold it to plaintiff by registered sale deed and delivered possession to him. The defendant No.1 filed a pre-emption case against the aforesaid transfer being miscellaneous case No.62 of 1956 under section 26F of the Bengal Tenancy Act against the plaintiff but the said Miscellaneous case was dismissed. In the meantime plaintiff was dispossessed from the suit land and then he was compelled to file the suit. The defendant No.1 contested the suit by filing written statement staung that the defendant is the real owner of the entire plot of land and has purchased the same in his name and also in benami of his 3 minor brothers and that Heba bill Ewaz deed of defendant No. 4 in favour of his wife Safatunnessa was a forged document and the plaintiff has acquired no title to the land by purchase. His further case is that, he is entitled to purchase the undivided share of the suit plot which is the homestead and filed the petition suit to buy the suit land under section 4 of the Partition Act. The trial Court decreed the suit. Defendant No.1 preferred appeal and the appellate Court by its judgment and decree dated 16-7-92 upheld the trial Court's judgment. Being aggrieved at the aforesaid judgment of the appellate Court the petitioners preferred this application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained the present Rule. 

4. Dr Rafiqur Rahman, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, submitted that the petitioner has been possessing the suit plot which is an undivided house for more that 30 years and he is entitled to buy the same under section 4 of the Partition Act and the learned Additional District Judge erred in law in deciding the case under section 4 of the Partition Act and as a result justice is denied to the petitioner. He further submitted that though the suit land is stated to be a chala land but it is a part and parcel of the petitioner's house where he grows vegetables and, as such, the suit land cannot be considered as a separate land from the dwelling house ?f the petitioner. In support of his above contention he relied on the decisions reported in 42 DLR (AD) 53; 40 DLR(AD) 150, 10 DLR 318, 12 DLR 649; 20 DLR 489, 22 CWN. 575, AIR 1960 (Cal) 467, ILR (Cal) 873, IC 1940, 117 and 12 CU 525. In the case reported in 40 DLR (AD) 150 wherein their Lordships made an observation, after discussing the case laws reported in the aforesaid 22 CWN, AIR 1960 (Cal), 12 CU and some other similar cases of Indian High Courts. Similarly, the observation made by their Lordships in 12 DLR and 20 DLR as stated above is almost same. I shall discuss the above observations later on. In reply to the above submission Mr. Reazul Karim, the learned Advocate for the opposite party, submitted that the petitioner filed the pre-emption case and he lost and, as such, he is debarred from purchasing the suit land under section 4 of the Partition Act. He further submitted that opposite party possessed the suit land after purchasing the same and he was subsequently dispossessed from the suit land which made him to file the suit. He also submitted that the petitioner did not disclose how the suit land belonged to undivided family of the petitioner as the land was transferred as chala land and not as homestead and, as such, section 4 of the Partition Act is not applicable in this case. In support of the above contention he cited a decision reported in 36 DLR 350. It is admitted that one co-sharer ie defendant No.1, transferred his share in favour of his wife Safatunnessa on 22-7-42 and Safatunnessa possessed the same for more than 11 years and transferred the same to the opposite party No.1 by registered Kabala dated 22-11-1953. The defendant No.1 of the original suit filed a pre-emption case against the said transferor but the same was dismissed as barred by limitation. In the petition suit under section 4 of the Partition Act the defendant No.1 stated that the suit property is an undivided homestead and the suit land is the land of his purchased plot by 4 brothers including the defendant No.1 The court below held the view that the entire suit plot is not the undivided dwelling house of the defendant No.1 as the suit land has been described in khatian as chala land where vegetables are grown. Since the suit land is a part and parcel of land where other 3 brothers have got dwelling house, it is an adjacent land and part of the suit plot. It is admitted that the plaintiff-opposite party is a stranger purchaser. In a case reported in 40 DLR (AD) 150 (Sree Jugal Kishori Sarker vs. Azizur Rahman and others) their Lordships observed: "As to the meaning of dwelling house for the purpose of section 4 it was noticed: "The terms house or dwelling house are ambiguous terms and for the purpose of section 4 of the Partition Act must be liberally construed. The terms should be taken to mean not only the structure or building but also adjacent buildings, garden, courtyard, orchard, and all that is necessary for the convenient occupation of the house. In support of the proposition, we need refer to the following, from amongst numerous decisions on the point." Section 4 of the Partition Act was enacted for the benefit of the undivided members of the family against the stranger purchaser. Their Lordships Amin Ahmed CJ and Asir J in a case reported in 12 DLR 649 (Bhaba Kanta Joddar and others VS. Satish Chandra Mandai and others) observed: "The language of section 4 does not militate against the view that the object of the legislature being to prevent intrusion by strangers to the dwelling house of an undivided family, the terms of section 4 should be liberally construed." Similar view has been taken in a case repotted in 20 DLR 489 (Mohammad Habibullah and another VS. Moulvi Saleh Chowdhury and others) wherein their Lordships held: "Section 4 of the Partition Act was enacted to afford protection to the members of an undivided family against stranger purchaser Its simple object was to prevent intrusion into the dwelling house of an undivided family by strangers on the basis of purchase of some share in such dwelling house."

5. In the instant case it is found that the suit land is a contiguous and parcel of an undivided homestead upon which house of the defendant No.1 and other members of his family is situated. Though the suit land is stated in the Kabala as chala land, it is part of undivided family which has not been partitioned previously. According to the decision of 40 DLR (AD) 150 as stated above adjacent buildings, garden, courtyard, orchard, and all that is necessary for the convenient occupation of the house is a part of the dwelling house. So, the suit land though stated in the Kabala as chala land is a part of dwelling house. The petitioner in his petition under section 4 of the Partition Act stated that the suit land is a part of his own undivided homestead. So the prayer made by the petitioner in the trial Court under section 4 of the Partition Act is considered legal. But both the Courts, below overlooked this fact and arrived at a wrong finding specially the appellate Court, that the suit land is not the undivided dwelling house of the defendant No.1 The lower appellate Court also held that the defendant No.1 and his wife transferred some land to strangers and they possessed the same since purchase. These purchasers are compromising persons as argued by Dr Rahman, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, and they have been accommodated by the defendant No.1 and by other co-sharers of the dwelling house and they did not enter into the suit land forcibly. There is force in his argument. The stranger purchaser who is not acceptable to other members of the family can not come into the undivided dwelling house and possess it forcibly and section 4 of the Partition Act does not permit it. In a case reported in 42 DLR (AD) 53 (Sayesta Bibi and others vs. Juma Sha and others) wherein their Lordships held: "After considering the mores of our people the co-sharers' attachment to their ancestral house and their anxiety to preserve the purdha and privacy of the members and inmates of the undivided dwelling house, the legislators made the provisions of section 4 of the Partition Act. The expression a dwelling house belonging to an undivided family is to be liberally construed." 
6. The learned appellate Court without considering the above facts of the case, came to an erroneous finding that the suit land is not the part of dwelling house of an undivided family. 

7. In view of the above discussion I, find substance in the argument put forward by the learned Advocate for the petitioner. 

8. In the result the Rule is made absolute without any order as to cost. 

9. The judgment and the decree of the Court below are 'hereby set aside. Send down the lower court records immediately. 

Cost assessed by the lower court in respect of the share of the suit land is maintained. 

End.

parties:
Raufique (Md) Hossain ------ Petitioner 
[In Writ Petition 88 of 1995] 
Md. Alauddin Khalid   ------ Petitioner 
[In Writ Petition 161 of 1995] 
vs.
Speaker, Bangladesh Parliament and others ------ Respondents 
[In all the Writ Petitions]
full_judgment:
AM Mahmudur Rahman J: The Writ Petition No.88 of 1995 filed under Article 102(2)(a)(i)&(ii) is for a writ of certiorari and Writ Petition No. 161 of 1995 filed under Article 102(2)(a)(i)&(ii) for a writ of mandamus arise out of an unprecedented event as happened in the Parliamentary democracy. And as these two petitions arise both question of great public importance and involve intricate interpretation of different provisions of the Constitution the Division Bench comprising myself and my learned brother Mr. Justice Hamidul Hoque issued the Rule Nisi in Writ Petition No. 88 of 1995 in the following terms:

"18.1.95

Mr. Md. Moksodur Rahman.......................for the petitioner.

Let the supplementary affidavit filed today be formed part of the main petition.

Let a Rule Nisi issue calling upon the respondent Nos. 1-5 only at the risk of the petitioner to show cause as to why the resignation letters submitted on behalf of 147 Members of the Parliament on 28.12.94 should not be declared to be illegal and void, or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

The respondent No.1 is restrained by order of this Court not to give his opinion regarding resignation letters of the Members of the Parliament numbering 147.

The Rule is made returnable within l(one) week from date.

In view of urgency of the matter we direct the petitioner to serve copy of the writ petition along with the Rules upon the respective respondent personally and the service of the notice of the Rule on those respondents through office is dispensed with.

Let this Rule be heard along with the Rule issued in Writ Petition No.161 of 1995."

And in Writ Petition No.161 of 1995 the Rule was issued in the following terms:

"Let a Rule Nisi issue calling upon the respondents to show cause why the respondent No.1 shall not be directed to take action as required under the Constitution on the resignation letters submitted by 147 Members of the Parliament, or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

The Rule is made returnable within 1 (one) week from date.

Let this Rule be heard along with the Rule issued in Writ Petition No. 88 of 1995.

Let this matter come up in the list on 25.1.95 at the top for hearing."

2. Thereafter the said Division Bench after perusing the application filed by respondents 3, 4 and 5 for constitution of a larger Bench on the ground that the petitions involve important and complicated questions of interpretation of several Articles of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh and hearing the learned Advocates of the applicants, the learned Attorney- General and the petitioner passed the following order.

"we have perused the two petitions and also heard the submission of the learned Advocates. As we feel that these petitions need to be heard by a Special Bench, we send these to the learned Chief Justice for his kind order."

The learned Chief Justice by his order dated 29.1.95 constituted this Bench comprising myself and my two learned brothers, namely, Mr. Justice Kazi Ebadul Hoque and Mr. Justice MA Karim and directed "to hear and dispose of the matter".

3. Both the writ petitions arise out of resignation of the seats of Parliament by 147 Members of the Parliament. But at the outset I must say that Writ Petition No. 88 of 1995 has been drafted haphazardly in an unusual manner and the events that led to file the petition are founded mostly on the news items published in the different national dailies of the country on different dates which are annexed to this petition in support of the statement of the petitioner. However, the narration of the episode, which led to the submission of the resignation letters and gave rise to these two petitions viz, Writ Petition Nos. 88 and 161 of 1995, in short, is that the election of the members of the 5th Parliament was held on 27.2.91 and after publication of the result in Gazette Notification the members elected took oath of their office. The respondents 3-5 were elected from respective constituencies. Respondent 3, Mrs. Sk. Hasina alias Sk. Hasina Wazed is the President of the Awami League and leader of the Opposition in the Parliament. Respondent 4 is the Acting Leader of the Jatiya Party in the Parliament while respondent No.5 is the leader of the Jamaat-e-Islami Party in the Parliament in Writ Petition No.88 of 1995. After the election the Parliament has been holding sessions regularly for legislative functions. But the respondents 3-5 along with the members of the Parliament belonging to their respective parties had been abstaining from attending the sessions of the Parliament from March 1, 1994 on the plea of non-acceptance of their demand by the Treasury Bench headed by the Prime Minister Begum Khaleda Zia for holding next general election of the members of the Parliament under a caretaker Government. That demand was made as they thought that no fair and free election could he held under the umbrella of the ruling party. It was further stated that not only the opposition members of the Parliament started boycott of the sessions of the Parliament but they also called hartals frequently to press home their demand and such boycott and hartals led one Mr. Anwar Hossain Khan to file Writ Petition No. 1001 of 1994 for a declaration, amongst others, that the unabated boycott by the opposition members was unconstitutional and void. The Constitutional Bench, however, on contest made the Rule absolute and declared, amongst others, the boycott and the demand for care-taker government void and unconstitutional with a further direction to the respondents 3-5 to attend the Parliament. It stated that demand for care-taker government was made following the result of by-election in the Magura-2 constituency held on 20.3.94 and the boycott of the Parliament created a serious political crisis and Sir Ninian Stephen, a Special Envoy of the Commonwealth Secretary General, came to Bangladesh to resolve the political deadlock He held dialogue between the competiting compass of political parties without any fruitful result and he left Bangladesh on 21.11.94. The petitioner further states that even after the failure of Sir Stephen attempts were made to continue the dialogue to solve the problem in different ways and the people were in serious tension every moment awaiting in anxious expectation for peaceful solution of the political impasse. But all were futile attempts and the opposition members of the Parliament submitted their resignation letters to the respondent 1 on 28.12.94 at 9-13 PM. The petitioner also states what happened on the eve of the submission of the resignation letters on that fateful night quoting from the news published in his petition. He states that on 28.12.94 at 7-15 PM Mrs. Sheikh Hasina along with other leaders went to the Chamber of the respondent 1 to submit resignation letters. But the respondent 1 led them to his "call-on-room" for another round of talks. After several rounds of telephonic talk a Government team of three members Prof Budruddoza Chowdhury, Mr. Abdus Salam Talukder and Mr. Oli Ahmed, came to the Parliament reportedly to sign an agreement with the opposition parties. But as the talk with the opposition leaders broke down the leaders of the ruling party left the Parliament around 9-10 PM and the Whips of the respective opposition parties submitted the identically worded resignation letters to the respondent 1 Mr. Sk. Rajjak Ali, the Speaker. The reason for failure of the talk was reported to be, according to the opposition parties, that ruling party introduced some new condition while the negotiators of the ruling party alleged that the opposition parties were going back from the commitment. It is stated that for accepting the demand of the opposition that the Prime Minister should not continue in office after the expiry of the term and the President was to conduct election the ruling party demanded a guarantee from the opposition parties that they would desist from calling any hartal or siege programme for the rest of the current term of the 5th Parliament. Imposition of this condition was considered by the opposition leaders an infringement of their fundamental political right of mass agitation and demonstration and for imposition of such conditions the last 'ditch-effort' fizzled out and 147 members of the Parliament tendered their resignation letters to the respondent 1. Mr. Azizur Rahman, Awami League Whip, submitted 93 resignation letters of the Members of the Parliament belonging to Awami League, Mr. Monirul Hoque Chowdhury submitted 34 resignation letters of the Members of the Parliament of the Jatiya Party while Mr. Latifur Rahman submitted 19 resignation letters of the Members of Parliament of the Jamaat-e-Islami and Mr. Salahuddin Kader Chowdhury, the leader of the Nationalist Democratic Party submitted his resignation letter peronally to the respondent 1. The resignation letters were worded in identical words stating that they were compelled to resign in the greater interest of the country as the Bangladesh Nationalist Party Government had rendered Parliament ineffective and each resignation letter contained the signature of the individual Member of the Parliament. After the resignation letters were submitted, it is stated by the petitioner, quoting from the newspaper, that as a part of the effort to save the nation from confrontation the opposition parties abstained from submitting the resignation letters even after the deadline mentioned and shifted from their original position but the Government foiled the sincere effort. The petitioner also quotes the statement of Moulana Matiur Rahman Nizami published in the newspaper saying that resignation letters were an expression of "........................no confidence in the 5th Parliament and the BNP Government, and both now lost their legitimacy." The petitioner again quoted a portion of the news published in the 'Daily Star' on 29.12.94. The summary of which is that former Minister and Jatiya Party Member of the Parliament Maj. Genl.(Retd) Mahmudul Hasan revolted against party decision on resignation from Parliament and joined Bangladesh Nationalist Party and Mr. Mizanur Rahman Chowdhury, acting Chairman of Jatiya Party, expressed his surprise at the joining of Mr. Mahmudul Hasan to Bangladesh Nationalist Party. He said that all Members of the Parliament of Jatiya Party had submitted their resignation letters to him a few days ago on the decision of the Presidium of the Jatiya Party decision to resign. He further quoted the news that the Awami League Chief Sk. Hasina announced at a huge rally that the Prime Minister should resign following the announcement of Election Schedule and the President would dissolve Parliament and form an interim government with either a serving or a retired judge of Appellate Division of the Supreme Court or a non-partisan personality as the Prime Minister with an Advisory Council and the members of the Council will be the nominee of the ruling party and the opposition parties. The Jatiya Party and the Jamaat-e-Islami also in their respective rallies announced that the interim government would be dissolved with the appointment of the new Prime Minister after the general election and the new frame-work would be ratified by the next elected Parliament. Mrs. Sk. Hasina also announced that after their resignation they would launch movement for the single demand for resignation of the Government of Begum Khaleda Zia to ensure free and fair election under non-party care-taker administration. He also quotes the news appeard in 'Daily Star' on 30.12.94, 31.12.84 and 5.1.1995 and 6.1.1995 which published the news that Prima Minister told at a public meeting opposition should revise the decision while Mrs. Hasina asked the Government to resign and to hold election as per opposition formula. It also reported that the Prime Minister had said that the country was to be run as per Constitution, and the Bangladesh Nationalist Party would not accept the Advisory Council and the opposition had said that the election was the only solution. It further reported that Mrs. Sk. Hasina wanted dissolution of the Jatiya Sangsad and hold a fresh election and Awami League urged the Government to return to the path of peace. But the Jatiya Party had said that there was no possibility of compromise but a discussion regarding when and how the government would resign and hold general election under the care-taker administration might be held. The petitioner also quoted the news appeared on 6.1.95 to the effect "efforts are still on for amicable solution to the persisting political impasse to avoid an apprehended confrontation between the opposing political camps following the en masse resignation of 147 opposition law-makers". The petitioner states further that resignation was piloted by the leaders of their respective parties including respondents 3-5 and the resigning members did not exercise their power of resignation in good faith under Article 67(2) which enables an individual member to resign for unavoidable reason and Article 67(2) does not contemplate en masse resignation under the pressure of the political parties. The petitioner further states that last parliamentary election held on 27.2.1991 was not held under a care-taker government as claimed by the opposition political parties but it was held under an interim Government when the former Chief Justice Mr. Justice Shahabuddin Ahmed performed the functions of the President being appointed the Vice President by the outgoing President HM Ershad to enable him to transfer power within the existing Constitutional scheme, the Presidential System of Government, which had nothing to do with holding an election of Members of the parliament and 12th Amendment of the Constitution has brought about a change in the method of transfer of power to the successor government through parliamentary election but the political leaders misled the people that the present government has come to power through election held under a care-taker Government. He states that the Government of Justice Shahabuddin Ahmed had no role in holding election except to place some necessary staff at the disposal of the Election Commission. He further states that members of the Parliament had taken oath to discharge their duties faithfully according to law but they have violated the oath by resigning seats. In the supplementary affidavit the petitioner states the 'Daily Dinkal' in its issue dated 3.1.1995 reported, that doubt had arisen in the mind of the Members of the Parliament belonging to the opposition parties that the resignation letters were not separately written. (Annexure-C to the supplementary affidavit is the copy of the daily Dinkal dated 3.1.1995).

4. In Writ Petition No. 161 of 1995 the petitioner states that he is an Advocate of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh and is a conscious citizen of this country and he is one of those who wants that nobody whoever he may be should be allowed to act against the provisions of the Constitution of Bangladesh and see that democracy should be allowed to function smoothly and democratic institution to act in accordance with law for establishment of equity and justice in the society. Thereafter he stated that 147 members of the Parliament handed over their resignation letters to the respondent 1 in the evening of 28.12.94. But Respondent 1 malafide got himself admitted in the Suhrawardy Hospital in the evening of 30.12.94 and was discharged on 4.1.95. But even after discharge from the hospital 12 days although passed the Respondent 1 willfully and intentionally withheld his imperative duty in respect of resignation letters received by him on 28.12.94. The petitioner further states that under the Constitution the Respondent 1 has no authority to sleep over the resignation on any plea and the delay in processing the matter is nothing but malafide one with the intention to frustrate the decision of 147 MPs which has put the nation in suspension which is encouraging deterioration of law and order situation in the country by resorting to hartals, aborods, etc. by opposition political parties.

5. In his affidavit-in-reply to the affidavit-in- opposition and the further affidavit-in-opposition of respondent 4 the petitioner of Writ Petition No. 88 of 1995 mostly reiterated his statements made in the writ petition. He, however, asserted that he did not file the writ petition for political motivation at the instance of any political party nor the petition was filed for vindication of a public interest as alleged by the respondent 4. He admitted that his source of information is the news items published in the newspapers which he terms as authentic and correct. He also denied the statement of the respondents that the petition is premature and asserts that the statements of para 29 of the affidavit-in-opposition were malicious. He also denies the truth of the statements of the respondent that the petition and the Rule issued created constitutional crisis and rather he asserts that the writ petition is filed to save the Constitution and the democratic process and states that it is the opposition parties who are bent upon to create constitutional crisis.

6. The Rule issued in Writ Petition No. 88 of 1995 is opposed by the respondents 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and respondent 7 by filing separate sets of the affidavit-in-opposition. Respondents 1 and 2 filed a joint affidavit-in-opposition while respondent 3, 4, 5 and 7 filed separate affidavit-in-opposition each.

7. The respondent 3 in her affidavit-in- opposition raised a preliminary objection to the maintainability of this writ petition on the ground that the petitioner has no locus standi to file the writ petition as he is not "a person aggrieved" within the meaning of Article 102 (2) of the Constitution and she including respondents 4, 5 are not "persons" within the meaning of Article 102(2)(a)(ii) of the Constitution inasmuch as they are not performing function in connection with the affairs of the Republic and in no way related to any statutory body and that the petition is premature, as according to the statement of the petitioner, the Speaker is yet to give decision on the submission of the resignation letters; The learned counsel for Respondent 3 also took the stand that this court is debarred from exercising its power as vested under Article 102 of the Constitution in view of Article 78(2) of the Constitution inasmuch as resignation relates to functioning of the Parliament, the powers and privileges of the members of the Parliament and is not amenable to judicial review by this court. There is no cause of action for this petition; the issues involved in this petition are of political nature and are beyond the ambit of Article 102 of the Constitution. As the petition is malafide and suffers from inordinate delay, filed after 9 months from the date all the opposition political parties launched movement for restoration of voting rights of the citizen by calling hartals, procession and holding meetings in order to ensure democracy, by holding free and fair election, this court should not exercise its discretion conferred under Article 102 of the Constitution; the petition suffers from defect of parties; it raises disputed question of facts regarding coercion in obtaining resignation letters from the resigning members of Parliament; the respondent 3 denies the truth of the statement of the petition that the 147 members of the Parliament resign their seat malafide to create political crisis and states that as the members acted in accordance with their constitutional right as envisaged under Article 67(2) of the Constitution this court cannot interfere with exercise of such constitutional right; the petitioner has failed to make out a case that his legal right is injured by reasons of resignation and that Article 67 (2) read with Rules 177 and 178 of the Rules of Procedure of Parliament of the People's Republic of Bangladesh (hereinafter shall be called the Rules) do not make any distinction between resignation and en-masse resignation. The respondent 3 also denied the allegations of the petitioner that the respondents are not performing their duties. And she, on the other hand, asserts that movement for care-taker government is a political movement for ensuring voting right of the people which is essential for democracy. She states that the petition founded on the statements made in paras 8-10 are based on the newspaper cutting relating to political issues cannot be considered by this court as news published in newspaper are not simpliciter admissible evidence; she asserts that each Member of the Parliament of the opposition parties specially of the Awami League had tendered their resignation letters separately and voluntarily in writing without any coercion in obedience to the decision of their respective parties and denies the statement that the resignation letters were submitted under coercion. She further states that none of the resigning members ever denied the fact that they voluntarily resigned on 28.12.94. She also asserts that the Election Commission has been rendered useless as it solely depends on the Government and the Bangladesh Nationalist Party government in by-election held in Mirpur and Magura proved that they are interested in corrupt practices. With reference to the statement of paragraph 16 of the writ petition respondent 3 states that all the opposition political parties represent 69% of the electorate and the Bangladesh Nationalist Party is afraid of holding election under care-taker government for losing in the election and it wants to remain in power practising fraud upon the electorate and the plea of amendment of the Constitution for care-taker government is fraudulent excuse to stay in power. It is further stated that as the present Government is the creation of care-taker Government it should have accepted the demand of the opposition parties but the government is not accepting as it wants to indulge in corrupt practices in election which it had adopted in by-election of Magura. She also denied the statements that by resignation the Members of the Parliament have faulted their oath.

8. Respondent 4 in his Affidavit-in-opposition states that the petitioner has no locus standi and the writ petition has been filed for political purpose as public interest litigation; the petition is also premature as the resignation letters are pending with the respondent 1 who has not yet given his decision thereon and he denies the statement of the petition that the leaders of the respective political party piloted resignation and that the members of the parliament had not exercised their power in good faith and that they were compelled to resign. He states that the resignation letters were submitted bonafide, voluntarily and those are genuine as they resigned after it was made clear to ruling party by announcing in the meeting of the respective parties held on 5.12.1994 that each member expressed his desire to resign voluntarily if the demand for amendment of the Constitution for care-taker Government is not accepted by the Government as similar decision was announced on 6.12.94 in the public meeting of the Jatiya Party that the members of the Parliament would resign on 28.12.94 if the demand was not accepted by 27.12.94. Respondent 4 denies the statement of the petitioner that submission of resignation is fraud upon the Constitution and the law. The respondent 4 like respondent 3 states that the present government came to power through a fair and free election held under a non-partisan government headed by the Chief Justice Mr. Justice Shahabuddin Ahmed. It is further stated that on 28.12.94 each member signed the resignation letter individually and when went to the Parliament accompanied by their leaders to submit resignation letters they were informed about the willingness of the government to come to an amicable settlement submission of resignation letters was withheld for two hours. Prof. Badruddoza Chowdhury. Mr. Oli Ahmed and Mr. Abdus Salam Talukder, however, arrived at 9-00 PM and informed that government accepted the demand of the opposition and the Prime Minister had agreed to resign 30 days prior to the national election. Respondent 4 also states that the Speaker was told that resigning members were present and should be available when called by the Speaker, In the further affidavit-in-opposition he stated that the petitioner is a political worker who filed the petition malafide at the instance of an influential faction of ruling party and the statements based on inaccurate news items cannot be relied upon.

9. Respondent 5 similarly states that the petitioner has no locus standi and the writ petition is outside the scope of judicial review under Article 102 of the Constitution. He also echoed the voice of respondent 3 that the opposition parties represent 69% electorate of the country and the demand for holding election under a care-taker government is a democratic demand. It is further stated that mere existence of Election Commission is not the guarantee for holding fair and free election and in 1991 the election held under the care- taker government was the free and fair one. He denies the statement that in 1991 parliamentary election was not held under care-taker government. He further denies that resignation by 147 Members of the Parliament is threat to the Constitutional deadlock and to peace and harmony in the society. He also states that news reports arc nothing but mere surmises and conjectures.

10. Respondents 1 and 2 state that petition is premature and not maintainable as it was filed when the resignation letters were awaiting the decision of the respondent 1. With reference to the statements made in paras 12 and 13 of the petition it states that on 28.12.94 at about 9-00 PM respondent 1 received 3 folders said to contain resignation letters submitted by the 147 Members of Parliament-one was filed by Mr. Matiur Rahman the other by Mr. Mizanur Rahman Chowdhury and another by Moulana Nizami. The respondent 1 immediately after receipt of the folders announced that those required scrutiny as per Article 67(2) and Rule 177 of the Rules of Procedure of the Parliament of the People's Republic of Bangladesh and requested the members of the Parliament who resigned their seats to appear before him in his office and when he called the name of some Members of the Jamaat-e-Islami he found nobody of the three political parties present except Mr. Salahuddin Kader Chowdhury of the National Democratic Party (NDP). Thereafter respondent 1 told the waiting journalists about receipt of the folders and of the absence of the members. He also told that he required time necessary to examine the resignation letters contained in the folders as per Constitution. These statements are also made on the basis of the news published on 29.12.94 (Annexures 1, 2, 3, 4& 5). It is further stated that on scrutiny it was found that signature on the resignation letters of two members of the Parliament belonging to the Awami League did not tally with their specimen signatures kept in the Parliament Secretariat and these letters did not bear any date. It is stated that the discrepancy required verification as to the genuineness of the resignation. It is stated further that Mr. Akhtaruzzaman MP was absconding and Mr. Mustafizur Rahman, MP by a letter informed on 28.12.94 that he did not submit any resignation letter. Maj. General (Retd.) Mahmudul Hasan of Jatiya Party by a letter dated 28.12.94 also informed that he had decided not to resign although his resignation letter was found in the folder submitted by Mizanur Rahman Chowdhury. It is also stated that some of the letters found in the folder were antedated showing the dates as 8.11.94 and 9.11.94. On 30.12.94 respondent 1 fell sick and was in Suhrawardy Hospital till 4.1.95. on his release, in spite of the advice of the Doctor to take rest, he resumed duty on 6.1.95 because of the urgency of the matter. It is stated that on verification respondent 1 found that in almost in all the resignation letters reason assigned was the failure of the ruling party to amend the Constitution for holding election under a neutral government and since the matter involves intricate constitutional and legal aspect he needed more time for scrutiny, etc. and he issued press release on 12.1.95 (Annexures 6-9). He denies the statement of the respondents 3-5 that Parliamentary election held on 27.2.91 was held under a care-taker government and states that it was held under the interim Government. It is further stated that neither the Constitution nor the Rule prescribes any time limit for scrutiny of the resignation letters and failure to complete verification and examination of resignation letters within two weeks is no failure to discharge his function calling for interference by this Court. It is further stated the even after submission of resignation letters negotiations between the ruling party and the opposition party continued to resolve the crisis which facts were published in the national daily as press briefing and the statements made by the leaders.

11. Respondent 7 also filed an Affidavit-in-opposition stating that although no Rule is issued against it but it appears as is impleaded as Respondent in the petition and states that filing of this Affidavit-in-opposition is necessitated for controverting and for denial of the allegation made against it by the Respondents 3-5 in the" Affidavit-in-opposition. Although it is stated that the extent of the authority of the Speaker to examine and decide as to the genuineness and voluntary nature of the resignation letters involves questions of interpretation of the Constitution and law, the privilege and the jurisdiction of the High Court Division to entertain writ petition. But also states that the petitioner is not a "person aggrieved" and, as such, cannot invoke writ jurisdiction and the petition is not maintainable. It terms the statement of the respondents 3-5 that if the Prime Minister remains in power she will influence the process of election of the Member of the Parliament and the voters of our country cannot exercise their franchise according to their free will as baseless and not correct. It further states that there is no provision for holding election under care-taker Government in the Constitution and such demand is contrary to the Constitution and submission of resignation by 147 members of the parliament created critical situation. It further states that as no Rule is issued on the respondent 7 the allegation made by respondents 3-5 in their affidavit- in-opposition against the respondent 7 are not justified and it denies the allegation made against the government. It further states that the statement of the respondents 3-5 that movement for care-taker government is constitutional and for ensuring the democratic right to the people is not correct and also denies the statements of respondent 3-5 that the Election Commission is totally and solely dependent on the Government. It further states that as the Bangladesh Nationalist Party is not impleaded as party in the writ petition it is unfair and unwarranted to make allegations against the said party which should go unconsidered by this court as these are motivated and are of political nature. It further states that allegations against Members who are not parties in this petition are ill founded and are denied. It further states that the statement of the respondent Nos. 3-5 that any democratic government would have responded to the demand of the respondents 3-5 is not correct inasmuch as the government is to function in accordance with the provision of law and it has no obligation to accept unconstitutional political demand. It further denies the truth of the statement of the respondents 3-5 that the Returning Officers being civil servants cannot work independently. It is stated that the allegation that there is intolerance, inaptness, insolence, arrogance, obstinacy and lack of experience and apprehension on the part of the government are irrelevant and unwarranted for the purpose of this Rule as those are political issues and ought not to have been raised in the writ petition. It further denies the statement made by respondents 3-5 that the present government has lost its popularity and legitimacy. It asserts that the statement made in paragraphs 43-45 of the Affidavit-in-opposition requires strict proof thereof by the makers of the statement. The allegation made against the Ministers who are not parties are unfair and unwarranted and denies the statement that a Member of the Cabinet was compelled to resign on the issue of Care-taker Government.

12. The Rule issued in Writ Petition No.161 of 1995 is opposed by respondents 1 and 2 filing affidavit-in-opposition wherein the respondents took a preliminary objection as to maintainability of the petition. It states that the petitioner has no cause of action and he not being a "person aggrieved" within the meaning of Article 102(2) (a) has no locus standi to file this petition. Secondly the respondents state that submission of resignation letter is an action taken under Article 67(2) of the Constitution and as it relates to the internal matter of the Parliament concerning regulation of procedure, conduct of business and maintenance of order in the Parliament this Court has no jurisdiction to issue the Rule. The respondents further state that whether resignation has been submitted duly or not is the subject matter of decision by the Speaker. It is further stated the discrepancies found in some letters and the failure of the members to appear before the respondent 1 when he made announcement for such appearance after receipt of three folders because it is imperative on his part to verify the genuineness of the signatures in the letters of resignation of MPs. in view of the Rule 177 of the aforesaid Rules. It further stated that according to Rule 177(2) respondent felt obliged as he considered it his constitutional obligation to examine whether or not the said resignation letters assigning reasons as aforesaid is contemplated by Article 67(2) of the Constitution. Even after filing of the resignation letters negotiations were going on making offer and counter-offer to resolve the matter and as such respondent 1 needed to examine the various legal aspects in the light of the aforesaid Constitutional provisions and the Rules. Respondent further states that matter involves complicacy as it involved interpretation of Constitution requiring to scrutinize the matter in greater detail and needed more time. Such views of the respondent 1 were published in the newspapers on 12.1.95 (Annexures 6, 7, 8 and 9 in affidavit-in-opposition). He further states that the Constitution and Rules do not contemplate that he is to act without satisfying himself as to the genuineness and legality of the resignation letters and more so in the backdrop and the manner the resignation letters were submitted by three leaders of the opposite parties. He states that submissions made in paragraphs 13 and 14 of the petition are misconceived, false and motivated. The statement made in paragraphs 15 and 16 of the petition is not maintainable. He categorizes the statements made in paragraph 17 as imaginary and baseless. He further states that there being no time limit provided in the Constitution and the Rules and for the stay order of the High Court it cannot be contended that he failed to discharge his responsibility under the Constitution. The petitioner also filed affidavit-in-reply. Except few statements most of those are by way of submission and reiteration of the statements made in the writ petitions. It is pertinent to observe that affidavit- in-reply insofar as it relates to submissions cannot be said to be a proper affidavit-in-reply. An affidavit- in-reply is meant to deny the truth of any false statement made in the affidavit-in-opposition and not to take a different stand from the original stand taken in the petition. But here we find petitioner made a departure from the original stand which I deprecate inasmuch as the Supreme Court as the highest Court of the country has cautioned in this regard.

13. Mr. KS Nabi the learned Advocate for the respondent 3, raised a preliminary objection on the maintainability of the Writ Petition No. 88 of 1995 and took a number of grounds on the merit of the writ petition. On the ground of maintainability he submits first that the petitioner has no locus standi as he is not a "person aggrieved" within the meaning of Article 102(2)(a) of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh (hereafter shall be called the Constitution). Secondly, the writ petition is premature. Thirdly, this Division has no jurisdiction under Article 102 of the Constitution to entertain the writ petition relating to the function, the business and the procedure of the Parliament as resignation from the seats of Parliament relates to the privileges of the Members and the Parliament is immuned from judicial review by this Division under Article 102 of the Constitution.

14. On the merit of the case he urged the petition raises political issues which cannot be settled by this court under Article 102, that there is no distinction between submission of a resignation letter and submission of resignation letters en masse in view of the language of Article 67 of the Constitution read with Rule 177 of the Rules of Procedure of the Parliament of the People's Republic of Bangladesh and that resignation was effective from 28.12.1994 the moment the Speaker received the resignation letters; that the writ petition suffers from defect of parties in that no other member except the resigning members was impleaded in the writ petition, that the petition alleges that the resignation letters were submitted under coercion and they were malafide, antedated and the signatures of the resigning MPs do not tally with their signature kept in the office of the Parliament, etc.

15. Mr. Moudud Ahmed, the respondent 3, appears in person and submits that as the petition is not founded on the ground of infringement or invasion of fundamental or any legal right of the petitioner there is no reason to declare en masse resignation void under Article 102 of the Constitution. He also echoes the contention of the respondent 3 that the petitioner is not "a person aggrieved" within the meaning of Article 102(2)(a) of the Constitution. He also submits that as the writ petition raised issues of political nature it should not have been entertained. He continues to say that where the petitioner fails to establish his petition on constitutional or on any legal right he is not entitled to invoke the jurisdiction of the High Court Division as confirmed upon it by Article 102 of the Constitution. Mr. Ahmed submits that the act done must invade a substantial and direct right of the petitioner which, according to him, is totally absent in this case before me. He further submits that as the petition suffers from vagueness and inadequate information it is liable to be dismissed summarily.

16. Mr. Abdur Razzaq the learned Counsel for the Respondent 5 also took the stand that the petitioner has no locus standi and being a crank and a busybody having no stake is not a "person aggrieved" within the meaning of Article 102(2) of the Constitution. He contends that in order to invoke writ jurisdiction not only the petitioner is to satisfy that his fundamental or any legal right has been violated but as well he must satisfy the court that he has got a direct and substantial interest in the subject matter. Mr. Razzaq stoutly argued that this court has transgressed its jurisdiction under Article 102 of the Constitution in issuing the Rule arising from submission of resignation letters by 147 MPs in that act of resignation relates to parliamentary privilege of the Members of Parliament and in view of the provisions of Article 78(2) of the Constitution the act done by the 147 Members of Parliament in resigning their seat of Parliament is not justifiable in court and, as such, is not amenable to judicial review by this Division under Article 102(2)(a)(ii) of the Constitution. He also submits that as the matter is pending before the Speaker the writ petition is premature. He also submits on merit that this Division is not empowered to give declaration that the resignation letters submitted are void and without lawful authority; that the writ petition suffers from defect of party that the issues involved in this petition are of political nature. He also contends that Article 102 provides for corrective measures of the records of the Subordinate Court or Tribunal but this court has no authority to issue Rules upon the respondent 1. Speaker of the Parliament, who is neither a subordinate Court nor a Tribunal and resignation letters not being before the court, there is no scope even for application of the corrective measure by this court in exercise of its power under Article 102 of the Constitution; that as respondents 3-5 the Member of the Parliament are not persons performing any function in connection with the affairs of the Republic or of a local authority this Division has no authority to issue the Rule under Article 102 upon them; Mr. Razzaq further submits that the Rule should be discharged as the petition is the outcome of the collusion between the petitioner and the respondents 1, 2 and 7 and raises the question of disputed facts.

17. Mr. Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, learned Additional Attorney-General, appearing for the respondents 1 and 2 also contends first, on the standing of the petitioner, saying that as the petitioner is not "a person aggrieved" within the meaning of Article 102(2)(a) of the Constitution the writ petition must fail. In other words, he submits that a person seeking to invoke the extraordinary writ jurisdiction as conferred upon the High Court Division under Article 102 of the Constitution must satisfy the court that he has a direct personal interest in respect of the matter for breach of which he seeks remedy.

18. Mr. Moksumul Hakim submits that the allegations made by the respondents 3-5 against respondent 7 and the Bangladesh Nationalist Party is indecorous and should not be considered by this Division at all. He submits that as the petition is premature and as no specific relief is sought for against respondent 7 it should fail. He continues to submit that wording of Article 78(2) is differently worded in our Constitution insofar as it relates to Parliamentary privilege from that of Britain where Parliament is supreme. He also submits that the statement of the petitioner is based on mere apprehension and, as such, it does not call for issuance of the Rule under Article 102 of our Constitution. He further submits that Article 67(2) read with Rules 177 and 178 of the Rules of Procedure of Parliament of the People's Republic of Bangladesh requires consideration by respondent 1 to examine whether for resigning the seat the members assign any reason and whether the resignation letters contain any extraneous matter.

19. Mr. Moksudur Rahman in reply to the preliminary objection raised by the respondents vehemently argued that petitioner, a citizen of Bangladesh and a member of the Dhaka District Bar, like other citizens who are politically conscious has got locus standi to file the writ petition before this court. He continues to argue that the resignation has affected the petitioner because the petitioner is vitally interested in orderly running of the Government and the election of the members of the Parliament according to the Constitution but resignation has posed an imminent danger to a Constitutional deadlock and threat to the peace and harmony in the society and holding of frequent hartals by the members of the opposition parties has affected the democratic process. On the contention of prematurity of this writ petition he submits that cause of action has not arisen as the matter of resignation of 147 is pending with the respondent 1 as contended by the respondent is not correct and submits that it has arisen from March 1, 1994 and cause of action is a recurring one continued till submission of resignation letters. He further submits on the merit of the case that the petition is made bonafide and shall not defeat on the ground of malafide as contended by the respondents.

He also argued that Article 67(2) does not conceive of en masse resignation and such resignation is malafide and constitutes fraud upon the Constitution and by such resignation the Parliament has been crippled and the democracy is halted. He further referred us to the preamble of the Constitution and Articles 8, 11, 21 and 75(i)(b) to contend that the resignation of the present nature is not only opposed to Article 67(2) but it is also opposed to the concept of the democracy as enshrined in the preamble, Articles 8 and 11 of the Constitution. Relying on Article 21 he submits that it is the duty of every citizen to observe the Constitution and the laws but the 147 members of Parliament by resigning en massee have violated the provision of Articles 8, 11 and 21. It is pertinent to say that those Articles fall under Part-II of the Constitution and relate to the Parliament Principles of State Policy. He further contends that the resignation letters were procured for collateral purpose to achieve the common goal for holding general election under a care-taker Government which is not contemplated under the Constitution.

20. Mr. Nabi on the contention on merits also replies and submits that contention of the petitioner that submission of the resignation letters was malafide and was obtained for collateral purposes is not correct as the members themselves submitted resignation letter bonafide out of their own decision and those were not obtained under coercion and no fraud on the Constitution has been practised by en massee resignation. He submits that the statements made in the petition and the affidavit give rise to the disputed question of fact which cannot be received on affidavits and on this ground this Division should discharge the Rule. He submits that the fundamental principles of state policy envisaged in Articles 8, 11 and 21 of the Constitution upon which the petitioner relies for the declaration sought in this Division are not justifiable in Court under Article 102 of the Constitution.

21. In support of their argument in both the cases the learned Advocates for the petitioners and the respondents referred us to a large number of decisions but I shall refer these in my judgment which I consider necessary.

<u>22. Before I enter into the question of maintainability I want to address on the jurisdiction of the High Court Division under Article 102 of the Constitution in issuing the Rule on the facts of the present parties as at the Bar a serious attempt was made to argue that by entertaining the writ petitions the High Court Division has entered into the exclusive domain of the parliamentary privilege and thereby invaded the sovereignty of the Parliament. In other words, the judiciary has come in conflict between the Supreme Court and the Parliament raised at the Bar it is necessary briefly to highlight the concept of sovereignty of the British Parliament which emerged out of long conflict of power between the House of Commons and the King and which has also inspired the founding fathers of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh and other countries to import that concept and its extent in their national constitutions and functioning of the British Parliament which does not work under a written Constitution and that of ours including the USA, the Republic of Ireland, India, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, etc. which work under the written constitution. But before tracing this conflict and growth of Parliamentary sovereignty of England I want to point out the difference between our Constitution and written constitution of other countries. Our constitution has its own distinctive characteristics unlike the constitutions of other countries specially that of India and Pakistan. The Constitution of Pakistan and India were the outcome of a peaceful transfer of power to the Dominions created by the British Rulers. But ours is an autochthonous constitution which has its root in the will of the people who won independence through "a historic war for national independence". To have a fair idea what is autochthonous constitution reference may be made to SA De Smith's treatise" Constitutional and Administrative Law", 3rd Edition In this work he has said "And a few countries have deliberately chosen to adopt a new constitution peacefully but in a manner unauthorized by the pre-existing constitution. This is an assertion of legal nationalism of what is called constitutional autochthony designed to demonstrate that the authority of the constitution is rooted in native soil, not derived from an imperial predecessor. Such a course has been followed in Eire (the Republic of Ireland), India and now Sri Lanka (Ceylon). A constitution is adopted by a Constituent Assembly in the name of the people, or presented to the people for their approval; it will not receive the royal assent like normal constitutional amendment". The difference between the Parliament of England and of ours and other countries where there are written constitution is that British Parliament unlike the Parliament of other countries enjoys absolute sovereignty subject to limitations imposed by its Houses. The contention leads me to examine the extent of the respective jurisdiction and function of the two organs of the State. There in no conflict between the function of the Parliament and that of the Superior Court meaning both the Divisions of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh. The Constitution clearly delineates their respective field of activities. The Parliament is competent to enact law and also to make amendment of the Constitution itself within the prescribed constitutional limitations. The function of the Supreme Court is to interpret the law given by the Parliament and the constitution in exercise of its power conferred by the constitution itself. Its function is to point out mistakes, if any it can declare any enactment ultra vires which is inconsistent and repugnant to the Constitution. Thus, both the Parliament and the Supreme Court act within their respective areas of activities under the Constitution. The Parliament of our country does not enjoy absolute sovereignty like the Parliament of the United Kingdom. The Parliament is the ultimate authority to give the law to the nation and that is not the function of the judiciary. In this respect it is pertinent to point out that the power of our judiciary to declare law ultra vires of the Constitution is not as wide as that of the Supreme Court of USA which has its stake on the doctrine of "due process of law". Be that as it may, the judiciary is not to function "as a kind of Third House" but it is to point out the wrong done, by the Legislature through interpretation of a provision of law given by the legislature. "It is not the function of any court or Judge to declare void or directly annul a law the moment it has been promulgated. Courts are not a supervisory body over the Legislature Their function is interpretative. In other words, upon any particular case coming before them in which the right of any party is involved, they decide whether the Act or any part of it is to be disregarded on the ground of its incompatibility with the Constitution." (vide Chotey Lal vs. State of Uttar Pradesh 1951 (Ali) 228). Thus, I find no conflict between the judiciary and the Parliament in functioning in their respective areas of activities. I must be failing in my duty if I do not say that it is necessary for both the organs—the Parliament and the Judiciary to function within restriction imposed by the constitution for the working of the Constitution and its preservation. And this also needs self-imposed restraint on the part of both the organs of the State. Now I look backward to state a historical background of the development of sovereignty of the Parliament of United Kingdom and privilege to the Houses and their members as we have fashioned our Constitution with the Parliamentary Sovereignty more in the line of the British Parliamentary System. May in his monumental treatise "Parliamentary Practice," 16th Edition under the heading "Jurisdiction of the courts of law in matters of privilege" at page 150 in a chronological form has given a brief sketch history of controversy, the long course of conflict resting on the acceptance of the limitation in regard to the internal proceeding of the House of Commons of England. As far back as 1330 AD on the basis of lex Parliament it was claimed that members of the Houses were to be tried exclusively by the Houses and they were not to be punished by any inferior court for their conduct in Parliament. Although such right no longer is recognized to the same extent "but a further branch of the lex Parliament, namely, that each House has the right collectively to discuss the subjects of its own choice without reference to the King, and that individual members in debate can speak their mind with immunity, is generally recognized and accepted." May also cites the case of one Thorpe of the year 1452. Thorpe was Speaker of the House of Commons. He was imprisoned in a suit. House of Lords in confirming order of imprisonment observed that Thorpe was entitled to release. In approaching the matter, however, the learned Judges of the House of Lords exhibited an extreme respect for the authority of the Parliament." In the case of Evelyn, a member of Parliament, Bridgman CJ, in 1664 "Foreshadowing the ultimate resolution of the conflict of jurisdiction, asserted the power and duty of the courts to determine the question of Parliamentary Privilege arising in a manner incidental to the proper jurisdiction, denied that Parliamentary decisions on privilege were necessarily conclusive, but at the same time admitted that the Parliamentary jurisdiction was exclusive over matter arising ab intra." In the case of Topam, Sergeant-at-arms of the House of Commons, decided in 1682 the King's Bench, the persons arrested by the Sergeant-at-arms brought an action. Topham pleaded privilege of the House of Commons. The King's Bench disallowed that the House of Commons had such privilege. The House of Commons after declaring the judgment of the King's Bench illegal and violation of the privileges and rights of the parliament sent for the judges and after hearing them they were directed to be imprisoned. The Judges, however, admitted that "when the entire matter is transacted in the House. it would have been proper to plead such matter to be outside the  jurisdiction of the court,"  In 1811 in the case of Abbot, the Speaker of the House of Commons, Abbot, directed imprisonment of Burdett on the order of the House of Commons. The matter went before the House of Lords. The House of Lords held that the House of Commons had acted in directing imprisonment of Burdett within its power which were no more than those enjoyed by the Superior Courts. In the case of Hansard, Hansard was a publisher of the House of Commons. He was sued for libel in 1836 for publication of certain papers on the order of the House of Commons. Hansard pleaded immunity on the ground of privilege that "the High Court of Parliament" was a Supreme Court and either House of Parliament was the final authority to decide the question of Parliamentary Privileges. In that case again all the Judges of the Court held that "Over its own internal proceedings the jurisdiction of the House was exclusive." In the case of Bradlaugh, Bradlaugh was elected a member of the Parliament and he was refused the right to take an oath and as he was disturbing the proceedings of the House of Commons. The House directed the Sergeant-at-arms to remove him from the House until Bradlaugh disengaged him from disturbing proceedings of the House. The matter went before the Queens' Bench. It refused relief to Bradlaugh against the denial of his rights to take an oath by the House of Commons. The observation of Stephen, J, in that case is in the following mariner: I think that the House of Commons is not subject to the control of Her Majestry's Courts in its administration of that part of the Statute-Law which has relation to its own internal proceedings. "We further observed "the order under which the Sergeant acted related to the internal management of the procedure of the House over which the Court had no jurisdiction." and refused the relief to Bradlaugh. May after survey of subsequent cases on the point of Parliamentary Privilege as claimed by the House of Commons concluded—"So far the position reached seems capable of being briefly stated as follows. The jurisdiction of House of Parliament over its own internal proceedings is exclusive; but the Courts claim jurisdiction over matters of privilege which affect the rights of persons exercisable outside Parliament".</u>

<u>Cornelius J in Pakistan vs. Ahmed Saeed Kirmani at page 423 of the Report observed "over the rest of the field of privilege as claimed by the House of Commons, there is yet no unanimity, so that it is possible for writers on constitutional law to say that "there may be at any given moment two doctrines of privilege the one held by the Courts the other by other House, the one to be found in the Law Reports the other in Hansard and there is no way of resolving the real point at issue should the conflict arise." He further observed with reference to Article 89 of the Constitution of Pakistan 1956. "If a proceeding is an internal proceeding of a Provincial Legislature........ Assembly and relates to its proper business, then under Article 89 it must be recognized as such by the courts and the courts must refrain from interfering with it." The decision in the case of Kirmani were out of certain allegations made by a member of the Provincial Assembly relating to dispute in connection with the election of Speaker of the Provincial Assembly and voting by the members of the Assembly. Article 89(1) reads as follows: "89 (1). The validity of any proceedings in a Provincial Assembly shall not be questioned in any court," Presently I shall quote Article 78(1) of the Constitution and it will be seen that the language used in Article 89(1) of the 1956 Constitution of Pakistan and that of Article 78(1) of the Constitution of Bangladesh is identical in nature. In that case Cornelius J, ultimately held that business of election of Speaker is the internal business of the Assembly itself and, as such, it is protected under Article 89(1) of the 1956 Constitution of Pakistan. In a summary of the conclusions to be reached on the basis of the decisions in the case cited May points out at page 174 that while Parliament which consists of the Sovereign and the two Houses is supreme, this is a legislative supremacy and is without effect upon the privilege jurisdiction of either House acting singly; that since it has been agreed since 1704 that neither House can itself add to its privilege, Parliamentary privilege is objective and its extent is ascertainable, and consequently, belongs to the law of Parliament which is a part of the law of the land. The Judges are therefore bound to take judicial notice of Parliamentary privilege. The Courts have also recognized certain exclusive jurisdictions of the House in the field of privilege of which only one is relevant namely that "the control of each House over its internal proceedings is absolute and cannot be interfered with by the Court". In the case Ahmed Sayeed Kirmani of the Supreme Court of Pakistan in an illuminating passage Cornelius, J. expressed the view of the court on the Parliamentary Privilege in delimiting the extent of the privilege of the Provincial Assembly as contemplated in Article 89 of the Constitution of Pakistan, 1956. The learned Judge in the facts of that case observed:</u>

<u>"In view which I have taken, this Rule which has statutory force, being made under power conferred by the Constitution, must be given the force of a law declaring that the announcement of the result of voting by division once made by the Speaker is not to be challenged in any court of law. It is of course amenable to correction, for instance, if a member votes who has a direct pecuniary interest in the question, his vote may be disallowed on a substantive motion carried by the Assembly subsequently. At pages 303 to 407 of May's Parliamentary Practice, there are discussed ways and means by which errors occurring in divisions may be corrected, and the votes of uncounted members may be allowed. In the same discussion will be found a reference to the case of a Member who through inadvertence votes in the wrong lobby The rule is that the vote is to be counted in the lobby in which such a Member presented himself, despite his intention to go to the other lobby, which clearly points to the fact that the choice of the Member becomes determined once and for all when he presents himself in a particular lobby. On consideration of all the facts as they appear in the case, I feel no hesitation in concluding that the proceedings in question were wholly within the privilege of the House, and wholly outside the jurisdiction of the Courts".</u>

<u>In the light of the observation made in the case referred to earlier in this judgment I am to see how far the contention raised at the Bar is tenable on the facts of this case and in view of the provision of Article 78(1) and 78(2) of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh. To appreciate the contention it is necessary to quote Article 78.</u>

<u>Article 78(1) reads:</u>

<u>"The validity of the proceedings in Parliament shall not be questioned in any court."</u>

<u>and Article 78(2) reads:</u>

<u>"A member or officer of Parliament in whom powers are vested for the regulation of procedure, the conduct of business or the maintenance of order in Parliament, shall not in relation to the exercise by him of any such powers be subject to the jurisdiction of any court."</u>

<u>The expression "proceedings-in-Parliament" does not find place in the interpretation in Article 152 of the Constitution nor in the definition Rule 2 of the Rules of Procedure of Parliament of the People's Republic of Bangladesh. Therefore in order to have a clear idea of the meaning of the expression guidance may be had from May's Parliamentary Practice, a valuable as well as trustworthy work. May at page 62 of his work says:</u>

<u>"The primary meaning, as a technical parliamentary term, of "Proceedings" (which it had at least as early as the seventeenth century) is some formal action, usually a decision taken by the House in its collective capacity. This is naturally extended to the forms of business in which the House takes action, and the whole process, the principal part of which is debate, by which it reaches a decision."</u>

<u>From a Canadian Judgment which was quoted by Maya fair impression of the meaning of the expression "proceedings" may be obtained. The quotation is as follows:</u>

<u>"I desire it to be understood, however, that I do not hold that a Member of Parliament is not amenable to the ordinary courts for anything he may say or do in Parliament. I merely say he is not so amenable for anything he may say or do within the scope of his duties in the course of Parliamentary business, for in such matters he is privileged and protected by lex at consuetudo Parliamenti."</u>

<u>May also referred to definitions contained in a report of the Select Committee on Official Secrets Act in the year 1930-39 which reads:</u>

<u>"It covers both the asking of a question and giving written notice of such question, and includes everything said or done by a Member in the exercise of his functions as a Member in a Committee of either House, as well as everything said or done in either House in the transaction of Parliamentary business,"</u>

<u>It is also necessary to understand what is called the privilege of the Parliament although the term "Parliamentary Privilege" is a difficult term for an exact definition. Prof Dicey in his introduction to the study "The Law of Constitution" says that-</u>

<u>"Nothing is harder to define than the extent of the indefinite powers or rights possessed by either House of Parliament under the head of privilege or law and custom of Parliament."</u>

<u>Parliamentary privilege is indeed, to use language of Redlich, which has been quoted by May in his "Parliamentary Practice":</u>

<u>"The sum of the fundamental rights of the House and of its individual members as against the prerogative of the Crown, the authority of the ordinary Courts of law and the special rights of the House of Lords"</u>

<u>The decision of Rajnarayan Singh vs. Atmaram Convind, 1954 (All) 319 may be referred to. In that decision their Lordships explained what is parliamentary privilege. It is held that Parliamentary privilege of the House of Commons of United Kingdom means that sum of the fundamental rights of the House and of its individual members as against the prerogative of the Crown, the authority of the ordinary Courts of law and the special rights of the House of Lords. The aforesaid observation is in the line of the observation made in the case of Bradlaugh vs. Grosett as referred to earlier in our judgment. In the case of Harendra Nalh Barua vs. Bev Kania Barua, 1958 Assam 160 a similar question fell for determination by their Lordships regarding the rights and privileges of the House of Parliament and the House of State Legislature. Sarjoo Prosad, CJ after reviewing the constitutional provision of Britain, Australia in this regard observed:</u>

<u>".................it is well established now that the House of Commons in England has certain well defined rights and privileges, honoured and sanctified by tradition and custom, one of the most important of them being the right to commit a persons for contempt of its high authority and dignity and for breach of its privilege. This power extends not merely to members of the House but even to person outside and when the acts are in vindication of these rights and privileges, the Courts of the land have no right to interfere. The proper forum is the House itself where the person affected can claim the redress of his rights. By virtue of the Indian Constitution, these powers and privileges are enjoyed by the House of Parliament in India and the Houses of the State Legislatures".</u>

<u>And ultimately his Lordship held that the privileges relate to the internal business of the House itself. In the light of the aforesaid observation there is no room for doubt to hold· that the resignation letters as submitted by 147 members of the Parliament to the respondent 1 is outside the ambit of Article 78(1) of our Constitution inasmuch as the act of submission of resignation to the Speaker by the members of Parliament though in connection with the business of the House but it does not form a part of the proceeding of the Parliament within the meaning of Article 78(1) of the Constitution of Bangladesh and that too is one stage ahead of the business of the Parliament. That stage will reach the moment when "the Speaker shall bring the fact to the notice of the House, if it is in session" in accordance with the provision of Rule 178(3) of the Rules of the Procedure of Parliament of the People's Republic of Bangladesh. In this regard Mr. Razzaq seriously contends that it is not only what is being done and talked in the Parliament attracts the immunity provision of the constitutional privilege insofar as it relates to the MP and officer of the Parliament but what is being done and talked outside the Parliament precinct.</u>

<u>Acceptance of such contention of Mr. Razzaq will be stretching the meaning of the expression "proceeding in Parliament" as appears in clause (1) of Article 78 of the Constitution too far. This contention seems to me unfounded in law and I am afraid to accept. Thus, from a close analysis of the decisions referred to above in the judgment it manifestly becomes clear that the action brought before the court in those cases had their origin in the proceeding-in-Parliament and were immuned from judicial service and were protected "Parliamentary Privilege". In the instant case, submission of resignation en masse (en bloc) to the Speaker is not immune from judicial review as under clause (2) of Article 67 of the Constitution a member of the Parliament may resign his -seat by writing under his hand addressed to the Speaker of the Parliament.
