The expression "addressed to the Speaker" used in Clause (2) of Article 67 has no protection of Article 78(1) of the Constitution inasmuch as resignation letters submitted to the Speaker does not fall within the ambit of the expression "proceeding of Parliament" as envisaged in Article 78(1) of the Constitution for the simple reason as neither resignation in writing "addressed to the Speaker" nor "submission of the resignation letters to him" is a proceeding of the Parliament by any of the definitions of which reference has been made earlier in this judgment notably the definition given by O' Conner, J, to RV Runting, 7 Ontario reported (vide page 62 of May's Parliamentary Practice, 16 Edn). Therefore, I am of the opinion that neither this Division in issuing the Rules in those two writ petitions has transgressed its jurisdiction conferred under Article 102(2) (a)(ii) and (i) far less to enter into conflict with the Parliament by invading the domain of Parliamentary Privilege or by stretching its sleeve to any proceeding of the Parliament or a member or officer of the Parliament as protected under clauses (1) and (2) of Article 78 of the Constitution. Thus, the contention raised at the Bar to oust the jurisdiction of this Division is the result of misconceived idea about the constitutional provision of this Article and accordingly, it fails.</u>

23. Now, I proceed to examine the contention as to maintainability of the Writ Petition No. 88 of 1995. Mr. Nabi contends that the petitioner has no locus standi to maintain this petition as none of his direct and substantial interest has been invaded by the resignation in question. He cites the following decision to contend that as in those decisions the petitioners were found to be aggrieved persons the writ petitions were maintainable before the courts. But as in the instant case the petitioner is not a "person aggrieved" within the meaning of Article 120(2) (a) the Rule must fail. Before I enter upon the discussion of the decisions cited by Mr. Nabi I refer to Article 102(2) (a) of our Constitution.

"102(1) The High Court Division on the application of any person aggrieved may give such directions or orders to any person or authority, including any person performing any function in connection with the affairs of the Republic, as may be appropriate for the enforcement of any of the fundamental rights conferred by Part III of this Constitution.

(a) on the application of any "person aggrieved" make an order-

(i) directing a person performing any functions in connection with the affairs of the Republic or of a local authority to refrain from doing that which he is not permitted by law to do or to do that which he is required by law to do; or

(ii) declaring that any act done or proceeding taken by a person performing functions in connection with the affairs of the Republic or of a local authority has been done or taken without lawful authority and is of no legal effect; or

(b).....................................................

(i)......................................................

(ii)...................................................

(3)...................................................

(4)...................................................

(a)...................................................

(b)...................................................

(5)...................................................

From Article 102(2) (a) it is seen that petitioner who wants a direction upon persons performing any functions in connection with the affairs of the Republic from this Division in the nature as contained in Article 102(2) (a) (i) or a declaration that an act or proceeding taken by such persons has been done or taken under Article 102(2) (a) (ii) without lawful authority and is of no legal effect must satisfy the court that he is a "person aggrieved". Now, I revert back to the cases relied upon by Mr. Nabi. He cited the following decisions:- The cases Bar Council vs. MV Dabholkar, 1975 (SC) 2095, DC Nakara and others vs. Union of India, 1983 (SC) 103, Dr. DC Wadhwa and others vs. State of Bihar and others, 1987 (SC) 579, Bangladesh Sangbad Patra Parishad (BSP) vs. Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, 43 DLR (AD) 126. In the case of Bar Council Supreme Court of India, while expressing its opinion on the meaning of the words a "person aggrieved" held that "one of the meanings is that a person will be held to be aggrieved by a decision if that decision is materially adverse to him. Normally, one is required to establish that one has been denied or deprived of something to which one is legally entitled in order to make one a "person aggrieved". It further held "The test is whether the words a "person aggrieved" include a person who has genuine grievance because an order has been made prejudicially affects his interests". DS Nakara and others vs. Union India AIR 1983 (SC) 130 is a case of public interest litigation. The petitioner No.3, in that case, a registered Society under Society Registration Act of 1860, was a non-political, non-profit and voluntary organization. Its members consist of public spirited citizens seeking to espouse cause of legitimate public interest. The Society received a large number of representations from old pensioners who were individually unable to undertake the journey through "labyrinths" of legal judicial process, costly and protected......................... "The case of Dr. DC Wadhwa and others vs. State of Bihar and others AIR 1987 (SC) 579, is also a Social Action Litigation (SAL). In that case the petitioner was a professional economist and has spent a number of years in studying the constitutional functioning of Indian politics and was deeply interested in the preservation and promotion of constitutional functioning of the administration in his country. In that case the petition challenged the power of the Governor of Bihar under Article 213 of the Indian Constitution to repromulgate ordinances from time to time without getting them replaced by Acts of the Legislature under Article 32 of the Constitution of India. The Supreme Court held that the petitioner because of his substantial contribution through research in the field to ensure proper implementation of the Constitutional Provision had locus standi to challenge the practice of the Bihar State to promulgate and repromulgate the Ordinance from time to time without enacting them into Acts of the legislature for vindication of public interests although it held that a petition is not entitled to challenge an Ordinance merely as a member of public unless some legal right or interest of his is violated or threatened by such Ordinance.

24. Mr. Nabi also argued that the writ petition is premature as the resignation letters submitted to the Speaker becomes effective when the Speaker determines its genuineness and submits that as the Speaker has not taken any step the writ petition is premature. This contention of Mr. Nabi is in contradiction of his submission that the resignation takes it effect as soon as the Speaker receives the same. However, in support of his contention of prematurity of the writ petition he cites the decision in the cases of Surat Singh Yadav vs. Sudama Prasad Goswami and another, 1965 All 536, Jagat Singh and ors. vs. State of Uttar Prodesh and another, 1962 (All) 606, Mohammad Mohideen vs. State Wakf Board and others, 1963 Mad 132, and the case of Universal Imports Agency & another vs. Chief Controller of Imports and Exports and others, 1961 (SC) 41. In Sural Singh Yadav, Sree Sudama Prasad Goswami, the opposite Party 1, was elected a member of the Bidhan Sabha of Uttar Pradesh on the Congress ticket. He resigned his seat in the Vidhan Sabha on the ground of arrest of one Raghu Nath Singh in connection with a dacoity case. Raghu Nath was a member of Janshangha party. Sudama Prosad announced in a public meeting held on 7.10.1963 that he had resigned his seat and sent his resignation letter to the Speaker of the Vidhan Sabha. But it was found that the resignation letter was sent to the President of All India Congress Committee and copy of the same to the President of the UP Congress Committee and to the President of the District Congress Committee. It was not sent to the Speaker. Later on the Speaker received resignation letter and read out in the Vidhan Sabha pointing out that the resignation letter was not in proper form as it did not mention from which date the member was resigning nor did it mention the time of the resignation letter. Consequently the Speaker declared that he would take action under Rule 268 of the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business of UP Legislative Assembly, 1958, to satisfy himself regarding the genuineness and voluntary nature of the resignation letter before giving his decision. The writ petition was filed before the Speaker had taken decision in this regard. In Jagat Singh it was held, on the facts of that case, that although the petitioner was able to show that there was a potential threat to the invasion of his right to obtain an adequate compensation under S.299 of the Government of India Act, 1935 the petition was liable to be dismissed on the ground of being premature as potential threat cannot be the cause of action for a petition under Article 226 of the Indian Constitution. In Mohammad Mohideen it was held that as there was dispute as to the propriety of the removal of the petitioner from mutawalliship it was for the Board who had a prima facie jurisdiction to go into the question of merit and as the allegation was before the Board it was held that for purpose of deciding the allegations the Wakf Board had jurisdiction and accordingly, the petition under Article 226 of the Constitution was held to be premature. The case of Universal Import Agency (AIR 1961 (SC) 41) is on different facts. That was a case where goods imported by India from Pondicherry after its merger with India was imported under a contract entered into with foreign supplier in Pondicherry before French Establishment (Application of Laws) Order, 1954 was made were confiscated by the Customs Authorities and the Supreme Court on interpretation of Para 6 held that the word "things done" were comprehensive enough to take in a transaction effect before the merger and it saved the transaction and the authorities had no right to confiscate the goods on the ground that they were imported without the licence required under the Imports and Exports (Control) Act, 1947.

25. Mr. Nabi argued that the petitioner is not entitled to have the relief as sought for in this Writ Petition as the resignation from the seats of the Parliament has already taken effect from the moment those were received by the Speaker. To substantiate the argument he cites the decision in the case of M Kunjukrishnan Nadar vs Hon'ble Speaker, 1964 Kerala 194 and the case of Union of India vs. Gopal contention requires interpretation on Article 67(2) and other relevant Articles and the preamble of the Constitution as raised in the writ petition but as I propose not to decide the matter on merit I do not think it necessary to consider these decisions for reason that the Rule is liable to be discharged on the preliminary objection as to maintainability.

26. Mr. KS Nabi next submits that the writ petition is filed malafide as the same has been filed after 9 months from the date when all the opposition political parties launched movement for restoration of rights of the people of Bangladesh in order to ensure democracy in the country for which people have sacrificed in term of lives and material benefits in the form of hartals, procession, meetings, etc. He submits that as writ jurisdiction is discretionary jurisdiction this Division as conferred under Article 102 of the Constitution should not be exercised in respect of the belated and motivated writ petition. In support of this contention he cites the case of State of Punjab vs. Staya Pal Dang & others, 1969 (SC) 903. He further submits that all the resigning members of the Parliament not being impleaded in the writ petition except the respondent 3-5 the petition fails and in support of his contention he cites decision in the case of Makhan Lal Chakraborty vs. SK Chatterjee and others, 1954 (Cal) 208, the case of British India Corporation Ltd, & others vs. Industrial Tribunal, Punjab, 1957 (SC) 354, and the case of Smt. Maneka Gandhi vs. Union of India 1978 (SC) 597. In Makhan Lal the court held that defect of parties in Writ Petition is a material defect and it cannot be put right by amendment of a writ. Mr. Nabi submits relying on these decisions that as no other member of the Parliament except the respondents 3-5 is impleaded in the writ petition as respondents this Rule should be discharged as the petitioner cannot obtain relief in absence of those members of the Parliaments and as no amendment is sought by the petitioner in this regard. The case of Maneka Gandhi on this point hardly has any relevancy. In the case reported in 1957 (SC) 354 the High Court summarily rejected the petition under Article 226 of the Indian Constitution although the petitioner alleged malafide against the Government. Supreme Court on appeal held that it was the duty of the High Court to accord a hearing to the parties after issuing notice to the respondents and record its decision after considering all the circumstances of the case which have thus been brought to its notice. It further observed that the High Court, however, adopted a course which prevented the parties from presenting their respective cases before it and dismissed the petition in limine. Which is not justified and cannot be maintained This decision has no bearing on the points raised by Mr. Nabi and does not deserve consideration. The case of Mrs. Maneka Gandhi, 1978 (SC) 597 is altogether on different facts and has no application in the facts of the present case. Mr. Nabi also contends that the allegation that resignation was not voluntary is not correct and he submits that the Members of the Parliament resigned their seats in accordance to the decision of the Presidium of the political parties. In this regard he cites decision in the case of In re vs. Chakkarai Chettiar, AIR 1953 (Mad) 94 wherein it has been held that under Article 226 no writ lies for agitating political question and a person can only maintain the petition for protection of his legal right. Mr. Nabi contends that it is the fundamental right of a member of political party to resign his seat of the Parliament and as 147 Members of the Parliament have exercised their Constitutional right under Article 76(2) of the Constitution and there being no question of coercion this court should not declare resignation illegal. He cites the decision in the case of Mohammad Newaz Sharif vs. President of Pakistan and others PLD 1993 (SC) 473. The fact of this case was that the President of Pakistan declared that the government of Federation could not be carried on in accordance with the provision of the Constitution of Pakistan, 1973 and in exercise of power conferred under Article 58(2) (b) of the Constitution he ordered dissolution of the National Assembly, dismissed the Prime Minister and his Cabinet and called for general elections in the country. A care-taker Government was also sworn in. The President did so because Mia Mohammad Newaz Sharif, the Prime Minister of Pakistan addressed the nation on the National Radio and Television Networks emotionally alleging, inter alia, that conspiracies were hatched up to destabilize his Government. He also alleged that all these were done under the patronage of the President of Pakistan. He concluded his speech saying "I will not resign; I will not dissolve the National Assembly; and I will not be dictated". On the facts of that case, inter alia, it was held with reference to Article 17(2) of 1973 Constitution of Pakistan that Article 17(2) of the Constitution confers upon every citizen right to form or to be a member of a political party which includes the right to participate in and contest an election. It was further held that the rights guaranteed under Article 17(2) not only extends to the right to form a political party or the right to become a member of a political party or to all political processes culminating in the election of its member to the National Assembly but also includes the right to form Government provided the member of that particular political party possesses the requisite majority. Therefore, according to Mr. Nabi, as the political party is recognized under Article 70 of the Constitution of Bangladesh and as the functioning of the political party has been prescribed therein right of resignation of the seat of the Parliament is a fundamental right of the resigning members of the political parties as right to form association as envisaged under Article 38 of the Constitution is a constitutional right. Therefore, he submits that Article 38 read with the Article 70 it is clear that the Members resigning has exercised their fundamental right according to Constitution. Mr. Nabi further submits that as this petition is founded on speculation and political issues this Division ought to have rejected it summarily and in support of his contention he cites a number of decisions including the decision in the case of MK Agarwall and another vs. Union of India and others 1994 Del. 242. I do not want to discuss this decisions cited by Mr. Nabi on merit of the instant case as I propose to discharge this Rule on the ground of maintainability.

Mr. Moudud Ahmed relied upon Article 102(2) (a) of the Constitution and the case of Ex parte Sidebothan. In re Sidebotham (1886) 14 Ch. D. 458), the case of Md. Abdus Salam vs. Chairman, East Pakistan Election Authority and others 17 DLR (Dac) 191, the case of Bangladesh Sangbad Patra Parishad vs. Government of People's Republic of Bangladesh, 43 DLR (AD) 126 and in the case of Anjuman Arain vs. Abdur Rashid and others, PLD 1982 (SC) 303, in support of his contention on the maintainability of the Writ Petition No. 88 of 1995. I have already quoted earlier Article 102(2) of our Constitution wherein the expression a "person aggrieved" has been employed. The decision cited by Mr. Moudud Ahmed seems to me explained the meaning of "person aggrieved". In re Sidebotham James, J, Lord Justice observed:

"But the words "person aggrieved" do not really mean a man who is disappointed of a benefit which he might have received if some other order had been made. A "person aggrieved" must be a man who has suffered a legal grievance, a man against whom a decision has been pronounced which has wrongfully deprived him of something, or wrongfully refused him something, or wrongfully affected his title to something".

In the case of Abdus Salam in delivering the judgment of the Division Bench of the Dhaka High Court Abu Sayeed Chowdhury, J observed that the definition of "person aggrieved" is not an exhaustive one and whether a person is aggrieved or not is to be decided on the facts of each case. In Abdus Salam Abu Sayeed Chowdhury, J. considered the decision in the case of Ex Parte Sidebotham and the case of Ex-Parte Official Receiver-In re Reed Bowen and Company, (1887) 19 QBD 174 I have already examined the decision in the case of Bangladesh Sangbad Patra Parishad earlier in this judgment. Therefore, I do not propose to discuss that case any further to burden the judgment any more. The case of Anjuman Arain Bhara was in the nature of pro bono public. While construing Article 98 of the 1962 Constitution of Pakistan the Supreme Court observed that:

"However, this Court has not held in several decisions that a party acting pro bono publico had no locus standi to call in question the transfer of property in favour of a third party unless he has a personal interest in the matter. We may add that a person can be deemed to be "aggrieved" if he has some interest in the corpus of the property to which the law attaches sanctity. It is only if the appellant can demonstrate some interest in the property, to which some legal sanctity was attached can he be considered as an aggrieved party."

This case directly has no bearing on the case before us inasmuch as it was a public interest litigation but in our case although the petitioner states that like other citizens of the country he is also aggrieved by en masse resignation of 147 Members of the Parliament from their seat but in ultimate analysis his petition is found not for vindication of the right of others but his own. Therefore, the case of Anjuman Arain has little application to the fact of the present case. Mr. Moudud Ahmed further argued on merit of the case submitting that the reliefs sought for in this petition on the plea of en masse resignation is without any basis as it raises ex facie question of disputed facts and the writ petition is not maintainable. In this regard Mr. Moudud Ahmed cites the decision in the case of Abdul Hamid Khan vs. Mia Nurul Islam and others, 42 DLR (AD) 49. He also cites the decision in the case of New India Tea Company Ltd. vs. Bangladesh and others BSCR (Vol. 1 and 11) 185. I do not feel necessary to discuss the cases cited on merit of the case, on the same ground for which I do not discuss the case cited by Mr. Nabi.

Mr. Abdur Razzaq also submits that the Rule should be discharged for in order to invoke writ jurisdiction under Article 102(2) (a) of the Constitution the petitioner first, is to satisfy the court that he is an "aggrieved person" and has a direct and substantial interest in the matter agitated before the Writ Bench. He also cites the cases of Bangladesh Sangbad Patra Parishad, 43 DLR (AD) 126, Dada Match Workers Union vs. Government of Bangladesh and others, 29 DLR 188. Mr. Razzaq also referred us to Order 53, rule 1 of the Rules of Supreme Court of England, 1977. Order 53, rule 3 (5) reads "The court shall not leave unless it considers that the applicant has a sufficient interest in the matter to which the application relates......................" and submits that as in this court the petitioner has no "sufficient interest" he is not entitled to invoke the writ jurisdiction. As I have already dealt with the case of Bangladesh Sangbad Patra Parishad earlier I need not discuss the same again. In the case of Dada Match Workers Union, 29 DLR 188 Supreme Court of Bangladesh held that a trade union is not an aggrieved person within the meaning of Article 102 of the Constitution and it cannot maintain an application under Article 102 of the Constitution as it has no locus standi in its representative capacity. In delivering judgment Ruhul Islam, J further observed:

"the expression "person aggrieved" contemplates a person directly affected by the impugned action. Such relief cannot be asked for by a person in his representative capacity."

Although the observation on just case is made relating to a representative litigation it has a direct bearing on the instant case before us. Mr. Razzaq also canvassed that where in a writ petition political issues fall for consideration this Court should not entertain the petition. He relies upon a passage from the book titled Constitutional Law of India written by HM Seerval 3rd Edition at page 124 which is "The Courts in India started with the ingrained traditions of the British administration of justice according to which judges do not get involved in political or social controversies." He also cites decision in the case of LC Golak Nath and others vs. State of Punjab and another AIR 1967 (SC) 1643, the petitioners of the 3 writ petitions challenged the authority of the Parliament to amend the Constitution in a manner to injure or destroy its indestructible character. In one the petitioner challenged that Punjab Security or Land Tenures Act X of 1953, read with section 10-B of declaring the land owned by the surplus as void on the ground that they infringed the rights of the petitioners under Clauses (f) and (g) of Article 19 and Article 14 of the Constitution of India and sought for direction that the Constitution (First Amendment) Act. 1951, Constitution (Fourth Amendment) Act 1955, Constitution (Seventeenth Amendment) Act 1964, insofar as they affected the fundamental rights of the petitioners were unconstitutional and inoperative. In other two writ petitions the petitioners sought for a declaration that the Mysore Land Reforms Act (Act 10 of 1962) fixing ceilings on the land holdings and conferring ownership of the surplus lands on the tenants infringed Articles 14, 19 and 31 of the Constitution and was therefore unconstitutional and void. Thus, it is seen that Golak Nath case was on the power of the Parliament to amend the Constitution. This case has no relevancy on the point that falls for determination by us. We are not called up in the instant case to examine the extent of the power of the Parliament to enact any law abridging the fundamental right of the citizen. Therefore, I need not proceed to discuss the case further. To substantiate his contention that the petition is premature as the resignation letters are pending decision of the Speaker he referred us to Rules 177 and 178 of the Rules of Procedure of Parliament. He placing reliance on Rule 178(5) of the Rules submits that unless the Speaker gives his decision and reads to the Parliament it cannot be said that the resignation reached finality and until that stage is reached no declaration as to the validity of resignation can be sought under Article 102 of the Constitution. He relies on the decision in the case of Federation of Pakistan and others vs. Moulvi Tamizuddin Khan, 7 DLR (FC) 291 at 330. The facts of that case was that Pakistan came into existence as an Independent Dominion and a member of the British Commonwealth of Nations on 15th August, 1947 with a provisional of the Constitution of the Federal Pattern, under the Indian Independence Act, 1947. Under that Act Government of Pakistan was to be carried on under the Government of India Act, 1935 subject to the adaptations and modifications necessary on attaining the status of an Independent Dominion. For the Governance of the Dominion a Governor-General was appointed to represent His Majesty, The function of the Legislature of the Dominion were to be performed by a Constitution Assembly which had also to function as the Federal Legislature under the adapted Act of 1935, Mr. Tamizuddin Khan was president of the Constituent Assembly at the relevant time, Before making any Constitution it was dissolved by the Governor-General on 24th October, 1954 by proclamation which, inter alia, proclaimed that until elections of the people's representative are held the administration of the country will be carried on by a reconstituted Cabinet. On 25th October, 1954 the constituted Council of Ministers was announced consisting of

(1) Mr. Muhammad Ali

(2) Ch. Muhammad Ali

(3) Major-General Iskander Mirza

(4) Mr. A H Ispahani,

(5) Dr. M A Malik,

(6) General Muhammad Ayub Khan,

(7) Mr. Ghyasuddin Path an and

(8) Mr. Ghulam Ali Talpur.

In the reconstituted Council of Ministers subsequently Dr. Khan Sahib was included. Respondent Tamizuddin Khan filed Writ Petition No. 43 of 1954 in the Chief Court of Sind in its Extraordinary Special Jurisdiction alleging that Major General Iskander Mirza had informed him on 26th October, 1954 that the Assembly was dissolved and he and members of the Assembly has been forcibly prevented from entering the premises of the Constituent Assembly Building in Karachi on the 27th October, 1954. He alleged that the dissolution of the Constituent Assembly by the alleged proclamation interfered with his duties as the President of the Assembly and preventing him from exercising his function and appointment of the members of the Council of Ministers was unconstitutional, illegal, ultra vires, without jurisdiction, inoperative and void inasmuch as inclusion of appellant Nos. 4, 5, 7, 8 and 10 in the Council was contrary to the provisions of the Act of 1935 since they were not the members of the Federal Legislature. The writ petitioner ultimately prayed that a writ in the nature of mandamus should be issued against the Federation of Pakistan restraining them from implementing or otherwise giving effect to the proclamation of the 24th October, 1954 and from interfering with the exercise of the respondent's functions and duties as the President of the Constituent Assembly. It was argued, inter alia, on behalf of the Federation of Pakistan that since Government of India (Amendment) Act, 1954 inserting section 223-A in the Government of India Act, 1935 empowering the High Court to issue writs of mandamus and quo-warranto had not received assent of the Governor-General it was not a law and therefore the Sind Chief Court had no jurisdiction to issue writ. The Full Bench of the Chief Court of Sind hearing the parties held that acts of the Constituent Assembly, when it did not functions as the Federal Legislature did not require the Governor-General's assent and the dissolution of the Assembly was illegal. The Supreme Court of Pakistan on appeal in an elaborate judgment ultimately held, that:

"the Constituent Assembly when it functions under sub-section (1) of section 8 of the Indian Independence Act, 1947, acts as the Legislature of the Dominion within the meaning' of section 6 of that Act, that under sub-section (3) of the latter section the assent of the Governor-General is necessary to all legislations by the Legislature of the Dominion, that since section 223-A of the Government of India Act under which the Chief Court of Sind assumed jurisdiction to issue the writs did not receive such assent, it is not yet law, and that therefore, that Court has no jurisdiction to issue the writs."

Mr. Razzak also cited the case of Bangladesh vs. Professor Golam Azam and others, 46 DLR (AD) 192 to contend that this Court should not deal with political issue and as the writ petition involves political issue the Rule should be discharged. In support of this submission he referred us to the observation at page 216 which is

"However, the Court's concern is not politics but law and only law. It is for the people of this country either to accept or reject the politics of the respondent. They are the best judge of their own welfare. The court cannot shirk its responsibility from doing justice according to law on an unfounded assumption of alleged national catastrophe."

This observation seems to me is made by way of obiter dicta as because the Appellate Division has in spite of such observation decided the case which according to me, is hardly distinguishable from the issue raised in the instant case but resting on constitutional and legal right of different nature. On collusion between the petitioner and the respondent Nos. 1, 2 and 7 Mr. Razzaque contends that the petition is not maintainable as it raises disputed question of facts to be resolved by taking evidence legally which cannot be done in a summary proceeding of Article 102 of our Constitution. I also do not propose to examine this point as it requires decision on merit.

27. In order to substantiate his argument that the petitioner has no locus standi to maintain the petition Mr. Bhuiyan referred us to the relevant section of the Government of India Act, 1935 and relevant Article of the Constitution of India. Mr. Addl. Attorney-General also relied upon a number of decisions viz; the cases of Tarik Transport Company vs. Sargodha Bhera Bus Service, 11 DLR (SC) 140, Mazaharul Huq Chowdhury vs Returning Officer and Circle Officer, 27 DLR (AD) 11 and Dada Match Workers Union vs. Government of Bangladesh, 29 DLR 188. He contends that in view of the decision of these cases the petitioner before us has no locus standi to obtain the relief in the form of declaration that the resignation from seats of Parliament by 147 Members is void and illegal inasmuch as the petitioner is not "a person aggrieved" within the meaning of Article 102 of our Constitution. He submits that in order to invoke Article 102 of the Constitution the petitioner must satisfy the court that his fundamental rights guaranteed under PART-III of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh or any legal right has been invaded. He submits that as the petitioner has stated in the writ petition that like any other citizen he is shocked and deprived of his right of franchise he has no direct and substantial interest which can be said to have been destroyed by the resignation of the 147 members of the Parliament from the seats. He submits that as there is no invasion on his fundamental right or any legal right the Rule must fail. Now I take up the question of maintainability of the petitions founded on the contention of standing of the petitioners and prematurity of the writ petitions. And in order to examine this point I shall first deal with Constitutional provisions of the Government of India Act, 1935 and different Articles of the Constitution of Bangladesh, Pakistan and India. Section 223-A of the Government of India Act, 1935 as amended in 1954 reads:

"223-A-Power of High Courts................Every High Court shall have power throughout the territories in relation to which it exercises jurisdiction to issue to any person or authority including in appropriate cases any Government within those territories writs including writs in the nature of habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, quo warranto and certiorari or any of them."

Article 170 of the Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan of 1956 is as follows:

"170. Notwithstanding anything in Article 22, each High Court shall have power, throughout the territories in relation to which it exercises jurisdiction to issue to any person or authority, including in appropriate cases any Government, directions, orders or writs, including writs in the nature of habeas corpus mandamus, prohibition, quo-warranto and certiorari, for the enforcement of any of the rights conferred by Part II and for any other purpose."

Article 98 of 1962 of the Constitution of Pakistan reads :

"98. (1) A High Court shall have such jurisdiction as is conferred on it by this Constitution or by Law.

(2) Subject to this Constitution, a High Court of a Province may, if it is satisfied that no other adequate remedy is provided by law.........

(a) on the application of any aggrieved party, make an order 	.

(i) directing a person performing in the Province functions in connection with the affairs of the Centre, the Province or a local authority to refrain from doing that which he is not permitted by law to do, or to do that which he is required by law to do; or....................."

Article 199 of 1973 Constitution of Pakistan reads:

"199........................Jurisdiction of High Court ................. (1) Subject to the Constitution, a High Court may, if it is satisfied that no other adequate remedy is provided by law..................................

(a) on the application of any "aggrieved party", make an order.................

(i) directing a person performing, within the territorial jurisdiction of the Court, functions in connection with the affairs of the Federation, a Province or a local authority, to refrain from doing anything he is not permitted by law to do, or to do anything he is required by law to do; or

(ii) declaring that any act done or proceeding taken within the territorial jurisdiction of the Court by a person performing functions in connection with the affairs of the Federation, a Province or a local authority has been done or taken without lawful authority and is of no legal effect; or..........................."

Article 226 of the Indian Constitution reads:

"226. Power of High Courts to issue certain writs..........................

(1) Notwithstanding anything in Article 32, every High Court shall have power, throughout the territories in relation to which it exercises jurisdiction, to issue to any person or authority, including in appropriate cases, any Government within those territories directions, orders or writs, including writs in the nature of habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, quo-warranto and certiorari, or any of them, for the enforcement of any of the rights conferred by Part III and for any other purpose.

(2)...........................................................

Article 102 (2) (a) of the Constitution of People's Republic of Bangladesh reads:

"102. (2). The High Court Division may, if satisfied that no other equally efficacious remedy is provided by law..............................

(a) on the application of any person aggrieved, make an order................

(i) directing a person performing any functions in connection with the affairs of the Republic or of a local authority to refrain from doing that which he is not permitted by law to do or to do that which he is required by law to do; or

(ii) declaring that any act done or proceeding taken by a person performing functions in connection with the affairs of the Republic or of a local authority has been done or taken without lawful authority and is of no legal effect";

Now, I deal with the decision cited by the learned Addl. Attorney-General. In Tarik Transport it was held by the Supreme Court of Pakistan that in a petition for a writ the first question that the court has to consider is whether the petition has the locus standi to invoke the extraordinary jurisdiction of the Court and it is a basic principle that a person seeking judicial review must show that he has a direct, personal interest in the act. It further held that an application for an order of certiorari can only be made by an aggrieved party and not merely by one of the public. In that case Supreme Court of Pakistan has considered the standing of petitioner for invoking Article 170 of the 1956 Constitution of Pakistan although the Constitution in Article 170 has not employed the expression" person aggrieved" as employed in Article 98 of 1962 Constitution and in the Constitution of People's Republic of Bangladesh under Article 102(2)(a). In the case of Mazahal'ul Huq Chowdhury 27 DLR (AD) 11 the Appellate Division held that a voter cannot be said to be "a person aggrieved" within the meaning of Article 102(2) of the Constitution and as such he has no locus standi to move High Court in its writ jurisdiction. In the case of Dada Match Workers Union, 29 DLR 188 the High Court held that a trade union cannot maintain an application under Article 102 in its representative capacity, it not being a "person aggrieved" within the meaning of that expression in Article 102. It further said that expression "person aggrieved" contemplated a person directly affected by the impugned action.

28. Mr. Moksudur Rahman stoutly made an attempt to repel the contention of the Respondent on the maintainability of the writ petition under Article 102 of our Constitution. He contends that the petitioner has got locus standi and heavily relied on the decision in the case of Kazi Moklesor Rahman vs. Bangladesh and others, 26 DLR (AD) 44. The fact of this case was that the petitioner filed a writ petition under Article 102(2)(a)(ii) of the Constitution for a declaration that agreement between the Governments of the People's Republic of Bangladesh and the Republic of India signed on 16.5.1974 by the Prime Ministers of the two countries involving cessation of Bangladesh territory was without lawful authority and of no legal effect. The petition relates to Barubari Union No. 12 and the adjacent enclaves which were under the administrative control of Indian state. The writ petition was summarily dismissed by the High Court Division holding that the petitioner had no locus standi. The petitioner admittedly was not a resident of any part of the territories in the aforesaid agreement which is called the Delhi treaty. The respondent contended before the Supreme Court that the petitioner as such had no interest which could be affected by the treaty and as such was not" a person aggrieved" within the meaning of Article 102(2) of the Constitution. The Supreme Court referred a large number of decisions of India, Pakistan, Australia, US and of English jurisdiction on this point. In delivering the judgment of the report Sayem, CJ observed "It appears to us that the question of locus standi does not involve the court's jurisdiction to hear a person but of the competency of the person to claim a hearing so that the question is one of discretion which the court exercises upon due consideration of the facts and circumstances of each case. The appellant has complained that he is under an impending threat of deprivation of his fundamental rights under Article 36 of the Constitution and his right of franchise. Because of this as well as of the exceptional and extraordinary Constitutional issue raised in this case involving consideration of an international agreement between this country and the friendly Republic of India, we decided to hear the appellant". But the Supreme Court having taken the view that the treaty making power though falls within the ambit of the executive power under Article 55(2) of the Constitution the present treaty involving cessation of territory can only be concluded by amendment of Article 2(a) by taking recourse to Article 142 of the Constitution. It was further held that as no such amendment was made the writ petition before the High Court was premature and upon such finding the appeal was dismissed. Mr. Moksudur Rahman also referred to the decision in the case of Anwar Hussain vs Bangladesh, popularly known as Constitution 8th Amendment case, 41 DLR (AD) 165 and referred to paragraph Nos. 61 and 62 of the judgment. The facts of that case, in short, are that by Martial Law Proclamation Order No. 11 of 1982 High Court Division of the Supreme Court was bifurcated by establishing seven permanent Benches at Dhaka, Rangpur, Jessore, Comilla, Chittagong, Sylhet and Barisal. Lawyers started movement against such fragmentation of the High Court Division. When the Constitution was revived the permanent Benches outside the capital were treated as Sessions of the High Court Division outside the capital. Lawyers contended that this was unconstitutional and there was stalemate. On 9.6.1988 Article 100 of the Constitution was amended setting up six permanent Benches at Rangpur, Jessore, Barisal, Chittagong, Com ilia and Sylhet and as the President was authorized to fix the territorial jurisdiction of the High Court Division in the permanent seat he issued notifications conferring upon the High Court Division and the permanent Benches mutually exclusive jurisdiction. The Chief Justice also framed rules importing the concept of "cases arising out of an area" and providing for transfer of pending proceedings from High Court Division to permanent Benches. Writ petitions were filed challenging the amendment of Article 100 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh and the Rules on various grounds, the most important ground was that High Court Division of the Supreme Court with plenary judicial power over the Republic is a basic structure of the Constitution which cannot be altered or damaged and the amendment is void having rendered the High Court Division with plenary judicial power over the entire Republic non-existent. The High Court Division refused to issue a Rule holding that the impugned amendment has not destroyed or damaged the basic stricture of the Constitution as the High Court Division has full powers and jurisdiction subject to Article 100(5) of the Constitution. On appeal to the Appellate Division by a majority of 3: 1 Appellate Division held that amendment of Article 100 was void. As in that case the writ petition challenged on the authority of the President for amendment of Article 100 of the Constitution and the decision was given on the power of the President to promulgate Ordinance to set up permanent Benches of the Supreme Court and as in the instant writ petition no such question on the amending power of the Parliament is raised for our determination this case of Anwar Hossain is of no assistance to him. He further cited the case of Pakistan vs. Ahmed Sayeed Kirmani, PLD 1958 (SC) 397, the case of SP Gupta and others vs. M Tarkunde and others AIR 1982 (SC) 149, (para 17-23), the case of Gali Kondaiah vs Gali Ankamma AIR 1988 (AP) 69. In Sayeed Kirmani "Mr. Ahmad Sayeed Kirmani, presumably a member of the Opposition, approached the High Court of West Pakistan for a writ of quo-warranto, mandamus, or any other appropriate writ, order or direction, declaring the election of the Speaker of the 20th May, 1956 to be null and void, directing Choudhri Fazal Elahi to prove his lawful authority to function as Speaker and directing Choudhir Fazal Elahi and the Secretary of the West Pakistan Legislative Assembly to enable Mir Muhammad Bakash Talpur and Mr. Varyani " to cast their votes according to their free will for the lawful election of the Speaker of the Assembly". The fact of this case is quite distinguishable from that facts of the case before us. The petitioner as a member of the West Pakistan Assembly had substantial interest in the matter of election of the Speaker and to see that his right to elect Speaker is not deprived of by any illegal decision of the Chairman who conducted the election. But before us the petitioner is not a member of the Parliament and his interest is not of the nature of the petitioner of writ petition before the West Pakistan High Court. Thus, this case does not help Mr. Moksudur Rahman. The case of SP Gupta is a case on public interest light and the principle laid down therein was enunciated relating to standing of a petitioner who brings an action before the Court to vindicate the right of socially disadvantaged group of people. That is not so here as the petitioner does not seek declaration for vindicating the right of the people, rather he moves this court in the writ jurisdiction to vindicate his own right. Thus, this case also does not help the petitioner to establish locus standi. The case of Goli Kondaiah has no relevance as it is cited to argue on defect of parties. As this Rule is discharged on the ground of maintainability this case does not require consideration.

29. In this respect I may profitably refer a decision from the Supreme Court of USA. It is the case of Ex Parte Albert Levitt reported in 302 US at page 633 is exactly on the point before us. The judgment is very short but very illuminating on the point and we are tempted to refer this judgment in extenso in our decision. The judgment is "The grounds of the motion are that the appointment of Mr. Justice Black by the President and the confirmation thereof by the Senate of the United States were null and void by reason of his ineligibility under Article 1, section 6, clause 2, of the Constitution of the United States, and because there was no vacancy for which the appointment could lawfully be made. The motion papers disclose no interest upon the part of the petitioner other than that of a citizen and a member of the Bar of this Court. That is insufficient. It is an established principle that to entitle a private individual to invoke the judicial power to determine the validity of executive or legislative action he must show that he has sustained or is immediately in danger of sustaining a direct injury as the result of that action and it is not sufficient that he has merely a general interest common to all members of the public." In delivering the judgment the learned Judge referred to a large number of cases in his judgment. This case is exactly identical with the case before us because the petitioner in that case was a member of the Bar like ours and the petitioner challenged an appointment of an acting Justice of the Supreme Court of United States but the petition failed on the observation which has already been referred to by us. With this citation I close my discussion on standing of the petitioner in the instant writ petition.

<u>30. The observation made in the decision of Indian jurisdiction were on the cases on either public interest litigation or on cases on social action litigations. The case before us is a litigation not of social action litigation or of public interest litigation as admitted by the petitioner in this case. Article 102 of our Constitution because of the expression a "person aggrieved" and expression "enforcement of any fundamental rights conferred by Part III of this Constitution" has narrowed down the scope of this writ jurisdiction unlike that of India under Article 226 in which the fathers of the constitution in their attempt to meet the social economic condition and for enforcement of such right widened the jurisdiction consciously. The decisions of Indian jurisdiction altogether are founded on different view on the finding of locus standi on the facts of each case based on the rights with reference to Article 226 of the Constitution of India which is differently worded other than fundamental rights as contemplated in Article 102 but it helps us indirectly to hold that unless the petitioner satisfied this Court about infringement of any constitutional rights or rights accrued under any Act of the Parliament no action as has been brought before us can stand. As I have examined several decisions cited at the Bar of the Indian jurisdiction I think that those are on the language employed in the Indian Constitution which is much wider in scope to apply high prerogative writs by the Supreme Court under Article 32 and by the respective High Courts of India under Article 226. But in view of the provision and the language used in Article 102 of our Constitution I must go by the pronouncements of this Division and Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh. The most important decision seems to me is the decision in the case of Bangladesh Sangbadpatra Parishad vs. Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh in 43 DLR (AD) 126 wherein it has been held that "Therefore the decisions of the Indian jurisdiction on public interest litigation are hardly apt to our situation. We must confine ourselves to asking whether the petitioner is a "person aggrieved", a phrase which has received a meaning and a dimension over the years". In the light of the aforesaid observation made in the cases just referred to by me and the expression "aggrieved party" which finds place in Article 102(2)(a) of the Constitution of Bangladesh I am of the opinion that in order to invoke writ jurisdiction of this Court under Article 102(2)(a) of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh in a writ of certiorari the petitioner must establish that by act done either his constitutional right or any legal right has been invaded and he has a direct and substantial interest in the matter. Because of en masse resignation it cannot be held that the petitioner is a "person aggrieved" within the meaning of Article 102(2) (a) as in the present case by such resignation no direct and substantial Constitutional or legal right of the petitioner has been infringed or he has been deprived of his right of franchise as contended by Mr. Moksudur Rahman nor resignation has acted as an imminent danger to any of constitutional or legal rights of the petitioner.</u>

<u>31. To sum up, in the light of the aforesaid observations, I can safely say that the petitioner, who styles himself as a voter and because of submission of resignation letters by 147 members of the Parliament his right of franchise has been curtailed if election is held, does not stand on sound constitutional and legal foundation. His contention on locus standi on that count does not find favour with the observation made in the decisions referred to above specially the decision in the cases of BSP and Ex-Parte Albert Levitt. Consequently I hold that the petitioner does not qualify as a "person aggrieved" to bring the action before us under Article 102(2) (a)(ii) of the Constitution and has no locus standi, on the ground of maintainability. Further argument at the Bar is that the petitions are premature because no decision has yet been obtained and the matter rests with the Speaker. This is so. Neither the Speaker has yet passed his view on the resignation letters after receipt of those and communicated such receipt to the House. That being the position I hold the contention of the respondent that it is premature is well founded in the light of the observations made in the cases referred to earlier in this judgment. Thus I hold that the petitioner has no locus standi to maintain this petition and this petition is also premature.</u>

<u>32. Mr. Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, learned Additional Attorney-General, submits that the proceeding under Article 102 of our Constitution is akin to civil suit to which the Code of Civil Procedure is applicable and placing reliance upon section 151 CPC he submits that the period consumed before this Court is to be excluded in order to secure the ends of justice or in other words a harmonious interpretation in this regard should be given to avoid conflict between Article 67 and Article 123(4) of the Constitution and for keeping the Constitutional provision alive so that it can work properly. He further submits that this Court having had issued order restraining the Speaker from giving his opinion on submission of resignation letter it should exclude the period for which the Speaker was restrained for no fault of his own from the period contemplated under Article 123(4) of the Constitution. Mr. Moudud Ahmed seriously opposes this contention saying that it will be improper to enter into the merit of the case. I cannot agree with Mr. Moudud Ahmed that the submission of Mr. Bhuiyan is on merit of the case. The respondents 3-5 also contend that acceptance of the submission of the Additional Attorney-General would mean amendment of the Constitution which is the exclusive domain of the Parliament. Merit of the case and exercise of our power to keep the Constitution running are quite different matters. Merit involves and raises question of facts to be resolved on taking admissible evidence which is not conceived of in this summary jurisdiction under Article 102 of the Constitution. Now. I proceed to examine section 151 CPC. It reads:</u>

<u>"151. Saving of inherent powers of Court. Nothing in this Code shall be deemed to limit or otherwise affect the inherent power of the Court to make such orders as may be necessary for the ends of justice or to prevent abuse of the process of the Court."</u>

<u>Now, the question is whether Section 151 CPC applies to writ petition. On this point in the decision of the Madras High Court in the case of M. Ramayya vs. State of (Mad) 1952 (Mad) 300 it is held that proceeding for certiorari is a civil proceeding. In other case of the same jurisdiction it has been held that under Article 226 there is nothing restricting the power of the High Court to apply provision of Civil Procedure Code wherever the Court thinks necessary for proper adjudication. In the case of Jagatt Singh and others vs. State of Uttar Prodesh and another, 1962 (AU) 606 it has also been held. Beside the application of the CPC the submission of the Additional Attorney-General is also acceptable applying the rule on nunc protunc wherein it propounded that power if not satisfactorily conferred upon the court necessary to prevent injustice it can assume such power in fit case. This view finds support in the decision in the case of Sham Das vs. Umer Din, 1930 Lal 497. Tek Chand, J. silting in a Full Bench of Lahore High Court in delivering the judgment observed:</u>

<u>"The applicability of the rule of nunc protunc which is really based on the maxim actus curiae neminem gravabit is confined to those cases only in which some hardship would be visited upon a party without any fault of his, unless he were relieved from it by allowing a proceeding as to be taken now for them..................................."</u>

<u>The pronouncement of Tek Chand, J. seems to me has full force in the facts of the present case. In Maxwell on "The Interpretation of Statutes" Twelfth Edition at page 45 the principle is laid down as follows: "Where alternative constructions are equally open, that alternative is to be chosen which will be consistent with the smooth working of the system which the statute purports to be regulating, and that alternative is to be rejected which will introduce uncertainty, friction or confusion into the working of the system". In the light of the above principle and the observation made in the aforesaid cases I also say that such principle is also applicable in case of interpretation of a provision of a Constitution and the Rules of Procedure of Parliament of our country. Applying such principle I hold that the period for which the Speaker was restrained from taking action under the Rules 177 and 178 of the Rules unless excludes in computing the period under Article 123(4) smooth working of the Constitution will be obstructed. In the case of Chandra Mohan vs. State of Uttar Prodesh and others, reported in AIR 1966 (SC) 1987, the Indian Supreme Court held "........................... it should be remembered that the fundamental rule of interpretation is the same whether one construes the provisions of the Constitution or an Act of Parliament, namely, that the court will have to find out the expressed intention from the words of the Constitution or the Act, as the case may be. But, "if, however, two constructions are possible then the Court must adopt that which will ensure smooth and harmonious working of the Constitution and eschew the other which will lead to absurdity or make well established provisions of existing law nugatory." The Supreme Court of India in a case reported in 1960(3) SCR at page 887 (905) observed, "It is true that any other Article of the Constitution may exclude the operation of the fundamental rights in respect of specific matter for instance, Articles 31A and 31B. It may also be that an Article embodying a fundamental right may exclude another by necessary implication, but before such a construction excluding the operation of one or other of the fundamental rights is accepted, every attempt should be made to harmonize the two Articles so as to make them co-exist, and only if it is not possible to do so, one can be made to yield to the other." The Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of our country in the case of AKM Ruhul Amin vs. District Judge and others, 38 DLR (AD) 172 observed as follows:</u>

<u>"In Collquhon vs. Brooks (1889) 14 App. Case 493 (496) Lord Harscheel said:</u>

<u>"It is beyond dispute, too, that we are entitled, and indeed, bound, when construing the terms of any provision found in a statute, to consider other parts of the Act which throw light on the intention of the legislature, and which may serve to show that the particular provisions ought not be construed as it would be alone and apart from the rest of the Act." and Lord Devey in Canada Sugar Refining-C. vs. R (1898) AC 735 (74) said; "Every clause of a statute should be construed with reference to the context and the other clauses of the Act, so as, so far as possible, to make a consistent enactment of the whole statute or series of statutes relating to the subject matter."</u>

33. Mr. KS Nabi on behalf of the respondent No.3 submits that this ought to have been argued in filing an application restraining for vacating the order of the Speaker and after hearing the lawyer appearing on behalf of the Speaker and without hearing the lawyer of the Speaker the Court should not pass order on this point. Accordingly, we want to hear Mr. Asrarul Hossain, the learned Counsel for the respondent 1. Mr. Hossain took us back to what he addressee us on the very first day on this point. He submits that he has already submitted that on Gazette Notification vacancy will take effect and contends that vacancy shall take effect from the date of Gazette Notification. It seems to us that his argument is a bit one step forward that what was argued by the learned Additional Attorney-General. Mr. Asrarul Hossain's argument based on Rule 316 of the Rules does not appeal to me.

34. In view of the aforesaid observations made in the decision discussed above I am of the opinion that the contention of the learned Additional Attorney-General has got substance. Accordingly, the period from 18.1.95 to 23.2.95 during which the Rule was pending before the Division is to be excluded for computation of the period contemplated under Article 123(4) of the Constitution.

35. Now, I proceed to deliver judgment in Writ Petition No.161 of 1995. Mr. ABM Nurul Islam, the learned Advocate for the writ petitioner in Writ Petition No. 161 of 1995 contends that as the respondent 1 has failed to do his duty as contemplated under Article 67(2) read with Article 123(4) of the Constitution this Court by a writ of mandamus should direct him to do what is required of him under the Constitution and law. He submits that respondent 1 had nothing to do except to bring the facts of submission of resignation to the notice of the House. Mr. Nurul Islam, therefore, submits that Respondent 1 is merely a post office. He continues to say that it is unusual on the part of respondent 1, not a custodian of those resignation letters, and the Secretary of the Parliament being custodian, to keep the resignation letters with him in breach of the Rules of Procedure of the Parliament. He further submits that once a resignation it is always a resignation and resignation takes effect as soon as respondent 1 received the same. According to Mr. Nurul Islam, the respondent 1 by not doing his duty and discharging his obligation on submission of resignation under Article 67(2) of the Constitution and under the Rules 177 and 178 of the Rules of Procedure of the Parliament faultered the democratic process of the country. He drew our attention to Rules 14-16 of the Rules. On reference to these Rules on facts of this case they do not require any consideration by me and Mr. Nurul Islam without understanding the application of these rules made an unnecessary exercise for long only to detain us from switching over on the real point calling for our decision. He further submits that inaction of respondent 1 is malafide and politically motivated and placed reliance on the decisions namely 34 DLR 222, 38 DLR (AD) 11, 39 DLR (AD) 1, and 1993 (SC) 873. The last decision of Indian jurisdiction relates to the proceeding in the Parliament. As I find that the petition is not maintainable on the ground of standing and prematurity and in view of the observation made in several cases of the Appellate Division that when the petition fails on the ground of preliminary objection the court is not called upon to give opinion on merit of the case and thus it is not necessary to discuss the cases cited by Mr. Nurul Islam. I resist myself from discussing the merit of the case as I have done in Writ Petition No. 88 of 1995.

36. Mr. Asrarul Hossain, the learned counsel appearing for the respondents 1 and 2, on the other hand, seriously contends that there being no provision to submit resignation letters to the Election Commission and as under clause (2) of Article 67 of the Constitution resignation letters are to be submitted to the Speaker it clearly indicates that the Speaker has got to do something with regard to submission of the resignation letters which is implicit under Article 67. He further submits that Article 67 had 2 parts. If conditions enumerated under clause (1) occur the vacation of seat of a member of the Parliament is automatic. But under clause (2) of Article 67 there is no automatic vacation of seat. Pointing out to the difference between two clauses of Article 67 the learned counsel submits that because of this different constitutional consequence the respondent 1 requires time to examine the resignation letters. He submits that this view finds force in proviso to clause (1) of Rule 177 and clause (2) of Rule 178 as the same has the force of law, the Rules being framed under the authority of Article 76(1) of the Constitution. Therefore, Mr. Hossain submits that the contention of the petitioner that once a resignation always a resignation and so the resignation letters submitted to the respondent 1 takes automatic effect as contended by Mr. Nurul Islam cannot be accepted. Mr. Asrarul Hossain secondly, submits that the Court should not have hastened to issue this Rule because the petition is premature and the matter rests with the Speaker. Mr. Hossain argued also referring to Rule 316 that the matter of submission of resignation letters arise in connection with the business of the House and the decision of the Speaker is final. He puts great stress that as the resignation letters arise in connection with the business of the House this Court has got no jurisdiction to issue the Rule. I am unable to accept the contention of the learned counsel of the respondents 1 and 2. My reading of the Article 67(2) and Rule 316 is contrary to what he says. In the Writ Petition No.88 of 1995 I have addressed myself on the jurisdiction of this Court on submission of the resignation letters. I, therefore, do not want to give a repeated view of mine in this regard with a view to avoid lengthening the judgment any further. But just I read a few pages from AK Brohi's book "Fundamental Law of Pakistan" appearing at paragraph 77. The learned author speaks as, "The business of the legislature thus falls into three broad categories, legislative, financial and critical; it has to pass laws, to vote supplies and keep the conduct of Government under the searchlight of public criticism. "Therefore, the contention of Mr. Hossain based on Rule 316 that the Court has no jurisdiction to issue Rule as it has done in the present case has got no legal stand in view of the aforesaid expression which just I have quoted in my judgment as submission or resignation although is in connection with the business of Parliament but submission to the Speaker simpliciter, until the Speaker brings it to the notice of the House as mandated by Rule 178(3), cannot be said "business of the House" on the interpretation of Rule 316 which Mr. Hossain wants us to give. Thus, I do not find force in the contention of Mr. Asrarul Hossain based on Rule 316. Now, I proceed to examine the standing of this petitioner. The petitioner is an Advocate of this Court and is a conscious citizen and he has filed the Writ Petition No. 161 of 1995 to vindicate the democratic right of the people for a direction on respondent 1 for the purpose which I have already stated. On the statements made in the petition, the affidavit-in-opposition and the reply to the affidavit-in-opposition it is seen that the petitioner does not claim that he has brought this action in the nature of public interest litigation nor social action litigation. Therefore, remedy sought to have arisen is on his independent right, either constitutional or legal. He founded his petition on the averments that he has right like the conscious citizen of the country that the respondent 1 should perform his function as contemplated under the Constitution and Rule and as withholding of his such function is contrary to the mandate of law this Court should direct him for performing such function. But it is surprising for us to see that none of the resigning members of the parliament has come forward to seek direction from us. The direction is sought by a person who has got no Constitutional right to enforce in the matter of acceptance of resignation letters because he cannot take advantage of any of the rights described under Part III of the Constitution nor could he successfully plead before us that any of his legal rights has been violated. In this writ petition his standing is identical to the standing of writ petitioner in Writ Petition No.88 of 1995. In Writ Petition No.88 of 1995 I have reviewed a large number of decisions starting from the Supreme Court of America, the Supreme Court of India, the Supreme Court of Pakistan and the Appellant Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh and I said that the petitioner has no locus standi to maintain the writ petition under Article 102 of the Constitution specially in view of the observation made in the Sangbadpatra Parishad case wherein it has been held that for the wording of Articles 32 and 226 of Indian Constitution which is different from wording of Article 102 of the Constitution Jurisdiction of the Indian Supreme Court under Article 226 and Article 32 is much more wider than that of ours because a limiting jurisdiction is conferred under Article 102 of the Constitution by the founding fathers of the Constitution. By resignation none of the fundamental rights guaranteed under Part-III of the Constitution of the petitioner seems to have been violated. Then what is his right. If it is not a fundamental right then it must be a legal right under an Act of the Parliament. From the statements made in the petition, the Affidavit-in-opposition, the affidavit-in-reply I am unable to bring the action before us under Article 102 of the Constitution and that being the position I am of the view that the petitioner is not a "person aggrieved" and has no substantial, direct personal interest in the matter. He may have some remote interest and for such remoteness of interest which is in common with other conscious citizens of the country he has no entitlement to proceed with the Rule before us on the ground of maintainability. Accordingly, I am of the opinion that this petition also fails on the ground of standing.

37. On the ground of prematurity it has been contended with reference to the decision of 1965 Allahabad 536 that it is premature. The fact of the case is also a bit different. But it is held that writ petition in respect of the same matter is premature. Here before us the matter is before respondent 1 and in view of clause (2) of Article 67 and Rules 177(1) and 178(3) I hold that this writ petition is also premature. As this petition is also premature on the view which I have taken in Writ Petition No. 88 of 1995 the period consumed in this court during which period the Speaker was restrained to give his opinion on the resignation letters is to be excluded from computation of the period as contemplated under Article 123(4) of the Constitution.

38. Before I part with this judgment I want to refer to other contention of the petition based on Rules 177,281,307 and Articles 102-103(4) of the Constitution. The contention resting on these provisions has no force as on the facts of the case the Rules and the Articles are irrelevant for our purpose.

39. In view of the discussions made above I hold that both the petitions must fail on the ground of maintainability. Consequently, I discharge the Rules issued in Writ Petition Nos. 88 and 161 of 1995 without any order as to cost.

The connected order restraining the respondent 1 in Writ Petition No. 88 of 1995 from giving his opinion on the resignation letters is hereby vacated.

Kazi Ebadul Hoque J: I agree with my learned brother to discharge the Rule in Writ Petition No.88 of 1995.

42. In Writ Petition No. 161 of 1995 Rule was issued on the respondent No. 1 Speaker of the Parliament and respondent No. 2 Secretary of the Parliament Secretariat calling upon them to show cause why the respondent No. 1, shall not be directed to take action as required under the Constitution on the resignation letters submitted by 147 members of the Parliament.

43. Both the respondents have opposed this Rule, by filing an affidavit-in-opposition, mainly amongst others, on the ground of lack of jurisdiction of this Court, as stated in paragraph No.4 thereof which is as follows:

"That this being an internal matter relating to procedure, conduct of business and maintenance of order in Parliament, it is respectfully submitted that the Supreme Court has no jurisdiction in this matter under Article 7R(2) of the Constitution."

44. Mr. Asrarul Hossain, learned Advocate of the respondents, conceded that this Court has jurisdiction under Article 102 of the Constitution of Bangladesh to issue Rule on the Speaker as he is "a person performing functions in connection with the affairs of the Republic" and he may be directed "to do that which he is required by law to do or refrain from doing that which he is not permitted by law to do" is inappropriate when parliamentary immunities are not affected. But he contended that jurisdiction of this Court is ousted under clause (2) of Article 78 of the Constitution to direct the Speaker to take action on the resignation letters submitted by the 147 members of the Parliament. Elaborating the point he further submitted that letters of resignation submitted by the 147 members under Article 67(2) of the Constitution are required to be examined by the Speaker under Rule 177(1) of the Rules of Procedure of the Parliament framed under Article 75 (1) of the Constitution to ascertain the genuineness and validity of the same and if the Speaker decides the matter then he is to bring the fact of such resignation to the notice of the House under Rule 178(3) of the said Rules and as soon as the matter is brought to the notice of the House the same forms part of the proceedings in Parliament and such decision of the Speaker being in exercise of his power "for the regulation of procedure, the conduct of business or the maintenance of order in Parliament" the same is not subject to the jurisdiction of any Court.

On the other hand Mr. ABM Nurul Islam, learned Advocate of the petitioner, contended that this Court has jurisdiction to give direction to the Speaker who has no power to accept or reject the letter of resignation submitted by 147 members and inordinate delay made by him after receipt of the same on the plea of giving a ruling as to acceptance is malafide and without jurisdiction.

45. Since my learned brother has not examined the question specifically raised in this Rule in detail in his judgment just pronounced except saying that this Court has jurisdiction to "issue Rule on the Speaker I like to consider this question in greater detail as no such question arose at any time from coming into force of our Constitution on the 16th day of December, 1972 and also to allay misgivings about the jurisdiction of this Court vis-a-vis the Parliament.

46. In this sub-continent Constitution of India is the earliest one after the partition and independence of the Indian Sub-continent in 1947 from British rule and the same came into operation on the 26th day of January, 1950. Then came the first Constitution of Pakistan in 1956 and then another Constitution in 1962 after the abrogation of the earlier one by the martial law authorities in October, 1958. After the Constitution of Bangladesh came into operation in 1972 another Constitution came into operation in 1973 in Pakistan.

47. There is no provision for resignation of a member of the British Parliament. Only by accepting an office of profit under the Crown a member of the British Parliament can get rid of his membership. Article 101 (3)(a) and Article 190(3)(a) of the Constitution of India provide for vacation of seat by a member of the Parliament and State legislature respectively after incurring involuntary disqualifications under Articles 102(1) and 191(1) of the said Constitution as the case may be. On the other hand, Articles 101(3)(b) and Article 190(3)(b) provide for vacation of seat by such a member of the Parliament and State legislature respectively by incurring voluntary disqualification by tendering resignation.

48. Earliest case over the resignation of a member of a State Legislative Assembly arose in the case of Thankama vs. Hon'ble Speaker reported in AIR 1952 TC 166. In that case petitioner wrote and signed a letter of resignation addressed to the Speaker before she was elected a member and made over the same to one of her supporters as a measure of strategy to put pressure for solving a current problem and subsequently she withdrew the same on 4.9.51 before her resignation letter reached the Speaker. But by notification dated 15.10.51 she was shown to have resigned with effect from 13.9.51 and the Speaker refused to administer oath to her. Petitioner challenged the same. Court held that the letter of resignation of the petitioner was void and that she had not lost her seat and directed the Speaker to administer oath to her rejecting the objection that taking or administering oath under Article 188 of the Constitution of India is not an item of conduct of business within the meaning of Article 212(2) of the said Constitution but only a condition precedent to entitle the member to take her seat in the Assembly and conduct the business. Hence wrongful refusal by the Speaker to allow a member to take oath and take her seat in the Assembly can be interfered with by the Court and Speaker cannot claim the protection given by Articles 212(2) of the Constitution of India. Provisions of the said Article quoted in the decision are substantially the same with Article 78 (2) of our Constitution.

49. Next case over resignation of another member of Kerala State Legislature arose in the case of Kunja Krishna vs. Speaker reported in AIR 1964 Kerala 194. In that case petitioner sent his letter of resignation on 23.11.63 to the Speaker, Kerala State Legislature to take effect on 1.12.63. But he withdrew the same on 29.11.63. In spite of receipt of the letter of withdrawal by the Speaker on 30.11.63 by Gazette Notification dated 10.1 2.63 petitioner's seat was made vacant. In that case it was held that withdrawal nullified the resignation and therefore Gazette Notification dated 10.12.63 was null and void. In that case no question of lack of jurisdiction of the Court was raised though there was a provision in Rule 162(2) of the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in Kerala Legislative Assembly providing for informing the Assembly about resignation of a member. But such question of lack of jurisdiction of the Court was raised in the subsequent case over resignation of a member of the State Legislature in the cases of Sural Singh vs. Sudama reported in AIR 1965 (All) 536. In that case Court found that the Speaker was yet to decide the matter arising from the resignation of the member concerned under Rule 278 of the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business and as the case was premature refrained from answering the question as to lack of jurisdiction of the Court under Article 212(2) of the Constitution of India. In the subsequent case of Raghabanandan vs. Chitrarasu reported in AIR 1973 (Mad) 50 however no such question as to lack of Court's jurisdiction under the said Article 212(2) was raised though the said case also arose from acceptance of resignation letter of a member of the Legislative Council. But in AIR 1952 TC 166 and AIR 1965 (All) 536 it was held that the Speaker can determine genuineness and voluntariness of a letter of resignation received by him.

50. After a long period of struggle between the King and the Parliament ultimately supremacy of the Parliament was achieved in England with the glorious revolution in 1688. To highlight the supremacy of English Parliament it is aptly said that Parliament can do and undo anything and everything except making a man a woman and woman a man.

51.
