After supremacy of English Parliament was achieved in 1688 with the flight of King James II Bill of Rights was passed in 1689 curtailing prerogative powers of the King and limiting powers of the Court to interfere with the powers and functions of the Parliament, its officers and members. By Article 9 of the Bill of Rights Court's jurisdiction was taken away in England in respect of speeches, debates and proceedings in Parliament. The said Article 9 of the Bill of Rights is as follows:

"That the freedom of speech and debate or proceedings in Parliament ought not to be impeached or questioned in any Court or place out of Parliament"

52. A Parliament under a written Constitution functions within the limits imposed by the Constitution specially when separation of powers between the three organs of the State is recognized in the Constitution. Our Constitution like the Constitution of India and Pakistan is a written one and powers of the three organs of the State have been clearly defined and each organ functions within the limits imposed by the Constitution. So Parliament of Bangladesh functions within its exclusive domain as set forth in the Constitution and as such, has limited supremacy and not absolute supremacy like the English Parliament which does not function under any written Constitution. Unlike the superior English Courts, Supreme Court of Bangladesh can declare void a law passed by the Parliament if it contravenes the Constitution. In the case of Anwar Hossain vs. Bangladesh (1989) BLD (AD) (Special 1 Issue) amendment of Article 100 of the Constitution made by the Eighth Amendment passed by the Parliament following all the formalities was declared void.

53. Let us now consider the powers, privileges and immunities enjoyed by a Parliament, its officers and members under a written Constitution and whether Court's jurisdiction is completely ousted in respect of such Parliament.

54. Articles 105 and 194 of the Constitution of India provides for powers, privileges and immunities of the Parliament and State legislatures respectively and members and officers of the respective House and Article 122 and 212 of that Constitution ousts Court's jurisdiction in respect of proceedings in Parliament and State legislatures respectively, On the other hand, Articles 56 and 89 of the Constitution of Pakistan 1956, Article 111 of the Constitution of Pakistan 1962 and Article 69 of the Constitution of Pakistan 1973 deal with the same. Article 78 of our Constitution similarly deals with the same. Clauses (1) and (2) of Article 78 of our Constitution dealing with Court's jurisdiction vis-a-vis the Parliament are as follows "-

"78(1) The validity of the proceedings in Parliament shall not be questioned in any Court.

(2) A member or officer of Parliament in whom powers are vested for the regulation of procedure, the conduct of business or the maintenance of order in Parliament shall not in relation to the exercise by him of any of those powers be subject to the jurisdiction of any Court."

Almost indentical provisions of Article 111 of the Constitution of Pakistan regarding ouster of Court's jurisdiction are as follows:

"111 (I)-The validity of any proceedings in an Assembly shall not be questioned in any Court.

(2) An officer or member of an Assembly in whom powers are vested for the regulation of procedure, the conduct of business or the maintenance of order in the Assembly shall not in relation to the exercise by him of any of those powers be subject to the jurisdiction of any Court."

For the first time Supreme Court of Pakistan dealt with the question of jurisdiction of the Court under the aforesaid Article 111 in a case arising from resignation of a member of the National Assembly of Pakistan. In that case, Fazlul Quader Chowdhury vs. Shah Nawa: reported in 18 DLR (SC) 62; PLD 1966 (SC) 105 respondent Mr. Shah Nawaz, a member of the National Assembly on 24.4.1964 sent a letter of his resignation addressed to the President of Pakistan and the same was subsequently made over to the Secretary of the National Assembly on 9.5.64. But in the meantime the respondent sent telegrams and wrote a letter on 27.4.64 to the Speaker informing him that he did not resign his membership and requested the Speaker not to accept the said letter of resignation addressed to the President. After the return of the Speaker to the country from abroad the said letter and telegrams were placed before him on 19.5.64 and the Speaker got a notification published in the Gazette on 20.5.1964 declaring that the respondent had resigned his seat in the National Assembly within the meaning of clause (a) of Article 107 of the Constitution of Pakistan, 1962. Respondent challenged the vires of the said Notification by filing an application under Article 98 of that Constitution. The Speaker took the plea that the jurisdiction of the High Court was barred under the provisions of Article 111 of the said Constitution. High Court of West Pakistan, Lahore allowed the petition of the respondent. The Speaker then appealed to the Supreme Court of Pakistan. The said appeal was dismissed and the objection about lack of jurisdiction of the High Court was negatived. SA Rahman J after considering the said Article 111 and case of Brodlaugh vs. Cosset held as follows:

"The case is not apposite in the circumstances under consideration here. Obviously, the dispute therein related to something that had happened within the chamber of the House of Commons. The question that falls for determination in the instant case relates more to the constitution of the Legislative Assembly itself, insofar as the point raised is whether on a true interpretation of the provisions of the Constitution, a sitting Member's seat has become vacant or not. No matter relating to "the regulation of procedure, the conduct of business or the maintenance of order in the Assembly" has been brought under review. Article 111 is consequently not attracted to the case and the Courts jurisdiction is not ousted. Indeed, the High Court's jurisdiction is eminently invokable under Article 98 to correct any error of law or any transgression of jurisdiction by any person or authority in circumstances akin to those prevailing in the instant case so long as the order to be passed is not repugnant to any other provisions of the Constitution. No such danger exists here. The Constitution contains a scheme for the distribution of powers between various organs and authorities of the State and to the superior judiciary is allotted the very responsible though delicate duty of containing all other authorities within their jurisdiction, by investing the former with powers to intervene whenever any person exceeds his lawful authority. Legal issues of the character raised in this case could only be resolved in case of doubt or dispute, by the superior Courts exercising judicial review functions, assigned to them by the fundamental law of the land, viz, the Constitution which must over-ride all other sub-constitutional laws."

55. Aforesaid Article 111 again came up for consideration of the Supreme Court of Pakistan in the case of Lt. Col Farzand Ali vs. Province of West Pakistan reported in 22 DLR (SC) 203 though in a different context regarding involuntary disqualification of some members of the National Assembly. In that case question was whether validity of 3rd, 4th and 6th Amendments of the Constitution of Pakistan could be challenged on the ground of disqualification of some members of the National Assembly and whether Court's jurisdiction was barred under Article 111 of the said Constitution. Hamidur Rahman CJ after reviewing the decisions of the Supreme Court of Pakistan in the case of Ahmed Syed Kirmani P.W 1958 SC 397; AK Badrul Huq 15 DLR (SC) 389=PLD 1963 (SC) 704, Bradlaugh vs. Gosset 12 QBD 273, Fazlul Quader Chowdhury vs. Md. Abdul Hoque 18 DLR (SC) 69=1963 (SC) 486, Fazlul Quader Chowdhury vs. Shah Newa: 18 DLR (SC) 62=PLD 1966 (SC) 105 along with some US decisions observed as follows:

"in this view of the matter, while I am prepared to concede that all that fairly concerns the internal proceedings of the House relating to its proper business is immune from challenge in Courts, I am not in a position to agree that a question relating to the title of a person to be a Member of the House or to continue to sit therein is a question pertaining to the internal proceedings of the House. It is a question affecting the constitution of the House and, therefore, it is not a question which can possibly be barred from enquiry by the Courts under Article 111 of the Constitution. This is not a matter which pertains either to the regulation of the procedure of the House or the conduct of its business or the maintenance of order in the Assembly or affecting any of its privileges. This -is not a question, therefore, which, in my opinion, relates to the "internal proceeding" of an Assembly. Clause (1) of Article 111 bars the Courts only from enquiring into the validity of "proceedings in an Assembly "in the formal sense and nothing more."

56. In that case it was further observed by his Lordship that: The words of Article 89(1) of the 1956 Constitution were to the same effect as the words of Article 111 (1) of the Constitution of 1962, and they were considered in the case of Ahmed Syed Kirmani to have given immunity only in respect of matters falling fairly within the scope of the "internal proceeding" of the House relating to its proper business. If under those provisions the immunity was held to be confined only to internal proceedings, I see no reason to think that their scope has been widened in Article 111 (1) of the 1962 Constitution. "

57. In the case of Tahir Beg vs. Kausar Ali reported in PLD 1976 (SC) 504 resignation letter of the appellant, a member of the Provincial Assembly allegedly obtained by the respondent by coercion at pistol point on 16.2.74, was placed before the Speaker who caused a Gazette Notification published on the same day about resignation of the appellant. In that case resignation of the appellant was considered by the House in a privilege motion adopted by the House on 24.5.74. So it was claimed that resignation of the appellant formed part of the internal proceeding of the House under Article 69 of the Constitution of Pakistan 1973 and Court has no jurisdiction to enquire into the matter. Md. Gul J after reviewing the decisions in the case Ahmed Syed Kirmani reported in PLD 1958 (SC) 379; Lt. Col. Farzand Ali Vs. Province of West Pakistan reported in 22 DLR (SC) 203=PLD 1970 (SC) 98 and Fazlul Quader Chowdhury vs. Md. Abdul Haque reported in 18 DLR (SC) 69=PLD 1963 SC 486 held that "Therefore, there is no merit in the second limb of the argument of the appellant's learned counsel. The question at the root is not validity of the resolution of the Provincial Assembly accepting the privilege motion on 24.5.74, but the right, title of the appellant to continue as member of the Assembly and therefore, inevitably a question relating to "composition" of the House, which the superior courts in the sub-continent have not hesitated to consider and decide in appropriate proceedings."

58. Article 69 of the Constitution of Pakistan 1973 considered in the aforesaid decision is as follows:

"69(1) The validity of any proceedings in Parliament shall not be called in question on the ground of any irregularity of procedure.

(2) No officer or member of Parliament in whom powers are vested by or under the Constitution for regulating procedure or the conduct of business, or for maintaining order in Parliament shall be subject to the jurisdiction of any Court in respect of the exercise by him of those powers."

59. The aforesaid provisions of Article 69 of the Constitution of Pakistan 1973 is almost identical with the provisions of Article 78 of our Constitution quoted hereinbefore.

60. Learned Advocate of the respondents could not lay his hand on any new decision in this respect except a decision of the House of Lords in the case of British Railway Board vs. Pickin reported in (1974) Weekly Law Reports 208. In that case validity of the British Railway Act 1968, a private Act of the Parliament, was challenged on the grounds of false recital in the preamble, want of notice to the owners and public notice of the intended compulsory acquisition at the time the Bill was moved in the Parliament. It was held that Court cannot investigate such allegations. Such challenge to the validity of an Act passed by our Parliament is also clearly barred under clause (1) of Article 78 of our Constitution. But in the facts and circumstances of the case before us principle enunciated in the said decision has no manner of application.

61. From a review of the aforesaid decisions of the Supreme Court of Pakistan it is seen that after interpreting the relevant provisions of the Constitution of Pakistan the said Court held that action taken by the Speaker on the letter of resignation of a member of the Legislature related to the title of such member and Court's jurisdiction was not ousted to decide the legality of such action. Indian High Court held that wrongful refusal of the Speaker to administer oath to a member did not relate to the internal business of the House.

62. Let us now examine the relevant provisions of the Constitutions of India, Pakistan and Bangladesh regarding vacation of seat of member of Parliament or legislature. Identical provisions of Articles 101(3) and 190(3) of the Constitution of India as the same stood before the 33rd Amendment of the Constitution dealt with vacation of seat by a member of the Parliament and the State Legislatures respectively. Original Article 190(3) before amendment on 14.5.1974 was as follows:

"If a member of a House of the Legislature of a State

(a) becomes subject to any of the disqualifications in clause (1) of Article 191; or

(b) resigns his seat by writing under his hand addressed to the Speaker or Chairman, as the case may be, his seat shall thereupon become vacant"

So clause (3) quoted above deals with involuntary and voluntary disqualification (by resignation) incurring which a member of the legislature vacates his seat in the legislature.

63. In AIR 1952 TC 166 and AIR 1965 (All) 536 High Court of Trivankar Cochin and High Court of Allahabad respectively held that the Speaker can determine the genuineness and voluntariness of the letter of resignation when such question is raised. By the 33rd Amendment of the said Constitution Speaker has been vested with the power to determine genuineness and voluntariness of the letter of resignation by enquiring if such question is raised and to accept the letter of resignation. Before the said Amendment there was no such power of the Speaker to accept letter of resignation under the unamended provisions of the said clause.

In spite of that in the aforesaid two decisions two High Courts held that Speaker can determine such question.

64. Article 107(a) of the Constitution of Pakistan 1962 regarding resignation of a member of the legislature was as follows:

"107. The seat of a member of an assembly shall become vacant if-

(a) he resigns his seat by notice in writing under his hand addressed to the Speaker of the assembly;"

Article 67 of our Constitution also provides for vacation of seat by Member of the Parliament under circumstances mentioned in clause (1) thereof including incurring involuntary disqualification under clause (2) of Article 66 and under clause (2) of the said Article 67 by incurring voluntary disqualification by tendering letter of resignation b) him to the Speaker. Article 67(2) of our Constitution regarding resignation of a Member of Parliament is as follows:

"A member of Parliament may resign his seat by writing under his hand addressed to the Speaker, and the seat shall become vacant when the writing is received by the Speaker or, if the office of Speaker is vacant or the Speaker is for any reason unable to perform his functions, by the Deputy Speaker."

From a reading of English and Bengali versions of the said clause (2) it appears that the resignation letter need not be written under the own hand of the Member resigning his seat and the same is only to be signed by him as Bengali version prevails over the English version in case of conflict between the two under the provisions of clause (3) of Article 153. Since there is such conflict as to writing of the letter of resignation under the own hand of the member concerned the Bengali version shall prevail as the same does not require the letter of resignation to be written under the own hand of the member resigning his seat. There is nothing in the aforesaid provisions authorizing the Speaker either to accept or reject a letter of resignation submitted by a member of Parliament after ascertaining genuineness or voluntariness or validity of the same. But in 18 DLR (SC) 62 it was held that Speaker is to arrive at the intention of the resigning member by construing the documents submitted by the member.

65. Let us now examine whether Speaker of the Parliament of Bangladesh can determine the genuineness and validity of the letter of resignation submitted by a member as contended by Mr. Hossain or he is a mere post box and must act in accordance with such letter without examining and determining the genuineness and voluntariness of the same and the same will take effect automatically as soon as the same is received by the Speaker as contended by Mr. Islam.

Rules 177 and 178 of the Rules of Procedure of the Parliament adopted on 22.7.1974 and amended up to date are as follows:

"177(1) A member who desires to resign his seat in Parliament shall intimate, in writing under his hand addressed to the Speaker, his intention to resign his seat in the House, and shall not give any reason for his resignation:

Provided that where any member gives any reason or introduces any extraneous matter, the Speaker may, in his discretion, omit such words, phrases or matter and the same shall not be read out to the House.

(2) The resignation shall take effect and the seat of the member shall become vacant under clause (2) of Article 67 of the Constitution when the intimation is received by the Speaker or if the office of the Speaker is vacant, or the Speaker is for any reason unable to perform his functions, by the Deputy Speaker.

178.(1) If any dispute arises as to whether a member has after his election, become subject to any of the disqualifications mentioned in clause (2) of Article 66 or as to whether. a member should vacate his seat pursuant to Article 70 of the Constitution, the dispute shall be referred by the Speaker to the Election Commission.

(2) If the decision of the Election Commission is that the member has become disqualified or should vacate his seat, as the case may be, the member shall cease to be a member.

(3) If a member resigns his seat, or is absent, without leave of the House, for ninety consecutive sitting days the Parliament, or fails to make and subscribe his oath of office within the time mentioned in clause (l) (a) of Article 67 of the Constitution or otherwise ceases to be a member, the Speaker shall bring the fact to the notice of the House, if it is in session;

Provided that when the Parliament is not in session the Speaker shall inform the House immediately after the House reassembles that a member has resigned or ceased to be a member, as the case may be, during the inter-session period.

(4) If the seat of a member becomes vacant, the Secretary shall cause a notification to that effect to be published in the Gazette and forward a copy of the notification to the member concerned and also to the Election Commission for taking steps to fill the vacancy thus caused."

66. Aforesaid sub-Rule (1) of the Rule 177 shows that when a member desires to resign his seat in Parliament he shall intimate his intention to the Speaker in writing under his hand and he shall not give his reason for his resignation. But there is nothing in this sub-Rule (1) that non-compliance of the said formalities makes the letter of resignation liable to be cancelled. So the said formalities are not mandatory but directory in nature as no consequence for such non-compliance of the said formalities has been provided thereunder. But reading the said sub-rule (1) in either version along with the said clause (2) of Article 67 it is clear that intention of the member concerned to resign his seat is to be conveyed to the Speaker. To ascertain such intention the Speaker is to be satisfied that the signature of the member appearing in the letter of his resignation is really that of the said member. Speaker can easily ascertain the genuineness of such signature by comparing the same with the signature of the member concerned contained in the Roll of Members kept in the Parliament Secretariat under Rule 6 of the aforesaid Rules. In case of any allegation of fraud or coercion applied to the member concerned in obtaining his signature in the letter of resignation the Speaker is also to examine voluntariness of such signature in the letter of resignation to ascertain the intention of the member to resign his seat. So even if there is nothing in Article 67(2) about ascertaining genuineness and voluntariness of a letter of resignation by the Speaker by making enquiry the aforesaid Rule 177(1) gives that power to the Speaker indirectly as he is to see that intention of the member concerned to resign his seat has really been conveyed to him in the letter of resignation. Under the proviso of the said sub-rule (1) of Rule 177 the Speaker may also omit the reason or extraneous matter introduced in the letter of resignation and when he omits the same he shall not read the same to the House. The said sub-rule (1) of Rule 177 having provided for the formalities for submitting letter of resignation by a member under Article 67(2) of the Constitution Speaker can examine the letter of resignation to ascertain the intention of the member in the aforesaid manner. But he cannot go beyond that to interpret the provisions of Article 67(2) which is the exclusive domain of this Court under the Constitution.

<u>67. Under sub-rule (3) of Rule 178 the Speaker is to bring the fact of resignation of a member to the notice of the House. But bringing the same to the notice of the House is not for the purpose of approval of the House as in the case of an application for leave of absence submitted by a member under Rule 179. No Rule or provision has been pointed out to us to show that action taken by the Speaker or his inaction over the letter of resignation or to bring the fact of such resignation to the notice of the House is taken by him in exercise of powers vested in him "for the regulation of procedure, the conduct of business or the maintenance of order in Parliament." Regulation of procedure by the Speaker is for the purpose of conduct of business or maintenance of order in Parliament. How can action taken by the Speaker or his failure to take action about the resignation letters of the Members of the Parliament be in exercise of his power of regulating procedure when such resignation is not subject matter of Parliamentary debate and decision? Had the resignation of the members been subject to Parliamentary debate or decision then it could very well be said that Speaker's decision in the matter is in exercise of his aforesaid power. Speaker takes action in respect of letter of resignation of a Member of the Parliament under the aforesaid Rules 177 and 178 only and the same gives him limited jurisdiction to ascertain the intention of the member by examining genuineness of the signature of the member concerned and, in case of complaint to him, to further ascertain the voluntariness of the letter of resignation. He may also omit the reasons and extraneous matters introduced in the letter of resignation. Obviously the Speaker is to exercise such jurisdiction within reasonable time as conceded by the learned Advocate of the respondents. I am not going to decide the reasonableness of the time taken by the Speaker as I am only considering the question of jurisdiction of the Court, raised in this Rule and seriously argued at the bar, in respect of the action or inaction of the Speaker in the matter of resignation letters submitted by the Members of the Parliament and for such limited purpose examining the relevant provisions of the Constitution and the Rules of Procedure of the Parliament. So, in my view, exercise of such jurisdiction by the Speaker is not related to "the regulation of procedure, the conduct of business or maintenance of order in Parliament" and the same is related to the right and title of the members of the Parliament and also to the proper constitution of the Parliament. Court can determine the right of a member or members to sit or not to sit in the Parliament if it did not arise from his or their committing any breach of privileges of the House but from his or their qualification or disqualification to sit in the Parliament. Resignation of a member is nothing but voluntary disqualification incurred by him to continue as such member. I am, therefore, of the view that action taken by the Speaker or his failure to take action on the resignation letters of 147 members of the Parliament is not sacrosanct from judicial review and Court's jurisdiction is not barred under Article 78(2) of the Constitution to examine the legality of any action or inaction of the Speaker if a really aggrieved person complains against the same. Since the petitioner is not an aggrieved person and has no locus standi in the matter before us and the Speaker has not yet taken any action in the matter as found by my learned brother this Rule also fails and is discharged.</u>

Md. Abdul Karim J: I agree with the judgment of my learned brother, AM Mahmudur Rahman, J, that the Rules be discharged. In my opinion, any discussion on immunity of the proceedings and the conduct of business in Parliament from the jurisdiction of the Court is not necessary in view of failure of the writ petitions on the threshold point of maintainability.

End.

full_judgment:
Mahmudul Amin Choudhury J: This Rule was issued calling upon the plaintiff-opposite party No.1 to show cause why order dated 17-8-97 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge and Artha Rin Adalat No.2, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 2 of 1995 should not be set aside.

2. The short fact leading to this Rule is that, Opposite Party No.1 as plaintiff instituted the aforesaid suit for realisation of Taka 93,35,483.00 from this petitioner by sale of the property mentioned in the schedule attached to the plaint which was mortgaged with the plaintiff opposite party No.1 and the plaintiff also prayed for realisation of interest and other incidental reliefs. The suit was instituted before the Artha Rin Adalat No.2 which was established under the Artha Rin Adalat Ain. The present petitioner who is defendant No.1 entered appearance in the suit and filed an application under Order 7, rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure for return of the plaint as the plaintiff is not a financial institution as contemplated under the Artha Rin Adalat Ain. According to the petitioner the suit has been wrongly filed in the Artha Rin Adalat instead of filing it before the ordinary Civil Court The Adalat then on hearing both the sides by order dated 17-8-97 rejected the petitioner's prayer holding that as the plaintiff is a registered Co-operative Credit Society there is no bar in proceeding with the suit before the Artha Rin Adalat. It was also observed that previously also the Court disposed of another suit of the same nature. With that observation the present petitioner’s prayer made under Order 7, rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure was rejected. The petitioner then moved this Court and obtained the present Rule.

3. Mr Miah Abdul Gafur, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner submits that the Artha Rin Adalat is not an ordinary civil Court. It is a civil Court of defined nature and only a financial institution or an organisation which has been given licence to act as financial institutions by the Bangladesh Bank can file a suit in the Adalat for realisation of any loan which is absent in the present case. It is submitted that the plaintiff is only a Co-operative Society and they have not obtained any licence from the Bangladesh Bank to operate as a financial institution within the meaning of Artha Rin Adalat Ain and as the present suit has been filed by the plaintiff which is nota financial institution the same cannot be maintained in that Court. The plaintiff has not obtained any licence and their status  is not that of a financial institution as contemplated under the Artha Rin Adalat Ain and the trial Court committed wrong and illegality in not returning the plaint to the filing Advocate for presentation before the proper Court.

4. Mr Ozair Faruque, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the plaintiff-opposite party No.1, at the very outset raised the question of maintainability of this petition before this Court under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure. He submits that the Artha Rin Adalat is not an ordinary civil Court, but it is a civil Court of defined nature and it is a self-contained court having its own forum of appeal. Section 6 of the Ain completely ousted the jurisdiction of the civil Court and no application under section 115 of the Code of   Civil Procedure is maintainable against any interlocutory order passed by the Artha Rin Adalat.

5. Before we proceed further we like to find out whether an application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure is maintainable before this Court against any order passed by the Artha Rin Adalat. In support of his submission that an application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure is maintainable Mr Miah Abdul Gafur first of all placed reliance in the case of Serajuddin Howlader VS. Pubali Bank Limited, reported in 4 BLT 80. Wherein it has been held that Artha Rin Adalat is a civil Court and is subordinate to the High Court Division and that being the legal position the petitioner may seek relief under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure. The Division Bench has held that "where no appeal lies" section 115 of the Code lies. That decision was given in a Writ petition and it was held that when an application under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure is maintainable against an order passed by the Artha Rin Adalat, the aggrieved party cannot invoke the jurisdiction under Article 102 of the Constitution. Mr Miah Abdul Gafur placed another decision of the High Court Division, reported in 48 DLR 57 (Sonali Bank VS. Ali Tannery Ltd. and others), where it has been held that the Artha Rin Adalat, though a special Court, is nevertheless a Court subordinate to the High Court Division and it is 'therefore' amenable to the revisional jurisdiction of this Division.

6. As against this Mr Ozair Faruque placed the decision reported in 14 BLD 195 (HCD) (Messers MAC-Proprietor Mahatabuddin Choudhury and another VS. Agrani Bank) in which decision one of us (Mahmudul Amin Choudhury J) was a party, where it has been held that the Artha Rin Adalat Ain is a special law under which Courts have been constituted with their own forum of appeal. By analyzing the provisions of section 5(4) and (5), it cannot be found that an Artha Rin Adalat is an ordinary civil Court for all purposes and all the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure are applicable in a proceeding under this Act. It has been held that provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure are applicable subject to the provisions of this special law. The same view has been expressed in another decision reported in 1994 BLT 118 (Sultan Alam vs. Rupali Bank). Mr Ozair Faruque then placed the decision reported in 14 BLD (AD) 196 (Sultana Jute Mills Ltd. and another vs. Agrani Bank and others) wherein it has been held that the Artha Rin Adalat is not a full-fledged Civil Court with all the powers and jurisdiction of a Civil Court. It is a Civil Court of a defined and limited jurisdiction. The Artha Rin Adalat Ain has not given the Adalat any jurisdiction to adjudicate upon any matter other than that provided in section 5(1) of the Act. Mr Ozair Faruque relying on this decision argued that it has been clearly spelt out by the Appellate Division that any interlocutory order passed by the Adalat is not revisable under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure by the High Court Division.

7. In 48 DLR 57, the High Court Division assumed jurisdiction under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure in the following manner.

"13. It had been held in a number of decisions that the Artha Rin Adalat is not an ordinary Civil Court but a special forum of limited jurisdiction. The question, therefore, arises whether an order passed by a Court of Special jurisdiction is revisable by this Court under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure. We can resolve this question, easily if we can find the answer to the question, is the Artha Rin Adalat a Court subordinate to the High Court Division. In deciding this issue with regard to the special status the superior Courts of this sub-continent have formulated certain principles. If appeal lies from a Special Tribunal to the High Court then that Special Tribunal is subordinate to the High Court. Similarly, if the Special Court is under the administrative control of the High Court it is also subordinate to the High Court. If we examine the provisions of the Act we find that an appeal shall lie against a judgment and decree of the Artha Rin Adalat to the High Court Division. Section 4(2) of the Act provides that the Judges of the Artha Rin Adalat will be appointed from amongst the Subordinate Judges with consultation with the Supreme Court. Rule framed under the Act provides that the Artha Rin Adalat will be under the administrative control of the Supreme Court. It has been held in one case that if the court is one from which an appeal lies to the High Court though in certain specified case, then the Court is subject to the appellate jurisdiction of the High Court and that is sufficient to attract the power of superintendency conferred on the High Court. Besides Article 109 of the Constitution provides that the High Court Division shall have superintendence and control over all Courts subordinate to it and Article 114 provides that there shall be in addition to the Supreme Court such Courts subordinate thereto as may be established by Law".

8. The High Court Division held that Artha Rin Adalat though a Special Court is nevertheless a Court subordinate to the High Court Division and is, therefore, amenable to the revisional jurisdiction of the High Court Division. In 4 BLT 80 case in paragraph No. 9 of the decision quoting the provision of section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure It has been held that the Artha Rin Adalat is a Civil Court and is subordinate to the High Court Division. That being the legal position it was found that the petitioner can seek relief under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

9. We have gone through these decisions of our High Court Division and it appears that the decisions were given in the same line holding that when appeal lies before the High Court Division against any decree and judgment passed by the Artha Rin Adalat it is subordinate to the High Court Division and is under the control and superintendence  of this Division and, as such, it is a Civil Court and so section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure can be  invoked against any order passed by the Artha Rin  Adalat. It may be pointed out that 48 DLR 57 decision was given by the Division Bench on 25th July, 1994 and in BLT case the same was delivered on 20th March, 1995.

10. But the latest decision of our Appellate Division on this matter is reported in 14 BLD (AD) 196, where it has been specifically decided that Artha Rin Adalat is not a full-fledged Civil Court with all the powers and jurisdiction of a Civil Court. It is a Civil Court of a defined and limited jurisdiction, and it has also been held that only these suits which are concerned with the realisation of loan as defined in the Act and disbursed by the financial institution can be filed in the Adalat and no other kind of suit. The Appellate Division in this decision has held as follows:

"22. Revisional jurisdiction of the High Court Division is provided for in section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure and in making under section 6 the proceeding, order, judgment and decree of an Artha Rin Adalat not amenable to interference by any Court or authority, the aim of the Adalat Act was to create departures from the Code of Civil Procedure. Section 7, it may be said, was meant to be an exception to this complete ouster of interference. An exception has been made in respect of a judgment and decree in section 7(1). Another exception has been made in respect of a final order under Order 9, rule 13 CPC. In both cases appeal will be to the High Court Division. There is room for argument that both the appellate, revisional powers of interference with any order interlocutory or otherwise, is expressly barred by section 6. The proviso to section 7(1) barring an appeal against an interlocutory order has been provided for only as a measure of abundant caution. In other words, section 6 is the master ouster provision, section 7 is an exception to that ouster. The exception cannot render the ouster provision nugatory".

11. The aforesaid findings clearly indicate that any order passed by the Artha Rin Adalat is not amenable to the jurisdiction of this Division under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure as there is express bar in section 6 which is the master ouster of jurisdiction. Before the Appellate Division it was argued that proviso to section 7 indicate that no appeal shall lie against interlocutory order of the Adalat, which means the appeal is barred but a revision shall lie before the High Court Division in respect of both the appealable and revisional orders. The Appellate Division disposed of this in the aforesaid manner in paragraph No.22 of the decision. In section 6 of the Ain it has been provided that no order of an Artha Rin Adalat is amenable to interference by any Court or authority, the only exception is section 7 where a provision for appeal has been made in respect of any judgment and decree or an order passed under Order 9, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Admittedly, the Artha Rin Adalat Ain is a special forum set up under a special legislation and the remedies will follow as provided in the Ain itself and it has been indicated by our Appellate Division that if there is any exclusion indicated in the Ain, as in section 6, it will include a remedy under the general law. So, on going through this decision of the Appellate Division, we hold that there is a complete ouster of jurisdiction of the High Court Division for interference under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure against any interlocutory matter or orders passed by the Adalat. In the two High Court Division decisions as aforesaid, this decision of our Appellate Division has not been looked into considered. We on perusal of this decision of our Appellate Division, are of the view that the impugned order is not revisable under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure as there is total bar under the Ain.

12. The main contention of Miah Abdul Gafur is that the suit has been filed by the plaintiff-opposite-partyin the Artha Rin Adalat though the plaintiff is not a financial institution as defined under the Artha Rin Adalat Ain. It is well-settled that a financial institution as defined in section 2 of the Ain may institute a suit before the Artha Rin Adalat for realisation of the amount of loan they advanced and in this section there is a list of institutions which are termed as financial institutions. The plaintiff-society or any co-operative society has not been included in the list. Miah Abdul Gafur placing sub-section (6) of section 2 of the Ain submitted that the plaintiff-society has not obtained any licence from the Bangladesh Bank to operate as a financial institution as provided under section 2 (Ka) of Artha Rin Adalat Ain. It is submitted that any society or organisation on obtaining licence from the Bangladesh Bank under this Ain may operate is a financial institution. The plaintiff admittedly has not obtained any licence under this law from Bangladesh Bank though it is a registered co-operative society and as the plaintiff has not obtained any licence to operate as a financial institution it cannot file any suit before the Artha Rin Adalat. That they have not obtained any licence has not been controverted by the plaintiff-opposite party No. 1. Mr. Ozair Faruque, the learned Advocate, frankly concedes that the plaintiff has not obtained any license under the aforesaid law to operate as a financial institution.

13. As regards jurisdiction of the Adalat it has been provided in section 5(1) of the Ain as follows:

৫। (১) অন্য কোন আইনে যাহা কিছুই থাকুক নাকেন, অর্থিক প্রকিষ্ঠান ঋণ আদায় সংক্রান্ত যাবতীয় মামলা আদালতে দায়ের করিতে হইবে এবং উক্ত আদালতেই নিষ্পত্তি করা হইবে।”

<u>14. This indicates that only the financial institutions may institute suit in the Adalat for realisation of any advance made to any party as a loan. Here in the present case admittedly the plaintiff is not a financial institution as contemplated under the Artha Rin Adalat Ain and, as such, they have no right to institute the suit in the Adalat and the Adalat has no jurisdiction to entertain such a suit. The suit if otherwise maintainable may be instituted in any other appropriate forum but not before the Artha Rin Adalat. The precondition for filing the suit before the Artha Rin Adalat is that it must be a financial institution as contemplated under section 2 of the Ain which is very much absent in the case of present plaintiff-opposite party No. 1. So, the institution and continuation of the suit before the Adalat is illegal and beyond jurisdiction. It appears that, taking this ground that as the plaintiff is not a financial institution the filing and entertainment of the suit in the Artha Rin Adalat is illegal the present petitioner filed a petition under Order 7, rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure for return of the plaint which was rejected by the trial Court on the ground that the plaintiff is a society which advanced the money to the present petitioner and that the Court also disposed of certain other suits of similar nature. But to attract jurisdiction of the Adalat it must follow the provision of section 2 of the Ain. It must first examine whether the plaintiff is a financial institution and that the amount involved is a loan without which no suit can be entertained by the Adalat. Here in the present case admittedly the plaintiff is not a financial institution as contemplated under section 2 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, But the suit has been entertained by the Adalat. It is well-settled that Artha Rin Adalat Ain is a self contained Code and the Adalat is not a Civil Court having all the powers of the Code of Civil Procedure. It is a Civil Court of defined nature and jurisdiction. This Adalat can entertain only those suits as contemplated under the Ain Now if a suit is filed by an authority, which is not a financial institution, can it be allowed to proceed further? In the Ain no provision has been made for return or rejection of the plaint as contemplated under Order 7, rules 10 and 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure. In such a situation can the aggrieved party be left without any relief. We have considered this aspect of the matter and the observation of our Appellate Division in 14 BLD cases and we are of the view that the Court is not left without power and the party is not left without any relief. When it is apparent on the face of the record that the suit has been wrongly entertained and proceeded with in the Adalat, this Court may act under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure. It provided that nothing in this Code shall be deemed to limit or otherwise affect the inherent power of the Court to make such orders as may be necessary for the ends of justice or to prevent abuse of the process of the Court. The continuation of the suit before the Artha Rin Adalat is an abuse of the process of the Court as any decree passed by the Adalat in such a suit will be without jurisdiction and, as such, a nullity. As that has been filed under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure it is not maintainable against an order passed by the Artha Rin Adalat, we are inclined to act under section 151(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure and make the Rule absolute with a-direction to the Adalat to return the plaint to the filing Advocate for presentation before the proper Court.</u>

15. Thus, after consideration of the materials on record and after hearing the learned Advocates of both the sides and on perusal of the decisions as aforesaid we hold that the application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure is not maintainable. By acting under the provision of Section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure we are inclined to make the Rule absolute.

16. The Rule, is accordingly, made absolute without any order as to costs. The Artha Rin Adalat No. 2, Dhaka is hereby directed to return the plaint to the filing Advocate for presentation before the appropriate Court.

End.

Vs.

case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 12th February 1995 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 1400 of 2000
full_judgment:
Md Fazlul Karim J: This appeal at the instance of the/defendant arose out of judgment and order dated 12-2-1995 passed by Single Judge of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.1400 of 1993 discharging the rule issued against the judgment and decree dated 15-11-1992 of the Additional District Judge, First Court, Khulna in Title Appeal No.227 of 1979 allowing the appeal reversing those dated 28-8-1999 by the Munsif, Second Court, Khulna in Title Suit No. 174 of 1975 dismissing the suit.

2. Respondent No.1 and father of respondent Nos. 2 and 3 namely, Rampada Mondal as the plaintiff Nos. 1 and 2 respectively instituted Title Suit No.174 of 1995 in the Court of Second Munsif, Khulna against the appellants and one Phanindra Nath Baidya for specific performance of contract. That the case of the respondents as made out in the plaint, inter alia, are that the suit land belonged to the plaintiffs who sold the same to the defendant No.1 namely, Phanindra Nath Baidya for a consideration of Taka 2500 (Taka two thousand five hundred) only by kabala dated 5-2-1963; that on the same day the defendant No.1 executed an Ekrarnama in favour of the plaintiffs; terms of the Ekrarnama was that the defendant No.1 would reconvey the suit land to the plaintiff on receipt of the aforesaid consideration money within any Chaitra after harvest by 1377 BS the defendant No.1 with an ill motive created some documents of transfer in favour of defendant Nos.2 and 3; after harvest in the year of 1377 BS the plaintiff respondents approached the defendant No.1 on several occasions in the month of Falgoon and tendered the consideration money with a request to execute and register the deed of reconveyance; that the plaintiffs also tendered the consideration money to the defendant No.1 on 14-4-1970 and requested to execute and register the deed of reconveyance, but the defendant No.1 refused to execute and register the deed of reconveyance in favour of the plaintiffs; they filed an application before the Sub- Divisional Officer, Khulna under the provisions of President's Order No.88 of 1972 and President Order No.136 of 1972 for redemption of the suit land from the defendant No.1 but the case was stayed by the Government and hence the plaintiff filed the present suit for specific performance of contract.

3. Defendant Nos. 2 and 3, the present appellants contested the suit by filing a written statement contending, inter alia, that the plaintiffs have no cause of action to file the present suit; the suit is barred by limitation; that the defendant No.1 has been residing in India since 1971; the right of repurchase of the plaintiffs through Ekrarnama is extinguished after expiry of the period mentioned in the Ekrarnama and the transaction was treated as an out and out sale; the contesting defendants have purchased the suit land for valuable consideration bonafide without notice of Ekrarnama and have been possessing the suit land; the price of the suit land is increased meanwhile and, as such, the plaintiffs have filed the present suit on false statement and, as such, they are not entitled to any relief as prayed for and the suit is liable to be dismissed with cost.

4. The learned Munsif dismissed the suit and on appeal the suit was decreed and the High Court Division discharged the Rule.

5. Leave was granted to consider the ground urged by the learned Advocate that:

"The learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioners submits that the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division has failed to notice that section 95A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act has no application to the transaction in question which had been past and closed before the promulgation of President's Order No.88 of 1972 and, as such, the impugned judgment and order is liable to be set aside and that of the trial Court restored."

6. Mr Abul Kalam Mainuddin, the learned Advocate appearing for the appellants, submitted that the High Court Division wrongly relied on the decisions reported in 34 DLR (AD) L37 and 36 DLR 90 which are not applicable in the facts and circumstances of the present case. The learned Advocate further submitted that the High Court Division failed to take notice that section 95A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act has no application to a transaction which was past and closed before the promulgation of President's Order No.88 of 1972.

7. Mr AY Ahmed Ali, the learned Counsel appeared for the respondents though did not file the concise statement but in view of the importance of the point involved we have heard him, who has relied on the decision reported in 44 DLR (AD) 233 and submitted that admittedly the plaintiffs who were owners of the suit land sold the same by registered kabala dated 5-2-1963 to the defendant No.2 with a condition to re-purchase on payment of the consideration money and on the same day executed an Ekrarnama to return the suit land, within Chaitra 1377 BS making the contract an usufructuary mortgage for which Article 148 of the Limitation Act provided a period of limitation of 60 years to make the suit barred by limitation and he further submits that by operation of section 95 and 95A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act after expiry of 7 years, the suit land automatically vests in the plaintiff and the transaction is not past and closed as has been submitted by the learned Counsel.

<u>8. In the case of Bangladesh vs Haji Abdul Gani Biswas reported in 32 DLR (AD) 233 it was held that:</u>

<u>"Our conclusions, therefore, are that the President's Order Nos.88 and 136 of 1972 and No.24 of 1973 are all valid legislations for affecting necessary amendments in the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and those laws cannot be attacked on the ground of ultra vires; (2) any transfer of a holding or part thereof by a raiyat either by way of out and out sale with an agreement to recovery or where the transferor receives from the transferee any consideration and transferee acquires the right to possess and enjoy the usufruct, shall notwithstanding anything contained in the document relating to the transfer, be deemed to be a complete usufructuary mortgage for period of maximum 7 years and the provisions of section 95(4) and (5) shall apply to such transfers; (3) and such transfers are not to be understood in the light of the Transfer of Property Act because those are to be understood in the light of the enactment in question; (4) those transactions which are subsisting on the date of promulgation of President's Order No.88 of 1972 are hit by section 95A including the transaction entered into by way of an out and out sale with an agreement to recover, made whether before or after the promulgation of President's Order No. 88 of 1972; and (5) as far as the transactions which are not alive before the promulgation of President's Order No. 88 of 1972 they are concluded by the transactions, past and closed."</u>

<u>9. But in the case of Abu Bakkar vs Nazir Ahmed reported in 34 DLR (AD) 237. This Division held that:</u>

<u>"But on perusal of the judgment of the High Court Division it is found that learned Advocates of both the parties who appeared they were confused between the period of subsistence of a usufructuary mortgage and the period of limitation in the case of a suit for redemption of a mortgaged land. The maximum period for which a usufructuary mortgage can be entered into was fifteen years under section 95 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. But by Ordinance No. XXI of 1969, section 95 was amended and thereby the maximum period for a usufructuary mortgage was reduced to seven years. And unless earlier redeemed by repayment of the consideration a mortgagor acquires right to redemption on the expiry of the maximum period of seven years, and if the mortgager does not voluntarily restore possession of the land to the mortgagor, the latter may file a suit for redemption within a period of 60 years from the date of accrual of his right of redemption. In this case the suit was filed just on the accrual of the right of redemption and, as such, it is not barred by limitation.</u>

<u>Section 95 has been again amended by the President's Order No.88 of 1972 with effect from 3 August, 1972, but this amendment did not touch the period of a usufructuary mortgage which is still 7 years, nor did it affect the period of limitation for redemption suit which is 60 years. The amendment relates to two new provisions. One is that if, on the expiry of the period of a mortgage, the mortgagee does not restore possession of the land to the mortgagor, then the Sub-divisional Magistrate shall, on an application by the mortgagor, restore possession to the mortgagor by evicting the mortgagee. In other words, for getting back possession of a mortgaged land the mortgagor need not file any redemption suit, but may get quick remedy by an application to the Sub-divisional Magistrate. The other provision in the amendment is that notwithstanding anything contained in any other law in force, any transfer of a land by an out and out sale with a condition for recovery acne shall be deemed to be a complete usufructuary mortgage for a period not exceeding 7 years on the expiry of which the mortgagor may get "back possession by an application to the Sub- divisional Magistrate. The High Court Division in view of its own conclusion that the transaction under Exhibit A is an out and out sale, considered whether this sale should be deemed to be a usufructuary mortgage and found that the transaction was past and closed. But since the transaction is, as we have found, a mortgage, no question arises whether it should be treated as mortgage".</u>

<u>10. The moot question involved in this case has been resolved ultimately in the case of Abdul Khaleque Sarnamat vs Abdul Khaleque Sarnamat and another reported in 1 BLC (AD) 90. The fact of the case was that respondent No.1 therein purchased one acre of land from the appellant by a registered kabala dated 24-6-1967 for a consideration of Taka 2,000 and on the same date executed a registered agreement to recovery the kabala land if the consideration of money was repaid within 4 years from that date. The appellant filed the Miscellaneous Case No. 1227 of 1972-73 in the Court of the then Sub-Divisional Officer, Barisal (South) to get the land redeemed. The suit was dismissed and the appeal was also dismissed. The High Court Division, however, made the rule absolute holding that as the date of reconveyance expired on 1-3-1972 before the President's Order No.88 of 1972 came into force on 3-8-1972 the transaction in question could not, be treated as a usufructuary mortgage transaction in the light of the decision in Bangladesh vs Haji Abdul Gani Biswas reported in 32 DLR (AD) 233 and the appellant was not entitled to get back the case land on the basis of section 95A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act as the transaction was not subsisting one on the date of promulgation of PO No.88 of 1972 as contemplated under section 95 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. This Division further held that:</u>

<u>"The High Court Division although was not correct in making some findings as noticed above but the decision given by it ultimately following 32 DLR case was correct. TH Khan has been fair enough to concede that if the. transaction is construed to be a mortgage for 4 years only and not 7 years as mentioned in section 95A then he has no case because in that case it will be governed by the principle of transaction past and closed as laid down in 32 DLR case."</u>

<u>11. In view of the above, in the instant case the 7 years period have expired long before the promulgation of President's Order No. 88 of 1972. Accordingly, we find substance in the submission of the learned Advocate for the appellant.</u>

Accordingly, the appeal is allowed without any order as to costs and Title Suit No.174 of 1975 of the Court of Munsif, Second Court, Khulna is dismissed without any order as to costs.

End.

parties:

Vs.
Secretary, Ministry of Industries ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Md Tafazzul Islam J: This Rule Nisi was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the impugned order dated 29-6-92 (Annexure-C) purporting to cancel the appointment of the petitioner should not be declared to have been made without any lawful authority and is of no legal effect.

2. The case of the petitioner, in brief, is that, respondent No. 2 Bangladesh Standards and Testing Institution herein after referred to as BSTI, is a body corporate having perpetual secession and common seal, being established under the Bangladesh Standards and Testing Institution Ordinance 1985 (Ordinance No. XXXVII of 1985) and the petitioner was appointed as Project Director under BSTI vide Memo dated 31-12-1991 (Annexure-A) and vide memo dated 2-3-1992 (Annexure-B) his pay scale was fixed at Taka 7100×200-8900 and the petitioner since his appointment, had been performing his duties most satisfactorily. However suddenly he received the memo dated 29-6-92 (Annexure-C), issued from the office of respondent No. 2 whereby without showing any cause or reason whatsoever, was informed that his appointment as Project Director has been cancelled with immediate effect by the decision of the office of the Secretary, Ministry of Industries. The petitioner then submitted representation to the Industry, Secretary of respondent No. 1, on 30-6-92 (Annexure-D) and subsequently, submitted several representations to the concerned authorities. Thereafter, vide memo dated 24-4-1993 (Annexure-E) addressed to the Minister in charge of the Ministry of Industries, the Director General BSTI, respondent No. 3 recommended withdrawal and reconsideration of the aforesaid order of cancellation of the appointment of the petitioner but without any result and so having no other alternative the petitioner moved this court. The petitioner also filed supplementary affidavit dated 31-7-1996 annexing therein Annexure-F and F1, Annexure-F being the report of the Selection Committee which selected the petitioner as Project Director and Annexure F-1 being the letter informing the concerned authorities that "Technical Assistance to BSTI project has been finally approved. The petitioner also filed another supplementary affidavit dated 11-6-97 annexing therein Annexure-G which is a report of the evaluation of the various projects of BSTI under five years plan which was submitted to the government and was duly approved.

3. The respondent No. 1 contested the Rule and filed affidavit-in-opposition stating, inter alia, that the petitioner, on 30-4-91, retired from BSTI as Director Administration on attaining retirement age of 57 years and so at the time of issuance of the appointing letter dated 31-12-91 (Annexure-A) the petitioner was a public servant retired from his service and, as such, in terms of section 5(1) of the Public Servants (Retirement) Act of 1.974 (Act XII of 1974) he could not be re-employed in any manner in BSTI without the approval of the President and accordingly, the letter of appointment on 31-12-91 appointing the petitioner as Project Director under BSTI being illegal ab initio and without any lawful authority there was no illegality in cancelling the said appointment. Further, Regulation 53 of the Bangladesh Standard and Testing Institution Service Regulation, 1989 provided that regarding retirement and re-employment of BSTI employees the provisions of Public Servants (Retirement) Act. 1974 will be applicable but the petitioner, taking advantage of his connection with the respondent No.3 got re-employment with BSTI illegally and since the letter dated 31-12-91 appointing the petitioner was issued without obtaining the approval from the President, was illegal ab initio, the respondent No. 1 directed the respondent No. 2 to cancel the aforesaid appointment without any delay and so it was not necessary to issue any show cause notice upon the petitioner before cancelling his appointment which was illegal ab initio and did not confer upon the petitioner any right to continue in the post. Further, though the appointment of the petitioner was cancelled on 29-6-1992 the petitioner did not challenge the said order and remained indolent for a period of three years and it is only when steps were taken to evict him from the official quarter earmarked for Project Director the petitioner filed this writ petition on 20-6-95 only to prolong his illegal occupation in the official quarter.

4. The respondent Nos. 2 and 4 also contested the Rule and filed affidavit-in-opposition stating, inter alia, that the petitioner retired from his service on 30-4-1991 after attaining the age of 57 years and, as such, in terms of section 5 of Public Servants (Retirement) Act 1974 (Act XII of 1974) he was not entitled to get any re-employment in BSTI without the prior approval of the President, and so the appointment of the petitioner, without obtaining prior approval of the President was illegal ab initio and accordingly, after this fact was revealed, the respondent No. 1 directed the respondent No. 2 to cancel the appointment of the petitioner and so, in the facts and circumstances of the present case, there was no requirement to issue any show cause notice. Further the project title “বাংলাদেশ ষ্ট্যান্ডার্ডস এন্ড ট্রেনিং ইনষ্টিটিউশন প্রতিষ্ঠা ও শক্তিশালী করণ প্রকল্প।” for which the petitioner was appointed albeit without proper authority was for the period from 30-6-90 to 30-6-93 as stated in the advertisement published in the Sangbad on 30-9-1990 (Annexure-3) and only the work of the project in Khulna and Chittagong continued till 1994 and accordingly, the work of the project as being duly concluded and closed in March 1994, the respondent No. 2 vide letter dated 30-8-1994 (Annexures-4 and 5) addressed to the Ministry of Industries, also acknowledged conclusion of the above project and advised regarding the deposit into the Bangladesh Bank of the balance of the unused project money the Writ Petition is not maintainable,

5. Mr. Amirul Islam, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner, submits that the petitioner was not in the service of the Republic and the petitioner was all along in the service of Bangladesh Standards Institution BDSI and after incorporation of BSTI as, a corporate body by Ordinance No. XXXVII of 1985 he was absorbed in BSTI permanently. Mr. Islam next submits that Article 152 of the Constitution of Bangladesh, has defined "Public officer" and also "Service of the Republic" and the petitioner does not come neither within the definition of "Public officer" nor "Service of the Republic" and the petitioner is not also a "Public servant" as defined within section 2(d) of the Public Servants (Retirement) Act. 1974 because he is not an employee of any corporation, national enterprise or local authority and further in view of the principle as laid down in the case of Deputy Managing Director and Chairman National Bank of Pakistan vs Ataul Huq reported in 17 DLR (SC) 74 the term' 'Local authority' as mentioned in section 2(d) above Public Servants (Retirement) Act. 1974 should be regarded as only an authority which is ordinarily charged with the function of self-government and have power of making by-laws, of imposing and of maintaining and administering a local fund.

6. Mr. Islam referring to Article 20 of the Constitution, further submits that since Public Servant (Retirement) Act 1974 imposes a restriction on the right of work the terms "local authority" as mentioned in section 2(d) of the said Act, should be interpreted in restrictive manner so that the power of the government to retire an employee may not stretch to other organizations beyond those specifically defined in section 2(d) of the above Act.

7.  Mr. Islam, referring to Annexure-F, F-1 and G which were filed along with supplementary affidavits filed by the petitioner submits that the project in question is still continuing. However, since in spite of the prayer of the petitioner in the Writ petition for treating him in service with full benefit Rule issued in the present case is confined only to the cancellation of the appointment of the petitioner. Mr. Islam conceded that the issue as to whether the project is continuing or not is not a material question in the present Rule.

8. Mr. AKM Shafiuddin, the learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing for the respondent No. 1 and Mr. M Iman Ali, the learned Advocates of the respondent Nos. 2, 3 both submitted that the records maintained with the respondent Nos. 1 and 2 show that in the year 1961 the petitioner joined Pakistan Standards Institution (PSI) which was under the Ministry of Industries arid after emergence of Bangladesh he joined Bangladesh Standards Institution, BDSI in 1977 which was also a directory of the Ministry of Industries and the petitioner keeping his lien in government service joined IACB and then joined BSTI and accordingly, after his retirement in view of the bar as provided in section 5(3) of Bangladesh Public Servants (Retirement) Act. 1974 he cannot be re-employed in BSTI. Further, even if it is conceded that the petitioner retired as an employee of BSTI even then for reemployment in view of Regulation 53 of BSTI Service Regulation the petitioner will be regarded as public servant as defined in section 2(d) of Public Servants (Retirement) Act. 1974 and the provision of section 5(3) of the aforesaid Act will be applicable in the case of the petitioner. Further, although the appointment of the petitioner was cancelled on 29-6-92 he did not challenge the order of cancellation for long period of 3 years and only when the respondent No. 2 took step to evict the petitioner from the official quarter which he was illegally occupying since 30-6-92 the petitioner filed this Writ Petition on 20-6-95 and the Writ Petition is also not maintainable on the ground of delay and laches in view of the principles laid down in the decisions reported in 13 DLR 805 and 29 DLR (SC) 232,  Mr. Shafiuddin and Mr. Ali next submitted that BSTI was established by and under Ordinance No. XXXVII of 1985 and accordingly, BSTI being established by statute is very much "local authority "as defined in section 2(d) of Act of 1974. Further, in the case of A Z Rafique Ahmed vs Bangladesh Council of Scientific and Industrial Research and others reported in 32 DLR (AD) 83 similar issue as to definition of local authority as mentioned in Article 102 of the Constitution arose and the Appellate Division in the above case held that Bangladesh Council of Scientific and Industrial Research Laboratory is a local authority.

9. Mr. Shafiuddin and Mr. Ali lastly, submit that if the petitioner contends that the respondent No.2 is not a local authority, then the petitioner not being in the service of the Republic or local authority and relief not being claimed against local authority this writ petition must fail as being not maintainable.

10. Heard the learned Advocates, perused the contents of the petition, affidavit-in-opposition and the annexure annexed therein and also the file containing the service records of the petitioner which were produced before us.

11. From the contents of the service records of the petitioner, it appears that the petitioner joined PSI on 5-12-91 and then joined BDSI in the year 1977 and on 19-7-78 he joined IACB keeping his lien in BDSI. However as it appears by order dated 16-11-79, the earlier order-dated 19-7-1978 was cancelled and the petitioner was absorbed in IACB on permanent basis because of his lien being cancelled and the petitioner received his entire dues from BDSI after cancellation of lien. The petitioner used to receive salary from BDSI in the scale of 470- 1135 but he joined IACB in the higher scale of 1150-1800 and the petitioner continued in his service in IACB for next 8 years and then he joined BSTI. It thus appears that the petitioner retired as an employee of BSTI and not as a government servant.

12. So, next question arises as to whether the provision of section 5 of Act 1974 regarding re-employment, will be applicable to the petitioner. Rules 53 of the BSTI Employee Service Regulation 1989 provides as follows:

অবসর গ্রহন, ইত্যাদি বিষয়ে XII of 1974 এর প্রয়োগ। অবসর গ্রহণ এবং উহার পর পুননিয়োগের ব্যাপারে Public Servants Retirement Act 1974 (XII of 1974) এর বিধানাবলী প্রযোজ্য হইবে।

It thus appears that in case of re-employment of all the employees of BSTI, the provision of Public Servants (Retirement) Act 1974 will be applicable.

13. Further, section 2(d) of the Public Servants (Retiement) Act 1974 provides that the word "Public servant" will include any person in the service of a local authority. According to Mr. Islam, the petitioner is not a public servant as' defined in section 2(d) above because BSTI, not being charged with functions of self-government and not having power of imposing taxation and of maintaining and administering a local fund, is not a local authority and the term "local authority" should be given in a restrictive meaning and so "local authority" in view of the principle laid down in 17 DLR (SC) 74, does not include BSTI. In the aforesaid decision reported in 17 DLR (SC) 74 it was contended that the National Bank of Pakistan, which was set up by Central Ordinance, bears no resemblance to the recognized conception of a local authority mentioned in Article 98 of the Constitution of Pakistan and accordingly, writ could not be issued upon the above bank in terms of Article 98 of the Constitution, of Pakistan. So, it appears above submission of Mr. Islam is self-defeating because in the present case the petitioner has prayed for relief against the impugned order of cancellation dated 29-6-92 (Annexure-C) issued by BSTI and unless BSTI is regarded as local authority the petitioner cannot seek relief under Article 102(2) of the Constitution . .It further appears that though in the Constitution the word "local authority" has not been defined but Article 152(2) of the Constitution specifically provided that General Clauses Act 1897 shall apply in relation, to the Constitution as it applies in relation to any Act of Parliament and so the definition of local authority as provided in section 2(28) of the General Clauses Act 1897 which will be applicable in interpreting "Local authority" as, mentioned in' Article 102 of the Constitution and also in section 2(d) of the Public Servants (Retirement) Act 1974 and as it appears in terms of the definition as provided in section 2(28) "Local Authority" shall also mean and include any corporation, other body or authority constituted or established by the Government under any law.

<u>14. It further appears that initially and also at the time of delivery of the Judgment of the case reported in 17 DLR (SC) 74, in General Clauses Act 1897 the definition "Local authority" was not in the present form and it is by President's Order 147 of 1972 that the present form of section 2(28) was incorporated in General Clauses Act, 1897 and so while interpreting "local authority" as mentioned in section 2(d) of Public Servants (Retirement) Act 1974 the definition of "local authority" as mentioned in section 2(28) of General Clauses Act 1897 as in the present form will be applicable.</u>

<u>15. In the decision reported-in 32 DLR (AD) 83, wherein an employee of Bangladesh Council of Scientific and Industrial Research Laboratory filed Writ Petition challenging the order of his dismissal, question arose as to whether the above Council is a local authority or not within .the meaning of Article 102 of the Constitution and it was held by Appellate Division that the aforesaid Bangladesh Council of Scientific and Industrial Research Laboratories (which is a similar institution like BSTI established by or under a statute) is a local authority within the meaning of section 2(28) of the General Clauses Act 1897 as amended by General Clauses (Amended) Order 1972. In the case of Mofizul Huq vs Mofizur Rahman and others reported in 48 DLR (AD) 121 it was contended that a person serving as Head Master of Non-Government Secondary School within the meaning of section 2(1)(h)(i) of the Intermediate and Secondary Education Ordinance 1961 was disqualified from election to the post of Chairman of Union Parishad under section 7(2)(c) of the Local Government Ordinance 1983 as in view of the recognition of the High School by the Board of Secondary and Intermediate Education, the said School became a "local authority within the meaning of section 7(2)(c) 1983 of the local government order but it was held by the Appellate Division that under provision of General Clauses Act a body or authority constituted or established by government under any law is a local authority and so the said High School not being constituted or not a local authority established by the government under any law, is not a local authority. So the same rule of interpretation will also apply while interpreting "local authority" as mentioned in section 2(d) of Public Servants (Retirement) Act 1974 and accordingly, since Regulation 53 of BSTI Service Regulation 1989 provides that in case of re- employment of a retired employee like the petitioner in BSTI, the provisions of Public Servant (Retirement) Act, 1974 will be applicable and section 2(d) of the said Act provides that employee of local authority will also be regarded as public servant and BSTI is a local authority, the petitioner will be regarded as a public servant and there being no prior approval before issuing the letter of appointment dated 31-12-91 in terms of section 5(3) of the said Act, the appointment of the petitioner is illegal ab initio.</u>

16. Further, from the contents of the advertisement for the position of Project Director it appears that it is SSTI who made advertisement and from the contents of the appointment letter it also appears that it is BSTI who appointed the petitioner as Project Director and thus it is also clear case of re-employment in BSTI and not appointment in a project outside BSTI.

17. The petitioner referring to Annexure-Fl and G, to the supplementary affidavits filed by the petitioner, submitted that the project, in which the petitioner was appointed, is still continuing. But the respondent Nos. 2-3 referring to Annexure 4-5 of the Affidavit-in-Opposition submitted that the project, in which the petitioner was appointed, was concluded and closed in March 1994 and then BSTI by letter dated 30-8-1994 (Annexure-4) addressed to the Ministry of Industries, acknowledged conclusion of the project and advised regarding the deposit of the balance unused project money by Treasury Chalan (Annexure-5). However since we are of the view that the petitioner Servant (Retirement) Act 1974 and Rule was issued only calling in question the cancelling of the appointment of the petitioner and further, this issue as to whether the project is still continuing or not is a disputed question of fact, we refrain from giving any decision on this issue.

18. Since we are of the view that appointment of the petitioner in the project by letter dated 30-12- 90 (Annexure-A) is, in fact, re-employment of the petitioner in BSTI and the approval of the President having under section 5(3) Public Servants (Retirement) Act 1974 not been obtained before issuing Annexure-A, the appointment of the petitioner as Project Director was illegal ab initio, the said appointment could be cancelled by the respondent Nos. 1 & 2 and accordingly, we find no illegality in the impugned order cancelling re- employment of the petitioner and accordingly, no interference is called for.

In the result the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs.

End.

lawyer:
Shahidul Islam, Advocate ----- For the Petitioner.
